<p rend="bodytext"><hi rend="bold">Tayo saṅkhārā</hi>: the *saṅkhārā* fashion together and heap up co-nascent phenomena and fruit phenomena in the next life; therefore, they are *saṅkhārā*.
*Abhisaṅkharoti*: therefore, it is *abhisaṅkhāro*.
*Puñño abhisaṅkhāro*: a meritorious fashioning; therefore, it is *puññābhisaṅkhāro*.

<hi rend="bold">Tayo saṅkhārā puññābhisaṅkhāro.</hi>
<p rend="bodytext">‘‘There, what is the meritorious fashioning (*puññābhisaṅkhāro*)? Wholesome volitions (*kusalā cetanā*) pertaining to the desire realm (*kāmāvacarā*), pertaining to the form realm (*rūpāvacarā*), consisting of giving (*dānamayā*), consisting of ethical conduct (*sīlamayā*), consisting of development (*bhāvanāmayā*)’’: this is a designation for those eight volitions of great wholesome minds pertaining to the desire realm, and for the five wholesome volitions pertaining to the form realm.
And here, there are indeed eight volitions consisting of giving and ethical conduct.
And there are thirteen consisting of development (*bhāvanāmayā*).
Just as someone reciting a well-learned doctrine (*dhamma*), even having reached one or two connections (*anusandhiṃ*), does not know, [but] afterwards, adverting [to it], he knows, just so, for one doing preliminary work on a *kasiṇa*, experiencing well-learned absorption (*jhāna*), contemplating, even development (*bhāvanā*) disconnected from knowledge (*ñāṇa*) occurs.
Therefore, it was said, ‘‘There are thirteen consisting of development (*bhāvanāmayā*)’’.

There, among those consisting of giving etc., ‘‘The volition (*cetanā*), intention (*sañcetanā*), and volitional state (*cetayitattaṃ*) which arise dependent on giving (*dānaṃ ārabbha*), concerning giving (*dānamadhikicca*), this is called a meritorious fashioning consisting of giving (*dānamayo puññābhisaṅkhāro*).
Dependent on ethical conduct (*sīlaṃ ārabbha*), dependent on development (*bhāvanaṃ ārabbha*), concerning development (*bhāvanamadhikicca*), the volition (*cetanā*), intention (*sañcetanā*), and volitional state (*cetayitattaṃ*) which arise, this is called a meritorious fashioning consisting of development (*bhāvanāmayo puññābhisaṅkhāro*)’’: this is an explanation in brief.

But for one giving robes etc. among the four requisites, or among the six objects beginning with forms, or among the ten objects of giving beginning with food, at the time of producing each of those, in the prior part, at the time of bestowing, and afterwards, in the recollection with a glad mind, the volition (*cetanā*) occurring at these three times is called consisting of giving (*dānamayā*).
But for one going to a monastery thinking, ‘‘I will go forth for the sake of perfecting ethical conduct (*sīla*)’’, for one going forth, having brought the wish to the summit, thinking, ‘‘I am one who has gone forth, it is good, good!’’ adverting [to it], restraining the *pātimokkha*, contemplating the requisites beginning with robes, restraining the doors of the eye etc. among forms etc. which have come into the path, and for one purifying his livelihood, the volition (*cetanā*) occurring is called consisting of ethical conduct (*sīlamayā*).

In the *Paṭisambhidā*, by the path of insight (*vipassanā*) stated, ‘‘For one developing the eye as impermanent, as suffering, as not-self… mind…
forms.
phenomena.
eye-consciousness… mind-consciousness.
eye-contact… mind-contact.
feeling born of eye-contact… feeling born of mind-contact.
perception of forms, old age and death as impermanent, as suffering, as not-self, the volition (*cetanā*) occurring is called consisting of development (*bhāvanāmayā*)’’: this is a detailed account.

And that fashioning is unmeritorious; therefore, it is an unmeritorious fashioning (<hi rend="bold">apuññābhisaṅkhāro</hi>).
This is a designation for the volitions connected with the twelve unwholesome minds.
It was also said, "What is unmeritorious activity? Unwholesome intention in the desire realm; this is called unmeritorious activity."

"Imperturbable," still, peaceful, the result of which is formless; thus he generates, it is called "imperturbable activity." This is a designation for the four wholesome consciousnesses pertaining to the formless realm. As it is said, "What is imperturbable activity? Wholesome intention in the formless realm; this is called imperturbable activity."

"Unmeritorious activity."

"Imperturbable activity."

In the *Personal Dispositions*, a person is one of seven kinds, he undertakes three trainings, so he is called "one in training." One whose influxes are destroyed, who has completed the training, does not train again, so he is called "one no longer in training." An ordinary person is excluded from the trainings, so he is "neither in training nor no longer in training."

*Personal Dispositions*

"One in training."

"One no longer in training."

"Neither in training nor no longer in training."

In the *Elderly Dispositions*, an elderly householder by birth is called an "elder by birth."

"There are these four qualities, monks, that make one an elder. Here, monks, an elder is virtuous, learned, attains the four *jhānas*, destroys the *āsavas*, is learned, attains the four *jhānas*, and by destroying the *āsavas*, dwells having realized with his own insight, here and now, the *cetovimutti* and *paññāvimutti* that are free from *āsavas*. These, monks, are the four qualities that make one an elder" (A. Ni. 4.22).

Thus, in the teachings that were spoken, one who is endowed with one or many is called an "elder in the *dhamma*."

Another monk named Thera, thus named Thera, or whomever the novices and others see as an old man and call "elder," this is called a "conventional elder."

*Elder by birth*, *elder in the Dhamma*, *conventional elder*.

Among the *bases for meritorious action*, giving itself is "consisting of giving." That meritorious action and that object of those benefits is called a "base for meritorious action."

In the other two as well, this is the method. In meaning, however, these three bases of meritorious action should be understood along with the intention consisting of giving previously mentioned, and with the intentions of the prior and subsequent stages.

For each one, beginning from the prior stage, when one does it with the body, there is bodily action. While uttering speech for that purpose, there is verbal action. Without stirring the bodily and verbal actions, while thinking in the mind, there is mental action.

While giving food and so forth, also thinking, "I am giving food and so forth," or reflecting on the perfection of giving, there is a base for meritorious action consisting of giving at the time of giving.

While standing at the head of the bed and giving, it consists of ethical discipline.

Having established contemplation on cessation and decay, while giving, there is a base for meritorious action consisting of cultivation.

*Bases for meritorious action*, consisting of giving.

*Base for meritorious action*.

Furthermore, there are these seven other bases for meritorious action: a base for meritorious action accompanied by respect, accompanied by service, giving transference of merit, rejoicing in others’ merit, consisting of teaching, consisting of hearing, and consisting of straightening one’s view.
There, having seen an elder, it should be understood as being accompanied by honoring (*apaciti*), by way of rising to greet, receiving the bowl and robe, respectful salutation, offering a seat, and so forth.

Due to the practice of duties towards those who are older, having seen a *bhikṣu* who has entered a village for alms, taking his bowl, causing the village to be pleased with the alms, by way of approaching, having heard "Go, bring the bowl for the *bhikṣus*," going quickly, and by way of bringing the bowl and so forth, it should be understood as being accompanied by service (*veyyāvacca*).

Having given the four requisites, "May the merit be for all beings," it should be understood as giving the transfer of merit by way of bestowing the offering.

Having approved the merit given by others, "Good, excellent!" it should be understood as rejoicing in the merit of others.

One dwells with the intention that "In this way, they will recognize me as a preacher of the *dharma*," becoming heavy with gain, he teaches; that is not of great fruit.

One, not expecting reward, teaches the qualities of his own excellence to others; this is called the meritorious object of teaching (*desanāmayaṃ puṇñakiriyavatthu*).

One, hearing, thinks "In this way, they will recognize me as faithful"; that is not of great fruit.

One, with a softened mind and diffusion of benefit, hears the *dharma* thinking, "In this way, great fruit will be mine"; this is the meritorious object of hearing (*savanamayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu*).

But the characteristic of fixed intention (*niyamalakkhaṇaṃ*) is for all those with right view (*diṭṭhi*).

Indeed, whatever merit one makes, due to right view (*diṭṭhi*) alone, it is of great fruit.

Thus, these seven meritorious objects (*puññakiriyavatthu*) are included in the former three.

Here, honoring (*apaciti*) and service (*veyyāvacca*) are in morality (*sīlamaye*).

Giving the transfer of merit and rejoicing in the merit of others are in generosity (*dānamaye*).

Teaching and hearing are in mental development (*bhāvanāmaye*).

Right view (*diṭṭhi*) goes to inclusion in all three.

The grounds for accusation (*codanāvatthūni*) are the causes for accusation (*codanākāraṇāni*).

"By sight (*diṭṭhenā*)" means having seen a transgression with the physical eye or with the divine eye, he accuses.

"By hearing (*sutenā*)" means having heard another's sound with the natural ear or with the divine ear, he accuses.

"Or by suspicion (*parisaṅkāya vā*)" means having been suspected by what is seen, or having been suspected by what is heard, or having been suspected by what is thought, he accuses.

This is the summary here; the expansion, however, should be understood in the same way as stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*.

Grounds for accusation (*codanāvatthūni*), by sight (*diṭṭhenā*), by hearing (*sutenā*), or by suspicion (*parisaṅkāya vā*):

"Enjoyments of sensual pleasure (*kāmūpapattiyo*)" means indulging in sensual pleasure, or the obtaining of sensual pleasure.

"Those with desires close at hand (*paccupaṭṭhitakāmā*)" means those with bound desires, with bound objects.

"Just as humans (*seyyathāpi manussā*)" means like humans.

Humans, indeed, constantly live under the control of an object.

Where their minds are attached, having given even a hundred or a thousand, having brought a woman, they enjoy constant enjoyment.

"Some gods (*ekacce devā*)” are those who dwell in the realm of the Four Great Kings (*catudevaloka*).

They, too, constantly live under the control of an object.

"Some beings in the states of loss (*ekacce vinipātikā*)” means having placed beings in *Naraka*, the remaining fish, turtles, and so forth constantly live under the control of an object.

The fish [is attached] to its female fish, the turtle to its female turtle.

"Having created and created (*nimminitvā nimminitvā*)" means whatever form they desire, according to blue, yellow, and so forth, having created that and that, like delightful deities with bodies, before the venerable Anuruddha.

"Delighting in creation (*nimmānaratī*)" means thus, in this way, delight is in the creation created by themselves; therefore, they are *nimmānaratī*.

"Controlling the creations of others (*paranimmitakāmā*)" means desires created by others.

For, having known their minds, others create whatever sensual enjoyment is pleasing to them; they live there under control.
How do they know another's mind? Through the habit of associating with them.

Just as a skilled cook, when the king is eating, knows what the king likes based on what he takes a lot of, so too, having known the object that is favored by nature, they create just that sort of thing.

They maintain their residence there and engage in sexual intercourse.

Some elders say, "Their sexual activity is accomplished merely by smiling, merely by glancing, and merely by embracing," but that is rejected in the commentary, saying, "But this is not so."

For, without touching tangible objects with the body, one cannot accomplish sexual activity.

For all beings in the realm of desire, desires are natural.

And this has been said:

The attainment of desires, desires that are present, just like humans.

Some gods, some are fallen.

Having created and created again.

Delighting in creation, causing others to create.

These six are beings in the realm of desire, successful in all desires;

How long is the lifespan of all of them counted together?

(Vibhanga 1023);

"Attainment of pleasure" means the acquisition of pleasure.

"Having produced and produced again, they dwell in happiness" means that they, having created happiness of the first *jhāna* below, experience the happiness of the resultant *jhāna* above—this is the meaning.

"Suffused with happiness" means soaked with the happiness of the second *jhāna*.

"Completely suffused" means soaked on all sides.

"Completely full" means perfectly full.

"Completely pervaded" is a synonym for that itself.

This too was said referring to only the happiness of the resultant *jhāna*.

"O happiness! O happiness!"—it seems great craving for existence arises in them.

Therefore, sometimes, occasionally, they utter such inspired utterances.

"It is peaceful indeed" means it is excellent indeed.

"Contented" means having become satisfied due to not desiring further happiness than that.

"Experiencing happiness" means they experience the happiness of the third *jhāna*.

Attainment of pleasure, having produced and produced again, they dwell in happiness, suffused with happiness, completely suffused, completely full, completely pervaded, O happiness! O happiness! It is peaceful indeed, contented, experiencing happiness.

"Learner's wisdom" means the seven noble wisdoms.

The wisdom of an *arhat* is "no longer learning."

The remaining wisdom is "neither learning nor not-learning."

Learner's wisdom, no longer learning.

Neither learning nor not-learning.

In regard to the *cintāmaya*, etc., this is the expansion: "There, what is wisdom born of thinking (*cintāmayā prajñā*)? Any preference, view, choice, opinion, judgment, liking for pondering over things, that concerns ownership of deeds or is in conformity with truth or is of such kind as to conform with ‘Materiality is impermanent’ or ‘Feeling … perception … formations … consciousness is impermanent’ that one acquires without hearing it from another—that is called wisdom born of thinking (*cintāmayā prajñā*).

There, what is wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayā prajñā*)? Any preference, view, choice, opinion, judgment, liking for pondering over things that concerns ownership of deeds or is in conformity with truth or is of such kind as to conform with ‘Materiality is impermanent’ or ‘Feeling … perception … formations … consciousness is impermanent’ that one acquires after hearing it from another—that is called wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayā prajñā*).

(There, what is wisdom born of meditation (*bhāvanāmayā prajñā*)?) All the wisdom of one who has attained is "wisdom born of meditation" (*bhāvanāmayā prajñā*)" (Vibhanga 768-69).

Wisdom born of thinking.

Wisdom born of thinking.

Wisdom born of hearing.
"**bhāvanāmayā paññā:**"

**sutāvudha** means *suta eva āvudhaṃ*. That is, the Tipiṭaka, the Buddha's word, is a weapon in the sense of its meaning. Indeed, relying on that, a bhikkhu, relying on the weapon of wisdom (paññāvudha), crosses the great wilderness of *saṃsāra* without being harmed, like a brave warrior who is unwavering in a great wilderness. Therefore, it was said: "An noble disciple with the *sutāvudha*, abandons the unskillful, cultivates the skillful, abandons the blameworthy, cultivates the blameless, and maintains a pure self” (A. Ni. 7.67).

**sutāvudha**

**pavivekāvudha** means “*kāyaviveko, cittaviveko, upadhiviveko*.” This threefold isolation itself is a weapon. Its distinction is that *kāyaviveka* is for those who are fond of renunciation, who have bodies that are the basis of isolation. *Cittaviveka* is for those with perfectly pure minds, who have attained the highest purification. *Upadhiviveka* is for individuals without defilements. Indeed, one who is fond of this threefold isolation is not afraid of anything. Therefore, this too is called a weapon in the sense of being a refuge. Wisdom (paññā), both mundane and supramundane, is a weapon, hence **paññāvudha**. Whoever has that is not afraid of anything, nor is anyone afraid of him. Therefore, that too is called a weapon in the sense of being a refuge.

**pavivekāvudha**, **paññāvudha**

**anaññātaññassāmītindriya** means the faculty that arises in one who has undertaken to know the Dhamma, which was previously unknown and unlearned. This is a designation for the knowledge of the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti).

**aññindriya** means the faculty that has the nature of knowledge, that is the nature of understanding. This is a designation for knowledge in six instances, beginning with the fruit of stream-entry.

**aññātāvindriya** means the faculty in those who have reached the end of the task of knowing among those who have known. This is a designation for the knowledge of the fruit of arahantship.

**anaññātaññassāmītindriya**, **aññindriya**, **aññātāvindriya**

**maṃsacakkhu** is eye-sensitivity ( cakkhupasādo).

**dibbacakkhu** is knowledge based on light.

**paññācakkhu** is wisdom, both mundane and supramundane.

**maṃsacakkhu**, **dibbacakkhu**, **paññācakkhu**

Among **adhisīlasikkhā** etc., **adhisīlasikkhā** is higher morality ( adhisīla ) and the training because it is to be trained ( sikkhā ). The same method applies to the other two as well. There, it should be understood that this is the distinction: morality is *adhisīla*, mind is *adhicitta*, and wisdom is *adhipaññā*—

**adhisīlasikkhā**, **adhisīlasikkhā**

**sīla** means the five precepts and the ten precepts; the restraint of the *pātimokkha* is called **adhisīla**. The eight attainments are *citta*, the jhāna that is the basis of insight (*vipassanā*) is **adhicitta**. Knowledge of the ownership of karma is *paññā*, the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā*) is **adhipaññā**. Indeed, the five precepts and the ten precepts exist even when a Buddha has not arisen, thus it is merely morality (sīla); the morality of the *pātimokkha* restraint exists only when a Buddha has arisen, thus it is higher morality (adhisīla). The same method applies to mind and wisdom as well.
Moreover, for one desiring nirvāṇa, taking up the five precepts or the ten precepts is indeed higher morality (adhiśīla).
Having attained the eight attainments (aṭṭha samāpatti), it is indeed higher mind (adhicitta).
All worldly morality is simply morality (śīla), [while] supramundane is higher morality (adhiśīla).
The same method applies in the case of mental wisdom (cittapaññā).

Morality (śīla), Higher Morality (adhiśīla), Higher Mind (adhicitta).
Higher Wisdom (adhipaññā).

In cultivations (bhāvanāsu), the body consisting of the five sense doors of one with outflows destroyed is called body cultivation (*kāyabhāvanā*).
The eight attainments (aṭṭha samāpatti) are called mind cultivation (*cittabhāvanā*).
The wisdom of the fruit of arhatship is called wisdom cultivation (*paññābhāvanā*).
For one with outflows destroyed, the body consisting of the five sense doors is well cultivated simply and entirely.
And for him, the eight attainments are not weak like those of others, and his wisdom is cultivated; it is called the attainment of the fullness of wisdom.
Therefore, it is said thus.

In cultivations (bhāvanāsu), [there is] body cultivation (*kāyabhāvanā*), mind cultivation (*cittabhāvanā*), wisdom cultivation (*paññābhāvanā*).
In the unsurpassed things (anuttariyesu), insight (vipassanā) [is] unsurpassed vision (*dassanānuttariyaṃ*), the path [is] unsurpassed practice (*paṭipadānussariyaṃ*).
The fruit [is] unsurpassed liberation (*vimuttānuttariyaṃ*).
Or, the fruit [is] unsurpassed vision (*dassanānuttariyaṃ*).
The path [is] unsurpassed practice (*paṭipadānuttariyaṃ*).
Nirvāṇa [is] unsurpassed liberation (*vimuttānuttariyaṃ*).
Or, nirvāṇa [is] unsurpassed vision (*dassanānuttariyaṃ*), because there is nothing further to be seen.
The path [is] unsurpassed practice (*paṭipadānuttariyaṃ*).
The fruit [is] unsurpassed liberation (*vimuttānuttariyaṃ*).
"Unsurpassed" (*anuttariya*) means the highest, the most excellent.

In the unsurpassed things (*anuttariyesu*), [there is] unsurpassed vision (*dassanānuttariyaṃ*), [and] unsurpassed practice (*paṭipadānussariyaṃ*).
Unsurpassed liberation (*vimuttānuttariyaṃ*).
Unsurpassed (*anuttariya*).
In concentrations (samādhīsu), the concentration of the first *jhāna* [is] with initial application and sustained application (*savitakkasavicāro*).
By the method of the pentad, the concentration of the second *jhāna* [is] with only sustained application but without initial application (*avitakkavicāramatto*).
The remainder [is] without initial application and without sustained application (*avitakkaavicāro*).

In concentrations (samādhīsu), [there is that which is] with initial application and sustained application (*savitakkasavicāro*).
[That which is] with only sustained application but without initial application (*avitakkavicāramatto*).
[And that which is] without initial application and without sustained application (*avitakkaavicāro*).

In emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and so on, there are three kinds of talk: from the perspective of arrival, from the perspective of quality, [and] from the perspective of object.
From the perspective of arrival, a certain *bhikṣu* after thoroughly entering into not-self, after seeing not-self, after emerging from not-self, his insight is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Why? Because of the absence of defilements that make the characteristics of self.
By the arrival of insight, the concentration of the path (maggasamādhi) is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
By the arrival of the path, the concentration of the fruit (phalasamādhi) is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Another, after thoroughly entering into impermanence, after seeing impermanence, after emerging from impermanence,
his insight is called signless (*animittā*).
Why? Because of the absence of defilements that make the characteristics of signs.With the coming of insight (*vipassanā*), the path-samādhi is called "signless" (*animitto*). With the coming of the path, the fruit is called "signless" (*animittaṃ*).

Furthermore, having entered into suffering, having seen suffering, and having emerged from suffering, his/her *vipassanā* is called "desireless" (*appaṇihitā*). Why is that? Because of the absence of afflictions that are the makers of desires (*paṇidhikārakakilesābhāvā*). With the coming of insight, the path-samādhi is called "desireless" (*appaṇihito*). With the coming of the path, the fruit is called "desireless" (*appaṇihitaṃ*) - this is the talk from the perspective of coming (*āgamanato*).

Moreover, path-samādhi is empty (*suññato*) because of being empty of passion etc. (*rāgādīhi suññatattā*), signless (*animitto*) because of the absence of the signs of passion etc. (*rāganimittādīnaṃ abhāvā*), desireless (*appaṇihito*) because of the absence of the desires of passion etc. (*rāgapaṇidhiādīnaṃ abhāvā*) - this is the talk from the perspective of qualities (*saguṇato*).

Nirvāṇa is empty (*suññatañceva*) because of being empty of passion etc. (*rāgādīhi suññatattā*) and signless and desireless because of the absence of the signs and desires of passion etc. (*rāgādinimittapaṇidhīnañca abhāvā*).

The path-samādhi with that as its object (*tadārammaṇo*) is empty (*suññato*), signless (*animitto*), desireless (*appaṇihito*). This is the talk from the perspective of the object (*ārammaṇato*).

"Purity" (*soceyyānī*) means those things which make for purity, the practices of purity. The detailed explanation here should be understood in terms of the three kinds of good conduct mentioned in the passage that begins, "What is purity of body (*kāyasoceyyaṃ*)? Abstaining from killing," and so forth.

"Austerities" (*moneyyānī*) means those things which make for sagehood, the practices of sagehood. Their detailed explanation [is as follows]: "What is austerity of body (*kāyamoneyyaṃ*)? Abandoning the three kinds of bodily misconduct is austerity of body; the three kinds of good bodily conduct are austerity of body; knowledge related to the body is austerity of body; complete understanding of the body is austerity of body; the path associated with complete understanding is austerity of body; abandoning desire and passion for the body is austerity of body; the attainment of the fourth *jhāna* through the cessation of bodily functions is austerity of body. What is austerity of speech (*vacīmoneyyaṃ*)? Abandoning the four kinds of verbal misconduct is austerity of speech; the four kinds of good verbal conduct are austerity of speech; knowledge related to speech is austerity of speech; complete understanding of speech is austerity of speech; the path associated with complete understanding is austerity of speech; abandoning desire and passion for speech is austerity of speech; the attainment of the second *jhāna* through the cessation of verbal functions is austerity of speech. What is austerity of mind (*manomoneyyaṃ*)? Abandoning the three kinds of mental misconduct is austerity of mind, the three kinds of good mental conduct are austerity of mind, knowledge related to the mind is austerity of mind, complete understanding of the mind is austerity of mind. The path associated with complete understanding, abandoning desire and passion for the mind, the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling through the cessation of mental functions is austerity of mind."

Among skills (*kosallesu*), "growth" (*āyo*) means increase. "Decline" (*apāyo*) means non-increase. "Means" (*upāyo*) [is] the cause of that. Skillfulness is understanding them. But the detailed explanation has already been stated in the *Vibhaṅga*.

Indeed, it was said: "What is skill in growth? When one attends to these things, both unarisen unwholesome things do not arise, and arisen unwholesome things cease. Or when one attends to these things, both unarisen wholesome things arise, and arisen wholesome things conduce to greater abundance, expansion, cultivation, and perfection; that is, wisdom there, understanding…right view. This is called skill in growth. What is skill in decline? When one attends to these things, both unarisen wholesome things do not arise, and arisen wholesome things cease. Or when one attends to these things, both unarisen unwholesome things arise, and arisen unwholesome things conduce to greater abundance, expansion, cultivation, and perfection; that is, wisdom there, understanding…right view. This is called skill in decline. And all understanding of means thereto is skill in means."
This, however, should be understood as being solely by way of knowing the cause of its arising, for the purpose of treating it, when an emergent matter or a fear has arisen.

<hi rend="bold">Madā</hi> means those things that are occurring by way of the state of intoxication.
Among them, "I am healthy, sixty or seventy years have passed, I have never even eaten a harītakī fruit piece before, but these other people go around saying, 'Such-and-such a place is hurting, I will eat medicine,'" thus, making pride in this way is called <hi rend="bold">the intoxication of health.</hi>
"We will make merit in old age, for now, we are young," thus, staying in youth and making pride in this way is called <hi rend="bold">the intoxication of youth.</hi>
"I have lived long, I am living long, I will live long; I have lived happily, I am living happily, I will live happily," thus, making pride in this way is called <hi rend="bold">the intoxication of life.</hi>

306. ‘‘Atthi kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena cattāro dhammā sammadakkhātā. Tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ, na vivaditabbaṃ…pe… atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ. Katame cattāro?

‘‘Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Vedanāsu vedanānupassī…pe… citte cittānupassī…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ.

satipaṭṭhānā.

‘‘Cattāro sammappadhānā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati.

sammappadhānā.

‘‘Cattāro iddhipādā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu chandasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Cittasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Vīriyasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Vīmaṃsāsamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti.

iddhipādā.

‘‘Cattāri jhānāni. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) upasampajja viharati. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ dutiyajjhānaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) upasampajja viharati. Pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca viharati sato ca sampajāno, sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti, yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti – ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ tatiyajjhānaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) upasampajja viharati. Sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā, pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā, adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) upasampajja viharati.

306. “There are, friends, four *dharmas* that are rightly expounded by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, rightly self-awakened. So it should all be recited together, without dispute… for the welfare, benefit, & happiness of *devas* and human beings. What are the four?

“The four *smṛtyupasthānas*. Here, friends, a *bhikṣu* abides, contemplating the body as body, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, after removing avarice and sorrow regarding the world. And when he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… the mind in the mind… and mental objects in mental objects, earnestly, clearly comprehending, and mindfully, after having overcome desire and sorrow in regard to the world.

*Smṛtyupasthānas*.

“The four *samyakprahāṇas*. Here a *bhikṣu* generates desire, endeavors, activates persistence, upholds & exerts his intent for the sake of the non-arising of evil, unskillful qualities that have not yet arisen. He generates desire, endeavors, activates persistence, upholds & exerts his intent for the sake of the abandoning of evil, unskillful qualities that have arisen. He generates desire, endeavors, activates persistence, upholds & exerts his intent for the sake of the arising of skillful qualities that have not yet arisen. He generates desire, endeavors, activates persistence, upholds & exerts his intent for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, plenitude, development, & culmination of skillful qualities that have arisen.

*Samyakprahāṇas*.

“The four *ṛddhipādas*. Here, friends, a *bhikṣu* develops the base of power endowed with concentration founded on desire and the fabrications of exertion (*chandasamādhiprahānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ ṛddhipādaṃ bhāveti*). He develops the base of power endowed with concentration founded on persistence and the fabrications of exertion (*chittasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ ṛddhipādaṃ bhāveti*). He develops the base of power endowed with concentration founded on energy and the fabrications of exertion (*vīryasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ ṛddhipādaṃ bhāveti*). He develops the base of power endowed with concentration founded on discrimination and the fabrications of exertion (*vīmāṃsāsamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ ṛddhipādaṃ bhāveti*).

*Ṛddhipādas*.

“The four *dhyānas*. Here, friends, a *bhikṣu*, quite secluded from sensuality, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters & remains in the first *dhyāna*: rapture & pleasure born of seclusion, accompanied by directed thought & evaluation (*savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati*). With the stilling of directed thoughts & evaluations, he enters & remains in the second *dhyāna*: rapture & pleasure born of concentration, unification of awareness free from directed thought & evaluation—internal assurance (*avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dvitīyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati*). With the fading of rapture, he remains equanimous, mindful, & alert, and senses pleasure with the body. He enters & remains in the third *dhyāna*, of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous & mindful, one has a pleasant abiding’ (*upekkhako satimā sukhavihārīti tṛtīyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati*). With the abandoning of pleasure & pain—as with the earlier disappearance of elation & distress—he enters & remains in the fourth *dhyāna*: purity of equanimity & mindfulness, neither pleasure nor pain (*aduḥkhamasukham upekṣāsatipāriśuddhiṃ caturthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati*).
) Note: *upasampajja viharati*.

**Jhānas.**

306. Iti tikavasena sāmaggirasaṃ dassetvā idāni catukkavasena dassetuṃ puna desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha ‘‘satipaṭṭhānacatukkaṃ’’ pubbe vitthāritameva.

Sammappadhānacatukke chandaṃ janetīti ‘‘yo chando chandikatā kattukamyatā kusalo dhammacchando’’ti evaṃ vuttaṃ kattukamyataṃ janeti. Vāyamatīti vāyāmaṃ karoti. Vīriyaṃ ārabhatīti vīriyaṃ janeti. Cittaṃ paggaṇhātīti cittaṃ upatthambheti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo . Vitthāro pana sammappadhānavibhaṅge āgatoyeva.

chandaṃ janetī Vāyamatī Vīriyaṃ ārabhatī Cittaṃ paggaṇhātī

Iddhipādesu chandaṃ nissāya pavatto samādhi chandasamādhi. Padhānabhūtā saṅkhārā padhānasaṅkhārā. Samannāgatanti tehi dhammehi upetaṃ. Iddhiyā pādaṃ, iddhibhūtaṃ vā pādanti iddhipādaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana iddhipādavibhaṅge āgato eva. Visuddhimagge panassa attho dīpito. Jhānakathāpi visuddhimagge vitthāritāva.

commentary_english:
306. Having shown the meaning of the aggregate by way of the triad, he now begins the discourse again in order to show [it] by way of the tetrad. There, the “tetrad of the foundations of mindfulness” has already been extensively explained.

In the tetrad of right efforts, *chandaṃ janeti* means: “whatever desire, will to do, wish to act, or wholesome desire for the Dhamma” -- thus, he generates the wish to act that was spoken of in that way. *Vāyamati* means he makes an effort. *Vīriyaṃ ārabhati* means he generates energy. *Cittaṃ paggaṇhāti* means he supports the mind. This is the summary here. But the detailed explanation has already come in the *Sammappadhānavibhaṅga*.

*Chandaṃ janeti, vāyamati, vīriyaṃ ārabhati, cittaṃ paggaṇhāti.*

In the foundations of success, the concentration that arises dependent on desire is *chandasamādhi* (concentration due to desire). The principal formative factors are *padhānasaṅkhārā* (principal formative factors). *Samannāgata*nti means endowed with those qualities. *Iddhiyā pādaṃ*, or *iddhibhūtaṃ vā pādaṃ* means *iddhipādaṃ* (base of power). So with the rest. This is the summary here, but the detailed explanation has already come in the *Iddhipādavibhaṅga*. But its meaning has been explained in the *Visuddhimagga*. The discourse on *jhāna* has also been extensively explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.

*Chandasamādhi, padhānasaṅkhārā, samannāgata, iddhipādaṃ.*

mula_pali:
307. ‘‘Catasso samādhibhāvanā. Atthāvuso, samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāya saṃvattati. Atthāvuso, samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā ñāṇadassanapaṭilābhāya saṃvattati. Atthāvuso samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā satisampajaññāya saṃvattati. Atthāvuso samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā āsavānaṃ khayāya saṃvattati.

‘‘Katamā cāvuso, samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāya saṃvattati? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ…pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ, āvuso , samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāya saṃvattati.

‘‘Katamā cāvuso, samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā ñāṇadassanapaṭilābhāya saṃvattati? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu ālokasaññaṃ manasi karoti, divāsaññaṃ adhiṭṭhāti yathā divā tathā rattiṃ, yathā rattiṃ tathā divā. Iti vivaṭena cetasā apariyonaddhena sappabhāsaṃ cittaṃ bhāveti. Ayaṃ, āvuso samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā ñāṇadassanapaṭilābhāya saṃvattati.

‘‘Katamā cāvuso, samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā satisampajaññāya saṃvattati? Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno viditā vedanā uppajjanti, viditā upaṭṭhahanti, viditā abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Viditā saññā uppajjanti, viditā upaṭṭhahanti, viditā abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Viditā vitakkā uppajjanti, viditā upaṭṭhahanti, viditā abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Ayaṃ, āvuso, samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā satisampajaññāya saṃvattati.

‘‘Katamā cāvuso, samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā āsavānaṃ khayāya saṃvattati? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu udayabbayānupassī viharati. Iti rūpaṃ, iti rūpassa samudayo, iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo. Iti vedanā…pe… iti saññā… iti saṅkhārā… iti viññāṇaṃ, iti viññāṇassa samudayo, iti viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo. Ayaṃ, āvuso, samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā āsavānaṃ khayāya saṃvattati.
mula_english:
307. Four developments of concentration ( *samādhi-bhāvanā*):
There is, friend (*āvuso*), the development of concentration that, when developed and pursued, leads to a pleasant abiding in the here and now (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāya saṃvattati*).
There is, friend, the development of concentration that, when developed and pursued, leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassanapaṭilābhāya saṃvattati*).
There is, friend, the development of concentration that, when developed and pursued, leads to mindfulness and alertness (*satisampajaññāya saṃvattati*).
There is, friend, the development of concentration that, when developed and pursued, leads to the ending of the effluents (*āsavānaṃ khayāya saṃvattati*).

And which is the development of concentration that, when developed and pursued, leads to a pleasant abiding in the here and now? Here, friend, a *bhikkhu*, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states of mind, enters and abides in the fourth *jhāna*, which is with applied and sustained thought…
This, friend, is the development of concentration that, when developed and pursued, leads to a pleasant abiding in the here and now.

And which is the development of concentration that, when developed and pursued, leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision? Here, friend, a *bhikkhu* attends to the perception of light (*ālokasaññaṃ manasi karoti*), establishes the perception of day (*divāsaññaṃ adhiṭṭhāti*), as by day, so by night; as by night, so by day.
Thus with an open mind (*vivaṭena cetasā*), unhampered (*apariyonaddhena*), he develops a brightened mind (*sappabhāsaṃ cittaṃ bhāveti*).
This, friend, is the development of concentration that, when developed and pursued, leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision.

And which is the development of concentration that, when developed and pursued, leads to mindfulness and alertness? Here, friend, for a *bhikkhu* feelings are known as they arise (*viditā vedanā uppajjanti*), known as they are present (*viditā upaṭṭhahanti*), known as they disappear (*viditā abbhatthaṃ gacchanti*).
Perceptions are known as they arise, known as they are present, known as they disappear.
Thoughts are known as they arise, known as they are present, known as they disappear.
This, friend, is the development of concentration that, when developed and pursued, leads to mindfulness and alertness.

And which is the development of concentration that, when developed and pursued, leads to the ending of the effluents? Here, friend, a *bhikkhu* dwells contemplating arising and vanishing (*udayabbayānupassī viharati*) in the five aggregates subject to clinging (*pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu*):
'Such is form (*rūpaṃ*), such is the arising of form (*rūpassa samudayo*), such is the passing away of form (*rūpassa atthaṅgamo*).'
Such is feeling... such is perception... such are fabrications... such is consciousness, such is the arising of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.
This, friend, is the development of concentration that, when developed and pursued, leads to the ending of the effluents.
commentary_pali:
307.Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāyāti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve sukhavihāratthāya. Idha phalasamāpattijhānāni, khīṇāsavassa aparabhāge nibbattitajhānāni ca kathitāni.

Ālokasaññaṃ manasikarotīti divā vā rattiṃ vā sūriyacandapajjotamaṇiādīnaṃ ālokaṃ ālokoti manasikaroti. Divāsaññaṃ adhiṭṭhātīti evaṃ manasi katvā divātisaññaṃ ṭhapeti. Yathā divā tathā rattinti yathā divā diṭṭho āloko, tatheva taṃ rattiṃ manasikaroti. Yathā rattiṃ tathā divāti yathā rattiṃ āloko diṭṭho, evameva divā manasikaroti. Iti vivaṭena cetasāti evaṃ apihitena cittena. Apariyonaddhenāti samantato anaddhena. Sappabhāsanti saobhāsaṃ. Ñāṇadassanapaṭilābhāyāti ñāṇadassanapaṭilābhatthāya. Iminā kiṃ kathitaṃ? Middhavinodanaāloko kathito parikammaāloko vā. Iminā kiṃ kathitaṃ hoti? Khīṇāsavassa dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ. Tasmiṃ vā āgatepi anāgatepi pādakajjhānasamāpattimeva sandhāya ‘‘sappabhāsaṃ cittaṃ bhāvetī’’ti vuttaṃ.

Ālokasaññaṃ manasikarotī Divāsaññaṃ adhiṭṭhātī Yathā divā tathā ratti Yathā rattiṃ tathā divā Iti vivaṭena cetasā Apariyonaddhenā Sappabhāsa Ñāṇadassanapaṭilābhāyā

Satisampajaññāyāti sattaṭṭhānikassa satisampajaññassa atthāya. Viditā vedanā uppajjantītiādīsu khīṇāsavassa vatthu viditaṃ hoti ārammaṇaṃ viditaṃ vatthārammaṇaṃ viditaṃ. Vatthārammaṇaviditatāya evaṃ vedanā uppajjanti, evaṃ tiṭṭhanti, evaṃ nirujjhanti. Na kevalañca vedanā eva idha vuttā saññādayopi , avuttā cetanādayopi, viditā ca uppajjanti ceva tiṭṭhanti ca nirujjhanti ca. Api ca vedanāya uppādo vidito hoti, upaṭṭhānaṃ viditaṃ hoti. Avijjāsamudayā vedanāsamudayo, taṇhāsamudayā kammasamudayo, phassasamudayā vedanāyasamudayo. Nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ passantopi vedanākkhandhassa samudayaṃ passati. Evaṃ vedanāya uppādo vidito hoti. Kathaṃ vedanāya upaṭṭhānaṃ viditaṃ hoti? Aniccato manasikaroto khayatūpaṭṭhānaṃ viditaṃ hoti. Dukkhato manasikaroto bhayatūpaṭṭhānaṃ viditaṃ hoti. Anattato manasikaroto suññatūpaṭṭhānaṃ viditaṃ hoti. Evaṃ vedanāya upaṭṭhānaṃ viditaṃ hoti, khayato bhayato suññato jānāti. Kathaṃ vedanāya atthaṅgamo vidito hoti? Avijjānirodhā vedanānirodho.…Pe… evaṃ vedanāya atthaṅgamo vidito hoti. Imināpi nayenettha attho veditabbo.

Satisampajaññāyā Viditā vedanā uppajjantī

Itirūpantiādi vuttanayameva. Ayaṃ āvuso samādhibhāvanāti ayaṃ āsavānaṃ khayañāṇassa pādakajjhānasamādhibhāvanā.

Iti rūpa Ayaṃ āvuso samādhibhāvanā
commentary_english:
307. " *Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāyā* ti" means for the purpose of dwelling in pleasure in this very existence.

Herein, the fruitional attainments (*phalasamāpattijhānāni*) and the meditative absorptions (*nibbattitajhānāni*) in the latter part of the life of one whose defilements are destroyed (*khīṇāsavassa*) are spoken of.

" *Ālokasaññaṃ manasikarotī* ti" means he attends to the perception of light, thinking, "Light, light," whether by day or by night, in regard to sunlight, moonlight, the light of a lamp, jewels, and so on.
" *Divāsaññaṃ adhiṭṭhātī* ti" means having made it in his mind in this way, he establishes the perception of "day."
" *Yathā divā tathā ratti* nti" means just as light is seen during the day, just so he attends to it at night.
" *Yathā rattiṃ tathā divā* ti" means just as light is seen at night, exactly so he attends to it during the day.
" *Iti vivaṭena cetasā* ti" means thus, with an open mind.
" *Apariyonaddhenā* ti" means without being entirely bound.
" *Sappabhāsa* nti" means with radiance (*saobhāsaṃ*).
" *Ñāṇadassanapaṭilābhāyā* ti" means for the purpose of obtaining the gain of knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassanapaṭilābhatthāya*).

What is stated by this? The light that dispels drowsiness, or the light of preliminary work, is stated.
What is stated by this? The divine eye knowledge (*dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ*) of one whose defilements are destroyed (*khīṇāsavassa*).

Having reference to just the attainment of the absorption of the foundational level of absorption, whether that has come or has not yet come, it is said, "He cultivates a mind with radiance (*sappabhāsaṃ cittaṃ bhāvetī*)."

*Ālokasaññaṃ manasikarotī divāsaññaṃ adhiṭṭhātī yathā divā tathā ratti yathā rattiṃ tathā divā iti vivaṭena cetasā apariyonaddhenā sappabhāsa ñāṇadassanapaṭilābhāyā* *satisampajaññāyā*ti" means for the purpose of mindfulness and full awareness (*sattaṭṭhānikassa satisampajaññassa atthāya*).

" *Viditā vedanā uppajjantī* tiādīsu" means in these and other instances, the object (*vatthu*) of one whose defilements are destroyed (*khīṇāsavassa*) is known, the object of attention (*ārammaṇaṃ*) is known, the object-of-attention-as-object (*vatthārammaṇaṃ*) is known.
Through knowing the object-of-attention-as-object, thus feelings arise, thus they remain, thus they cease.

It is not only feeling (*vedanā*) that is spoken of here, but also perception (*saññā*), and so on, and volition (*cetanā*), and so on, even though not spoken of, are known, and arise, and remain, and cease.

Moreover, the arising (*uppādo*) of feeling is known, its appearance (*upaṭṭhānaṃ*) is known.
From the arising of ignorance (*avijjāsamudayā*) [comes] the arising of feeling (*vedanāsamudayo*); from the arising of craving (*taṇhāsamudayā*) [comes] the arising of action (*kammasamudayo*); from the arising of contact (*phassasamudayā*) [comes] the arising of feeling (*vedanāyasamudayo*).

Even while seeing the characteristic of production (*nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ passantopi*), he sees the arising (*samudayaṃ passati*) of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandhassa*).
Thus, the arising (*uppādo*) of feeling is known.

How is the appearance (*upaṭṭhānaṃ*) of feeling known? When attention is given to it as impermanent (*aniccato manasikaroto*), the appearance as exhaustion (*khayatūpaṭṭhānaṃ*) is known.
When attention is given to it as painful (*dukkhato manasikaroto*), the appearance as terror (*bhayatūpaṭṭhānaṃ*) is known.
When attention is given to it as not-self (*anattato manasikaroto*), the appearance as voidness (*suññatūpaṭṭhānaṃ*) is known.
Thus, the appearance (*upaṭṭhānaṃ*) of feeling is known; he knows exhaustion, terror, voidness.

How is the subsiding (*atthaṅgamo*) of feeling known? From the cessation of ignorance (*avijjānirodhā*) [comes] the cessation of feeling (*vedanānirodho*).
…pe… Thus, the subsiding (*atthaṅgamo*) of feeling is known.

In this way also, the meaning here should be understood.

*Satisampajaññāyā viditā vedanā uppajjantī* *iti rūpa*ntiādi" [is] just the manner that has been spoken of.
" *Ayaṃ āvuso samādhibhāvanā*ti" means this, friend, is the cultivation of absorption that is the basis for the knowledge of the destruction of defilements (*āsavānaṃ khayañāṇassa pādakajjhānasamādhibhāvanā*).

*Iti rūpa ayaṃ āvuso samādhibhāvanā*

mula_pali:
308. ‘‘Catasso appamaññā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati. Tathā dutiyaṃ. Tathā tatiyaṃ. Tathā catutthaṃ. Iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyāpajjena abyāpajjhena (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) pharitvā viharati. Karuṇāsahagatena cetasā…pe… muditāsahagatena cetasā…pe… upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati. Tathā dutiyaṃ. Tathā tatiyaṃ. Tathā catutthaṃ. Iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ upekkhāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyāpajjena pharitvā viharati.

‘‘Cattāro āruppā.arūpā (syā. kaṃ. pī.) Idhāvuso, bhikkhu sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati.

āruppā. arūpā (syā. kaṃ. pī.)

‘‘Cattāri apassenāni. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevati, saṅkhāyekaṃ adhivāseti, saṅkhāyekaṃ parivajjeti, saṅkhāyekaṃ vinodeti.

apassenāni.
mula_english:
308. "Four immeasurables: Here, friends, a monk abides pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second direction, likewise the third direction, likewise the fourth direction; thus above, below, and across, everywhere, in its entirety, he keeps pervading the all-encompassing world with an awareness imbued with goodwill—abundant, enlarged, immeasurable, without hostility, without ill will. And he dwells, letting his mind, filled with com­passion,… with sympathetic joy,… with equanimity, per­vade one quarter, likewise the second direction, likewise the third direction, likewise the fourth direction; Thus above, below, & all around, everywhere, in its entirety, he keeps pervading the all-encompassing cosmos with an awareness imbued with equanimity—abundant, enlarged, immeasurable, without hostility, without ill will.

“Four formlessnesses: There is the case, friends, where a monk—with the complete transcending of perceptions of form ( *rūpasaṃjñā* ), with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and not attending to perceptions of multiplicity, ‘Infinite space’ ( *ananto ākāso* )—enters & remains in the dimension of the infinitude of space (*ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ*). With the complete transcending of the dimension of the infinitude of space, ‘Infinite consciousness’ (*anantaṃ viññāṇa*)—enters & remains in the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ*). With the complete transcending of the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness, ‘There is nothing’ (*natthi kiñcī*)—he enters & remains in the dimension of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ*). By utterly transcending the sphere of nothingness, one attains to and abides in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ*).

Four supports: There is the case, friends, where a monk, contemplating one thing, associates with it; contemplating one thing, acquiesces to it; contemplating one thing, avoids it; contemplating one thing, subdues it.
commentary_pali:
308.Appamaññāti pamāṇaṃ agahetvā anavasesapharaṇavasena appamaññāva. Anupadavaṇṇanā pana bhāvanāsamādhividhānañca etāsaṃ visuddhimagge vitthāritameva. Arūpakathāpi visuddhimagge vitthāritāva.

Apassenānīti apassayāni. Saṅkhāyāti ñāṇena ñatvā. Paṭisevatīti ñāṇena ñatvā sevitabbayuttakameva sevati. Tassa ca vitthāro ‘‘paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cīvaraṃ paribhuñjatī’’tiādinā nayena veditabbo. Saṅkhāyekaṃ adhivāsetīti ñāṇena ñatvā adhivāsetabbayuttakameva adhivāseti. Vitthāro panettha ‘‘paṭisaṅkhā yoniso khamo hoti sītassā’’tiādinā nayena veditabbo. Parivajjetīti ñāṇena ñatvā parivajjetuṃ yuttameva parivajjeti. Tassa vitthāro ‘‘paṭisaṅkhā yoniso caṇḍaṃ hatthiṃ parivajjetī’’tiādinā nayena veditabbo. Vinodetīti ñāṇena ñatvā vinodetabbameva vinodeti, nudati nīharati anto pavisituṃ na deti. Tassa vitthāro ‘‘uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetī’’tiādinā nayena veditabbo.

Apassenānī Saṅkhāyā Paṭisevatī Saṅkhāyekaṃ adhivāsetī Parivajjetī Vinodetī

Ariyavaṃsacatukkavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
308. *Appamaññā* means *appamaññāva* by not grasping a measure (*pamāṇaṃ*), but by way of pervasion without remainder (*anavasesapharaṇavasena*).

Moreover, the commentary on the subsequent verses, the method of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and concentration (*samādhi*) have already been extensively explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.

The discussion of the formless realms (*arūpakathāpi*) has also been extensively explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.

*Apassenānī* means supports (*apassayāni*).

*Saṅkhāyā* means having known with knowledge (*ñāṇena ñatvā*).

*Paṭisevatī* means having known with knowledge (*ñāṇena ñatvā*), one cultivates precisely what is fit to be cultivated (*sevitabbayuttakameva sevati*).

And its exposition should be understood by the method beginning with "reflecting wisely, he uses the robe" (*paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cīvaraṃ paribhuñjatītyādina nayena veditabbo*).

*Saṅkhāyekaṃ adhivāsetī* means having known with knowledge (*ñāṇena ñatvā*), one endures precisely what is fit to be endured (*adhivāsetabbayuttakameva adhivāseti*).

The exposition here should be understood by the method beginning with "reflecting wisely, he is forbearing of cold" (*paṭisaṅkhā yoniso khamo hoti sītassā’’tiādinā nayena veditabbo*).

*Parivajjetī* means having known with knowledge (*ñāṇena ñatvā*), one avoids precisely what is fit to be avoided (*parivajjetuṃ yuttameva parivajjeti*).

Its exposition should be understood by the method beginning with "reflecting wisely, he avoids a fierce elephant" (*paṭisaṅkhā yoniso caṇḍaṃ hatthiṃ parivajjetī’’tiādinā nayena veditabbo*).

*Vinodetī* means having known with knowledge (*ñāṇena ñatvā*), one dispels precisely what should be dispelled (*vinodetabbameva vinodeti*), he pushes out, he removes, he does not allow it to enter within (*nudati nīharati anto pavisituṃ na deti*).

Its exposition should be understood by the method beginning with "he does not tolerate a arisen thought of desire" (*uppannaṃ  kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetī’’tiādinā nayena veditabbo*).

*Apassenānī*, *Saṅkhāyā*, *Paṭisevatī*, *Saṅkhāyekaṃ adhivāsetī*, *Parivajjetī*, *Vinodetī*

Commentary on the fourfold lineage of the Noble Ones (*ariyavaṃsacatukkavaṇṇanā*).

mula_pali:
309. ‘‘Cattāro ariyavaṃsā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu santuṭṭho hoti itarītarena cīvarena, itarītaracīvarasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī, na ca cīvarahetu anesanaṃ appatirūpaṃ āpajjati; aladdhā ca cīvaraṃ na paritassati, laddhā ca cīvaraṃ agadhito agathito (sī. pī.) amucchito anajjhāpanno ādīnavadassāvī nissaraṇapañño paribhuñjati; tāya ca pana itarītaracīvarasantuṭṭhiyā nevattānukkaṃseti na paraṃ vambheti. Yo hi tattha dakkho analaso sampajāno paṭissato, ayaṃ vuccatāvuso – ‘bhikkhu porāṇe aggaññe ariyavaṃse ṭhito’.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu santuṭṭho hoti itarītarena piṇḍapātena, itarītarapiṇḍapātasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī, na ca piṇḍapātahetu anesanaṃ appatirūpaṃ āpajjati; aladdhā ca piṇḍapātaṃ na paritassati, laddhā ca piṇḍapātaṃ agadhito amucchito anajjhāpanno ādīnavadassāvī nissaraṇapañño paribhuñjati; tāya ca pana itarītarapiṇḍapātasantuṭṭhiyā nevattānukkaṃseti na paraṃ vambheti. Yo hi tattha dakkho analaso sampajāno paṭissato , ayaṃ vuccatāvuso – ‘bhikkhu porāṇe aggaññe ariyavaṃse ṭhito’.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu santuṭṭho hoti itarītarena senāsanena, itarītarasenāsanasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī, na ca senāsanahetu anesanaṃ appatirūpaṃ āpajjati; aladdhā ca senāsanaṃ na paritassati, laddhā ca senāsanaṃ agadhito amucchito anajjhāpanno ādīnavadassāvī nissaraṇapañño paribhuñjati; tāya ca pana itarītarasenāsanasantuṭṭhiyā nevattānukkaṃseti na paraṃ vambheti. Yo hi tattha dakkho analaso sampajāno paṭissato, ayaṃ vuccatāvuso – ‘bhikkhu porāṇe aggaññe ariyavaṃse ṭhito’.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu pahānārāmo hoti pahānarato, bhāvanārāmo hoti bhāvanārato; tāya ca pana pahānārāmatāya pahānaratiyā bhāvanārāmatāya bhāvanāratiyā nevattānukkaṃseti na paraṃ vambheti. Yo hi tattha dakkho analaso sampajāno paṭissato ayaṃ vuccatāvuso – ‘bhikkhu porāṇe aggaññe ariyavaṃse ṭhito’.
mula_english:
309. “The four lineages of the Noble Ones (ariyavaṃsā):

Here, friends, a monk is content with any old robe cloth at all. He speaks in praise of being content with any old robe cloth at all. He doesn’t, for the sake of robe cloth, do anything unseemly or inappropriate. Not getting cloth, he isn’t agitated. Getting cloth, he uses it unattached to it, uninfatuated, guiltless, seeing the drawbacks, and discerning the escape from them. He doesn’t, on account of his contentment with any old robe cloth at all, exalt himself or disparage others. Any monk who is diligent, deft, alert, & mindful in this is said to be a monk standing firm in the ancient, original traditions of the noble ones.

“And further, friends, the monk is content with any old almsfood at all. He speaks in praise of being content with any old almsfood at all. He doesn’t, for the sake of almsfood, do anything unseemly or inappropriate. Not getting almsfood, he isn’t agitated. Getting almsfood, he uses it unattached to it, uninfatuated, guiltless, seeing the drawbacks, and discerning the escape from them. He doesn’t, on account of his contentment with any old almsfood at all, exalt himself or disparage others. Any monk who is diligent, deft, alert, & mindful in this is said to be a monk standing firm in the ancient, original traditions of the noble ones.

“And further, friends, the monk is content with any old lodging at all. He speaks in praise of being content with any old lodging at all. He doesn’t, for the sake of lodging, do anything unseemly or inappropriate. Not getting lodging, he isn’t agitated. Getting lodging, he uses it unattached to it, uninfatuated, guiltless, seeing the drawbacks, and discerning the escape from them. He doesn’t, on account of his contentment with any old lodging at all, exalt himself or disparage others. Any monk who is diligent, deft, alert, & mindful in this is said to be a monk standing firm in the ancient, original traditions of the noble ones.

“And further, friends, the monk finds pleasure & delight in abandoning, finds pleasure & delight in developing. He doesn’t, on account of his pleasure & delight in abandoning & developing, exalt himself or disparage others. Any monk who is diligent, deft, alert, & mindful in this is said to be a monk standing firm in the ancient, original traditions of the noble ones.
commentary_pali:
309.Ariyavaṃsāti ariyānaṃ vaṃsā. Yathā hi khattiyavaṃso, brāhmaṇavaṃso, vessavaṃso, suddavaṃso, samaṇavaṃso, kulavaṃso, rājavaṃso, evaṃ ayampi aṭṭhamo ariyavaṃso ariyatanti ariyapaveṇī nāma hoti. So kho panāyaṃ ariyavaṃso imesaṃ vaṃsānaṃ mūlagandhādīnaṃ kāḷānusāritagandhādayo viya aggamakkhāyati. Ke pana te ariyā yesaṃ ete vaṃsāti? Ariyā vuccanti buddhā ca paccekabuddhā ca tathāgatasāvakā ca, etesaṃ ariyānaṃ vaṃsāti ariyavaṃsā. Ito pubbe hi satasahassakappādhikānaṃ catunnaṃ asaṅkhyeyyānaṃ matthake taṇhaṅkaro medhaṅkaro saraṇaṅkaro dīpaṅkaroti cattāro buddhā uppannā, te ariyā, tesaṃ ariyānaṃ vaṃsāti ariyavaṃsā. Tesaṃ buddhānaṃ parinibbānato aparabhāge asaṅkhyeyyaṃ atikkamitvā koṇḍañño nāma buddho uppanno…pe… imasmiṃ kappe kakusandho, koṇāgamano, kassapo, amhākaṃ bhagavā gotamoti cattāro buddhā uppannā. Tesaṃ ariyānaṃ vaṃsāti ariyavaṃsā. Apica atītānāgatapaccuppannānaṃ sabbabuddhapaccekabuddhabuddhasāvakānaṃ ariyānaṃ vaṃsāti ariyavaṃsā. Te kho panete aggaññā aggāti jānitabbā. Rattaññā dīgharattaṃ pavattāti jānitabbā. Vaṃsaññā vaṃsāti jānitabbā.

Porāṇāti na adhunuppattikā. Asaṃkiṇṇā avikiṇṇā anapanītā. Asaṃkiṇṇapubbā atītabuddhehi na saṃkiṇṇapubbā. ‘‘Kiṃ imehī’’ti na apanītapubbā? Na saṅkīyantīti idānipi na apanīyanti. Na saṅkīyissantīti anāgatabuddhehipi na apanīyissanti, ye loke viññū samaṇabrāhmaṇā, tehi appaṭikuṭṭhā, samaṇehi brāhmaṇehi viññūhi aninditā agarahitā.

Santuṭṭho hotīti paccayasantosavasena santuṭṭho hoti. Itarītarena cīvarenāti thūlasukhumalūkhapaṇītathirajiṇṇānaṃ yena kenaci. Atha kho yathāladdhādīnaṃ itarītarena yena kenaci santuṭṭho hotīti attho. Cīvarasmiñhi tayo santosā – yathālābhasantoso, yathābalasantoso, yathāsāruppasantosoti. Piṇḍapātādīsupi eseva nayo. Tesaṃ vitthārakathā sāmaññaphale vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Ime tayo santose sandhāya ‘‘santuṭṭho hoti, itarītarena yathāladdhādīsu yena kenaci cīvarena santuṭṭho hotī’’ti vuttaṃ.

Ettha ca cīvaraṃ jānitabbaṃ, cīvarakkhettaṃ jānitabbaṃ, paṃsukūlaṃ jānitabbaṃ, cīvarasantoso jānitabbo, cīvarapaṭisaṃyuttāni dhutaṅgāni jānitabbāni. Tattha cīvaraṃ jānitabbanti khomādīni cha cīvarāni dukūlādīni cha anulomacīvarāni jānitabbāni. Imāni dvādasa kappiyacīvarāni. Kusacīraṃ vākacīraṃ phalakacīraṃ kesakambalaṃ vāḷakambalaṃ potthako cammaṃ ulūkapakkhaṃ rukkhadussaṃ latādussaṃ erakadussaṃ kadalidussaṃ veḷudussanti evamādīni pana akappiyacīvarāni. Cīvarakkhettanti ‘‘saṅghato vā gaṇato vā ñātito vā mittato vā attano vā dhanena paṃsukūlaṃ vā’’ti evaṃ uppajjanato cha khettāni, aṭṭhannañca mātikānaṃ vasena aṭṭha khettāni jānitabbāni. Paṃsukūlanti sosānikaṃ, pāpaṇikaṃ, rathiyaṃ saṅkārakūṭakaṃ, sotthiyaṃ, sinānaṃ, titthaṃ, gatapaccāgataṃ, aggidaḍḍhaṃ, gokhāyitaṃ upacikakhāyitaṃ, undūrakhāyitaṃ, antacchinnaṃ, dasācchinnaṃ, dhajāhaṭaṃ, thūpaṃ, samaṇacīvaraṃ, sāmuddiyaṃ, ābhisekiyaṃ, panthikaṃ, vātāhaṭaṃ, iddhimayaṃ, devadattiyanti tevīsati paṃsukūlāni veditabbāni.

cīvaraṃ jānitabba Cīvarakkhetta aṭṭha khettāni Paṃsukūla

Ettha ca sotthiyanti gabbhamalaharaṇaṃ. Gatapaccāgatanti matakasarīraṃ pārupitvā susānaṃ netvā ānītacīvaraṃ. Dhajāhaṭanti dhajaṃ ussāpetvā tato ānītaṃ. Thūpanti vammike pūjitacīvaraṃ . Sāmuddiyanti samuddavīcīhi thalaṃ pāpitaṃ. Panthikanti panthaṃ gacchantehi corabhayena pāsāṇehi koṭṭetvā pārutacīvaraṃ. Iddhimayanti ehibhikkhucīvaraṃ. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva.

Cīvarasantoso

Tattha sādakabhikkhunā temāsaṃ nibaddhavāsaṃ vasitvā ekamāsamattaṃ vitakketuṃ vaṭṭati. So hi pavāretvā cīvaramāse cīvaraṃ karoti. Paṃsukūliko aḍḍhamāseneva karoti. Iti māsaḍḍhamāsamattaṃ vitakkanaṃ vitakkasantoso. Vitakkasantosena pana santuṭṭhena bhikkhunā pācīnakkhaṇḍarājivāsikapaṃsukūlikattherasadisena bhavitabbaṃ.

Thero kira cetiyapabbatavihāre cetiyaṃ vandissāmīti āgato cetiyaṃ vanditvā cintesi ‘‘mayhaṃ cīvaraṃ jiṇṇaṃ bahūnaṃ vasanaṭṭhāne labhissāmī’’ti. So mahāvihāraṃ gantvā saṅghattheraṃ disvā vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pucchitvā tattha vuttho punadivase cīvaraṃ ādāya āgantvā theraṃ vandi. Thero kiṃ āvusoti āha. Gāmadvāraṃ, bhante, gamissāmīti. Ahampāvuso, gamissāmīti. Sādhu, bhanteti gacchanto mahābodhidvārakoṭṭhake ṭhatvā puññavantānaṃ vasanaṭṭhāne manāpaṃ labhissāmīti cintetvā aparisuddho me vitakkoti tatova paṭinivatti. Punadivase ambaṅgaṇasamīpato, punadivase mahācetiyassa uttaradvārato, tatheva paṭinivattitvā catutthadivase therassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Thero imassa bhikkhuno vitakko na parisuddho bhavissatīti cīvaraṃ gahetvā tena saddhiṃyeva pañhaṃ pucchamāno gāmaṃ pāvisi. Tañca rattiṃ eko manusso uccārapalibuddho sāṭakeyeva vaccaṃ katvā taṃ saṅkāraṭṭhāne chaḍḍesi. Paṃsukūlikatthero taṃ nīlamakkhikāhi samparikiṇṇaṃ disvā añjaliṃ paggahesi. Mahāthero ‘‘kiṃ, āvuso, saṅkāraṭṭhānassa añjaliṃ paggaṇhāsī’’ti? ‘‘Nāhaṃ, bhante, saṅkāraṭṭhānassa añjaliṃ paggaṇhāmi, mayhaṃ pitu dasabalassa paggaṇhāmi, puṇṇadāsiyā sarīraṃ pārupitvā chaḍḍitaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ tumbamatte pāṇake vidhunitvā susānato gaṇhantena dukkaraṃ kataṃ, bhante’’ti. Mahāthero ‘‘parisuddho vitakko paṃsukūlikassā’’ti cintesi. Paṃsukūlikattheropi tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne ṭhito vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā tīṇi phalāni patto taṃ sāṭakaṃ gahetvā cīvaraṃ katvā pārupitvā pācīnakkhaṇḍarājiṃ gantvā aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

Thero Paṃsukūlikatthero

Cīvaratthāya gacchantassa pana ‘‘kattha labhissāmī’’ti acintetvā kammaṭṭhānasīseneva gamanaṃ gamanasantoso nāma.

gamanasantoso

Pariyesantassa pana yena vā tena vā saddhiṃ apariyesitvā lajjiṃ pesalaṃ bhikkhuṃ gahetvā pariyesanaṃ pariyesanasantoso nāma.

pariyesanasantoso

Evaṃ pariyesantassa āhariyamānaṃ cīvaraṃ dūrato disvā ‘‘etaṃ manāpaṃ bhavissati, etaṃ amanāpa’’nti evaṃ avitakketvā thūlasukhumādīsu yathāladdheneva santussanaṃ paṭilābhasantoso nāma.

paṭilābhasantoso

Evaṃ laddhaṃ gaṇhantassāpi ‘‘ettakaṃ dupaṭṭassa bhavissati, ettakaṃ ekapaṭṭassā’’ti attano pahonakamatteneva santussanaṃ mattappaṭiggahaṇasantoso nāma.

mattappaṭiggahaṇasantoso

Cīvaraṃ pariyesantassa pana ‘‘asukassa gharadvāre manāpaṃ labhissāmī’’ti acintetvā dvārapaṭipāṭiyā caraṇaṃ loluppavivajjanasantoso nāma.

loluppavivajjanasantoso

Lūkhapaṇītesu yena kenaci yāpetuṃ sakkontassa yathāladdheneva yāpanaṃ yathālābhasantoso nāma.

yathālābhasantoso

Attano thāmaṃ jānitvā yena yāpetuṃ sakkoti, tena yāpanaṃ yathābalasantoso nāma.

yathābalasantoso

Manāpaṃ aññassa datvā attano yena kenaci yāpanaṃ yathāsāruppasantoso nāma.

yathāsāruppasantoso

‘‘Kattha udakaṃ manāpaṃ, kattha amanāpa’’nti avicāretvā yena kenaci dhovanupagena udakena dhovanaṃ udakasantoso nāma. Paṇḍumattikagerukapūtipaṇṇarasakiliṭṭhāni pana udakāni vajjetuṃ vaṭṭati.

udakasantoso

Dhovantassa pana muggarādīhi apaharitvā hatthehi madditvā dhovanaṃ dhovanasantoso nāma. Tathā asujjhantaṃ paṇṇāni pakkhipitvā tāpitaudakenāpi dhovituṃ vaṭṭati.

dhovanasantoso

Evaṃ dhovitvā karontassa idaṃ thūlaṃ, idaṃ sukhumanti akopetvā pahonakanīhāreneva karaṇaṃ karaṇasantoso nāma.

karaṇasantoso

Timaṇḍalappaṭicchādanamattasseva karaṇaṃ parimāṇasantoso nāma.

parimāṇasantoso

Cīvarakaraṇatthāya pana manāpasuttaṃ pariyesissāmīti avicāretvā rathikādīsu vā devaṭṭhāne vā āharitvā pādamūle vā ṭhapitaṃ yaṃkiñcideva suttaṃ gahetvā karaṇaṃ suttasantoso nāma.

suttasantoso

Kusibandhanakāle pana aṅgulamatte sattavāre na vijjhitabbaṃ, evaṃ karontassa hi yo bhikkhu sahāyo na hoti, tassa vattabhedopi natthi. Tivaṅgulamatte pana sattavāre vijjhitabbaṃ, evaṃ karontassa maggapaṭipannenāpi sahāyena bhavitabbaṃ. Yo na hoti, tassa vattabhedo. Ayaṃ sibbanasantoso nāma.

sibbanasantoso

Rajantena pana kāḷakacchakādīni pariyesantena na rajitabbaṃ. Somavakkalādīsu yaṃ labhati, tena rajitabbaṃ. Alabhantena pana manussehi araññe vākaṃ gahetvā chaḍḍitarajanaṃ vā bhikkhūhi pacitvā chaḍḍitakasaṭaṃ vā gahetvā rajitabbaṃ, ayaṃ rajanasantoso nāma.

rajanasantoso

Nīlakaddamakāḷasāmesu yaṃkiñci gahetvā hatthipiṭṭhe nisinnassa paññāyamānakapakaraṇaṃ kappasantoso nāma.

kappasantoso

Hirikopīnapaṭicchādanamattavasena paribhuñjanaṃ paribhogasantoso nāma.

paribhogasantoso

Dussaṃ pana labhitvā suttaṃ vā sūciṃ vā kārakaṃ vā alabhantena ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati, labhantena na vaṭṭati. Katampi sace antevāsikādīnaṃ dātukāmo hoti, te ca asannihitā yāva āgamanā ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Āgatamattesu dātabbaṃ. Dātuṃ asakkontena adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Aññasmiṃ cīvare sati paccattharaṇampi adhiṭṭhātuṃ vaṭṭati. Anadhiṭṭhitameva hi sannidhi hoti. Adhiṭṭhitaṃ na hotīti mahāsīvatthero āha. Ayaṃ sannidhiparivajjanasantoso nāma.

vissajjanasantoso

Anesananti dūteyyapahinagamanānuyogappabhedaṃ nānappakāraṃ anesanaṃ. Appatirūpanti ayuttaṃ. Aladdhā cāti alabhitvā. Yathā ekacco ‘‘kathaṃ nu kho cīvaraṃ labhissāmī’’ti. Puññavantehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ ekato hutvā kohaññaṃ karonto uttasati paritasati, santuṭṭho bhikkhu evaṃ aladdhā cīvaraṃ na paritasati. Laddhā cāti dhammena samena labhitvā. Agadhitoti vigatalobhagiddho. Amucchitoti adhimattataṇhāya mucchaṃ anāpanno. Anajjhāpannoti taṇhāya anotthato apariyonaddho. Ādīnavadassāvīti anesanāpattiyañca gedhitaparibhoge ca ādīnavaṃ passamāno. Itarītaracīvarasantuṭṭhiyāti yena kenaci cīvarena santuṭṭhiyā. Nevattānukkaṃsetīti ‘‘ahaṃ paṃsukūliko mayā upasampadamāḷeyeva paṃsukūlikaṅgaṃ gahitaṃ, ko mayā sadiso atthī’’ti attukkaṃsanaṃ na karoti. Na paraṃ vambhetīti ‘‘ime panaññe bhikkhū na paṃsukūlikā’’ti vā ‘‘paṃsukūlikaṅgamattampi etesaṃ natthī’’ti vā evaṃ paraṃ na vambheti. Yo hi tattha dakkhoti yo tasmiṃ cīvarasantose, vaṇṇavādādīsu vā dakkho cheko byatto. Analasoti sātaccakiriyāya ālasiyavirahito. Sampajāno paṭissatoti sampajānapaññāya ceva satiyā ca yutto. Ariyavaṃse ṭhitoti ariyavaṃse patiṭṭhito.

Itarītarena piṇḍapātenāti yena kenaci piṇḍapātena. Etthāpi piṇḍapāto jānitabbo. Piṇḍapātakkhettaṃ jānitabbaṃ, piṇḍapātasantoso jānitabbo, piṇḍapātapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ jānitabbaṃ. Tattha piṇḍapātoti ‘‘odano, kummāso, sattu, maccho, maṃsaṃ, khīraṃ, dadhi, sappi, navanītaṃ, telaṃ, madhu, phāṇitaṃ, yāgu, khādanīyaṃ, sāyanīyaṃ, lehanīya’’nti soḷasa piṇḍapātā.

Itarītarena piṇḍapātenā piṇḍapāto

Piṇḍapātakkhettanti saṅghabhattaṃ, uddesabhattaṃ, nimantanaṃ, salākabhattaṃ, pakkhikaṃ, uposathikaṃ, pāṭipadikaṃ, āgantukabhattaṃ, gamikabhattaṃ, gilānabhattaṃ, gilānupaṭṭhākabhattaṃ, dhurabhattaṃ, kuṭibhattaṃ, vārabhattaṃ, vihārabhattanti pannarasa piṇḍapātakkhettāni.

Piṇḍapātakkhetta

Piṇḍapātasantosoti piṇḍapāte vitakkasantoso, gamanasantoso, pariyesanasantoso paṭilābhasantoso, paṭiggahaṇasantoso, mattappaṭiggahaṇasantoso, loluppavivajjanasantoso, yathālābhasantoso, yathābalasantoso, yathāsāruppasantoso, upakārasantoso, parimāṇasantoso, paribhogasantoso, sannidhiparivajjanasantoso, vissajjanasantosoti pannarasa santosā.

Piṇḍapātasantoso

Tattha sādako bhikkhu mukhaṃ dhovitvā vitakketi. Piṇḍapātikena pana gaṇena saddhiṃ caratā sāyaṃ therūpaṭṭhānakāle ‘‘sve kattha piṇḍāya carissāmāti asukagāme, bhante’’ti, ettakaṃ cintetvā tato paṭṭhāya na vitakketabbaṃ. Ekacārikena vitakkamāḷake ṭhatvā vitakketabbaṃ. Tato paraṃ vitakkento ariyavaṃsā cuto hoti paribāhiro. Ayaṃ vitakkasantoso nāma.

vitakkasantoso

Piṇḍāya pavisantena ‘‘kuhiṃ labhissāmī’’ti acintetvā kammaṭṭhānasīsena gantabbaṃ. Ayaṃ gamanasantoso nāma.

gamanasantoso

Pariyesantena yaṃ vā taṃ vā agahetvā lajjiṃ pesalameva gahetvā pariyesitabbaṃ. Ayaṃ pariyesanasantoso nāma.

pariyesanasantoso

Dūratova āhariyamānaṃ disvā ‘‘etaṃ manāpaṃ, etaṃ amanāpa’’nti cittaṃ na uppādetabbaṃ. Ayaṃ paṭilābhasantoso nāma.

paṭilābhasantoso

‘‘Imaṃ manāpaṃ gaṇhissāmi, imaṃ amanāpaṃ na gaṇhissāmī’’ti acintetvā yaṃkiñci yāpanamattaṃ gahetabbameva, ayaṃ paṭiggahaṇasantoso nāma.

paṭiggahaṇasantoso

Ettha pana deyyadhammo bahu, dāyako appaṃ dātukāmo, appaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Deyyadhammo bahu, dāyakopi bahuṃ dātukāmo, pamāṇeneva gahetabbaṃ. Deyyadhammo na bahu, dāyakopi appaṃ dātukāmo, appaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Deyyadhammo na bahu, dāyako pana bahuṃ dātukāmo, pamāṇena gahetabbaṃ. Paṭiggahaṇasmiñhi mattaṃ ajānanto manussānaṃ pasādaṃ makkheti, saddhādeyyaṃ vinipāteti, sāsanaṃ na karoti, vijātamātuyāpi cittaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti. Iti mattaṃ jānitvāva paṭiggahetabbanti ayaṃ mattappaṭiggahaṇasantoso nāma.

mattappaṭiggahaṇasantoso

Saddhakulāniyeva agantvā dvārappaṭipāṭiyā gantabbaṃ. Ayaṃ loluppavivajjanasantoso nāma. Yathālābhasantosādayo cīvare vuttanayā eva.

Piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjitvā samaṇadhammaṃ anupālessāmīti evaṃ upakāraṃ ñatvā paribhuñjanaṃ upakārasantoso nāma.

upakārasantoso

Pattaṃ pūretvā ānītaṃ na paṭiggahetabbaṃ, anupasampanne sati tena gāhāpetabbaṃ, asati harāpetvā paṭiggahaṇamattaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Ayaṃ parimāṇasantoso nāma.

parimāṇasantoso

‘‘Jighacchāya paṭivinodanaṃ idamettha nissaraṇa’’nti evaṃ paribhuñjanaṃ paribhogasantoso nāma.

paribhogasantoso

Nidahitvā na paribhuñjitabbanti ayaṃ sannidhiparivajjanasantoso nāma.

sannidhiparivajjanasantoso

Mukhaṃ anoloketvā sāraṇīyadhamme ṭhitena vissajjetabbaṃ. Ayaṃ vissajjanasantoso nāma.

commentary_english:
309. "ariyavaṃsā" means the lineages of the noble ones (ārya). Just as there is the lineage of the Kṣatriyas, the lineage of the Brahmins, the lineage of the Vaiśyas, the lineage of the Śūdras, the lineage of the Śramaṇas, the family lineage, the royal lineage, so too, this eighth lineage of the noble ones, which is noble, is called the noble tradition (ariyapaveṇī). And this lineage of the noble ones is called the foremost, like the kālānusārika-gandha, etc., from the root fragrance, etc., of these lineages. But who are these noble ones whose lineages these are? The noble ones are called Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and disciples of the Tathāgata; the lineages of these noble ones are the "ariyavaṃsā." Before this, at the head of four asaṃkhyeyyas exceeding a hundred thousand kalpas, four Buddhas arose: Tṛṣṇaṃkara, Medhaṃkara, Saraṇaṃkara, and Dīpaṃkara; they are noble ones, the lineages of those noble ones are ariyavaṃsā. After the parinirvāṇa of those Buddhas, having passed asaṃkhyeyyas, a Buddha named Koṇḍañña arose...pe... In this kalpa, four Buddhas arose: Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and our Blessed One Gotama. The lineages of these noble ones are ariyavaṃsā. Moreover, the lineages of all Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddha disciples of the past, future, and present are ariyavaṃsā. These are to be known as "aggaññā," as foremost. "rattaññā" are to be known as long-lasting. "vaṃsaññā" are to be known as lineages.

"porāṇā" means not newly arisen. "asaṃkiṇṇā" means unmixed, not scattered, not removed. "asaṃkiṇṇapubbā" means not previously mixed by past Buddhas. "kiṃ imehī" means not previously rejected? "na saṅkīyantī" means even now they are not rejected. "na saṅkīyissantī" means even by future Buddhas they will not be rejected; those who are wise śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world, they are unreproached, unblamed, unrejected by wise śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.

porāṇā asaṃkiṇṇā asaṃkiṇṇapubbā na saṅkīyantī na saṅkīyissantī "santuṭṭho hoti" means he is content by way of contentment with the requisites. "itarītarena cīvarena" means with whatever, whether coarse, fine, rough, excellent, durable, or worn. But it means he is content with whatever, any kind of what is obtained, etc. For in regard to robes there are three kinds of contentment: contentment with whatever is obtained, contentment with whatever strength, contentment with whatever is suitable. The same method applies to piṇḍapāta, etc. Their detailed explanation should be understood in the same way as stated in the Sāmaññaphala [Sutta]. With reference to these three kinds of contentment it is said, "santuṭṭho hoti, itarītarena, with whatever is obtained, etc., he is content with whatever robe."

santuṭṭho hoti itarītarena cīvarena Here, the robe should be known, the robe field should be known, the rag robe (pāṃśukūla) should be known, contentment with the robe should be known, and the dhutaṅgas connected with the robe should be known. There, "the robe should be known" means the six robes of khoma, etc., and the six conforming robes of dukūla, etc., should be known. These twelve are allowable robes. But the unallowable robes are: robes of kusa grass, robes of bark, robes of fruit fibers, robes of human hair, robes of horsehair, blankets, hides, owl wings, tree bark cloth, creeper cloth, eraka cloth, kadali cloth, veḷu cloth, and so on. "cīvarakkhetta" means the six fields from which they arise: "from the Saṅgha, from the group, from relatives, from friends, or from one's own wealth, or a rag robe," and the eight fields should be known in terms of the eight matrices. "paṃsukūla" means: from the cemetery, from the market, from the road, from the heap of rubbish, from the lying-in place, from the bathing place, from the ford, gone and returned, burnt by fire, eaten by cows, eaten by white ants, eaten by rats, cut at the edge, torn at the edge, brought by a flag, from a stupa, a śramaṇa's robe, from the sea, for anointing, from the road, brought by the wind, made by magic, given by Devadatta; these twenty-three pāṃsukūlas should be known.

cīvaraṃ jānitabba cīvarakkhetta aṭṭha khettāni paṃsukūla Here, "sotthiya" means removing the impurities of the womb. "gatapaccāgata" means a robe that is covered over a dead body, taken to the cemetery, and brought back. "dhajāhaṭa" means brought from there, having raised a flag. "thūpa" means a robe worshiped in an anthill.
