commentary_english:
347. In the *kammapathas*, the *karmas* themselves are called *kammapathas* because they are the path to good and bad destinies. Among these, killing, taking what is not given, lying, and so forth, the first four, have already been extensively described in the *Brahmajāla* [Sutta]. As for *kāmesumicchācāra*, *kāmesu* means sexual intercourse or objects of sexual intercourse. *Micchācāra* means utterly blameworthy, base conduct. As to its characteristic, *kāmesumicchācāra* "sexual misconduct" is the volition to transgress bounds occurring through the body door by way of unrighteous intent.

Herein, *agamanīyaṭṭhānaṃ* means, firstly, for men, the ten kinds of women beginning with those protected by the mother, namely, “protected by the mother, protected by the father, protected by the mother and father, protected by the brother, protected by the sister, protected by relatives, protected by the clan, protected by the *dharma*, under protection, entailing a penalty.” The twenty [women] are the ten beginning with those purchased with money, namely, “one purchased with money, one who lives by her will, one who lives by her wealth, one who lives under protection, one who provides water, a kept woman, a female slave and a wife, a female worker and a wife, one captured in war, and a prostitute.” For women, other men are out of bounds for the twelve kinds of women consisting of the two, namely, under protection and entailing a penalty, and the ten beginning with those purchased with money. This is called *agamanīyaṭṭhānaṃ*. This sexual misconduct is less blameworthy when the one who is out of bounds is without good qualities such as ethical discipline, etc., and more blameworthy when the one who is out of bounds possesses good qualities such as ethical discipline, etc. There are four constituents of this act: an object which is out of bounds (*agamanīy वस्तु*), the mind to engage in that, the effort to engage, and consent to the union of sexual organs. The means (*upayoga*) is single: one’s own person.

*Agamanīyaṭṭhānaṃ*

*Abhijjha*, "covetousness": It covets, thus it is covetousness; the meaning is "having become directed towards others’ goods, it occurs through inclination towards them". It has the characteristic of coveting others’ goods thus: “Oh, that this were mine!” It is less blameworthy and more blameworthy as in the case of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*). Its constituents are two: another’s goods, and the inclination for them to be one’s own. For even though greed (*lobha*) has arisen based on another’s goods, it is not classed as a course of *karma* so long as one does not incline to them as one’s own, “Oh, that this were mine!”

*Abhijjha*

*Byāpādo*, "ill will": It destroys welfare and happiness. It is less blameworthy and more blameworthy as in the case of harsh speech, its characteristic is mental corruption for the destruction of another. Its constituents are two: another being (*parasattva*), and the wish for that being’s destruction. For even though anger (*kodha*) has arisen based on another being (*parasattva*), there is no breach of a course of *karma* so long as one does not wish, “Oh, that this being might be cut off and destroyed!”

*Byāpādo*

*Micchādiṭṭhi*, "wrong view": It sees wrongly due to the absence of a correct grasp of things, thus it is wrong view. Its characteristic is the mistaken view that “there is no giving,” etc. It is less blameworthy and more blameworthy as in the case of gossip (*samphappalāpa*). Moreover, it is less blameworthy when not fixed in destiny, and more blameworthy when fixed. Its constituents are two: a mistaken manner of grasping the basis (*vastu*), and the appearance of that in accordance with the manner in which it has been grasped.

*Micchādiṭṭhi*

Now the exposition of these ten courses of unwholesome *karma* should be understood in five ways: as to mental state (*dhammato*), as to category (*koṭṭhāsato*), as to object (*ārammaṇato*), as to feeling (*vedanāto*), and as to root (*mūlato*).

Herein, as to mental state (*dhammato*): The first seven among these are volitional states (*cetanādhammā*) only. The three beginning with covetousness (*abhijjhā*) are associated with volition.

*Dhammato*

As to category (*koṭṭhāsato*): the first seven in order, and wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*), these eight are courses of *karma* only, not roots (*mūlāni*).
Covetousness and ill will are courses of action (kamma) and also roots.
For covetousness, having arrived at a root, is the unwholesome root greed (lobha).
And ill will is the unwholesome root hate (dosa).

From the standpoint of…
From the standpoint of object: killing living beings has formations as its object because of the object that is the life faculty.
Taking what is not given has beings or formations as object; misconduct has formations as object by way of tangible object.
Some say that it has only beings as object.
False speech has beings or formations as object; likewise malicious speech.
Harsh speech has only beings as object.
Gossip has either beings or formations as object by way of the seen, heard, sensed and cognized.
Likewise covetousness.
Ill will has only beings as object.
Wrong view has formations as object by way of the states belonging to the three planes .

From the standpoint of feeling: killing living beings has painful feeling.
For although kings, seeing a robber, say laughingly, “Go and execute him,” their volition consummating the action is associated only with pain.
Taking what is not given has three feelings.
Misconduct has two feelings, pleasant and neutral.
But in the mind which consummates the action there is no neutral feeling.
False speech has three feelings.
likewise malicious speech.
Harsh speech has painful feeling only.
Gossip has three feelings.
Covetousness has two feelings, pleasant and neutral; likewise wrong view.
Ill will has painful feeling only.

From the standpoint of root: killing living beings has two roots, by way of hate and delusion.
Taking what is not given, by way of hate and delusion or by way of greed and delusion.
Misconduct, by way of greed and delusion.
False speech, by way of hate and delusion or by way of greed and delusion; likewise for malicious speech and gossip.
Harsh speech, by way of hate and delusion.
Covetousness has one root, by way of delusion.
Likewise ill will.
Wrong view has two roots, by way of greed and delusion.

Description of the ten wholesome courses of action
The abstaining from killing living beings and so on should be understood by way of undertaking, accomplishment, utter destruction, and abstention.

Abstaining from killing living beings
From the standpoint of the norm, in these, in due order, seven volitions occur, as well as abstinences.
the last three are associated with volition only.

From the standpoint of the norm, from the standpoint of division, in due order, there are seven courses of action only, not roots.
At the end of those, the courses of action and the roots...

And, for non-covetousness, having attained the root, non-greed (alobha) is a wholesome root (kusalamūla).

Non-ill will (abyāpāda) and non-hatred (adosa) are wholesome roots (kusalamūla).

Right view (sammādiṭṭhi) and non-delusion (amoha) are wholesome roots (kusalamūla).

From the aspect of sections...

From the aspect of object (ālambanato): the objects of actions such as killing living beings are indeed their objects.

For restraint is called abstinence.

Just as the noble path (ariyamagga), which has *Nirvāṇa* as its object (nibbānārammaṇa), abandons defilements (kilesa), so too should it be understood that these courses of action (kammapatha), which have the life faculty (jīvitindriya), etc., as object, abandon evil conduct (dussīlya) beginning with killing living beings (pāṇātipātādīni).

From the aspect of object (ālambanato)...

From the aspect of feeling (vedanāto): all have pleasant feeling (sukhavedanā) or neutral feeling (majjhattavedanā).

For there is no painful feeling ( dukkhavedanā) which arrives at the wholesome (kusala).

From the aspect of feeling (vedanāto)...

From the aspect of root (mūlato): in due order, for one who abstains by means of consciousness associated with knowledge (ñāṇasampayuttacittena), there are three roots (timūlāni) in terms of non-greed (alobha), non-hatred (adosa), and non-delusion (amoha); for one who abstains by means of consciousness dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇavippayuttacittena), there are two roots (dvimūlāni).

Non-covetousness (anabhijjhā) has two roots (dvimūlā) in one who abstains by means of consciousness associated with knowledge (ñāṇasampayuttacittena), one root (ekamūlā) by means of consciousness dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇavippayuttacittena).

Non-greed (alobha), however, is not its own root (mūla).

And the same method (nayā) applies in the case of non-ill will (abyāpāda).

Right view (sammādiṭṭhi) has two roots (dvimūlā) in terms of non-greed (alobha) and non-hatred (adosa).

From the aspect of root (mūlato)...

Explanation of the Decade on the Noble Life (ariyavāsadasakavaṇṇanā).

mula_pali:
348. ‘‘Dasa ariyavāsā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu pañcaṅgavippahīno hoti, chaḷaṅgasamannāgato, ekārakkho, caturāpasseno, paṇunnapaccekasacco, samavayasaṭṭhesano, anāvilasaṅkappo, passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro, suvimuttacitto, suvimuttapañño.

‘‘Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu pañcaṅgavippahīno hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno kāmacchando pahīno hoti, byāpādo pahīno hoti, thinamiddhaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, uddhaccakukuccaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, vicikicchā pahīnā hoti. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu pañcaṅgavippahīno hoti.

‘‘Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu chaḷaṅgasamannāgato hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā neva sumano hoti na dummano, upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno. Sotena saddaṃ sutvā…pe… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya neva sumano hoti na dummano, upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu chaḷaṅgasamannāgato hoti.

‘‘Kathañcāvuso , bhikkhu ekārakkho hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu satārakkhena cetasā samannāgato hoti. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu ekārakkho hoti .

‘‘Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu caturāpasseno hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevati, saṅkhāyekaṃ adhivāseti, saṅkhāyekaṃ parivajjeti, saṅkhāyekaṃ vinodeti. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu caturāpasseno hoti.

‘‘Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu paṇunnapaccekasacco hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno yāni tāni puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ puthupaccekasaccāni, sabbāni tāni nunnāni honti paṇunnāni cattāni vantāni muttāni pahīnāni paṭinissaṭṭhāni. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu paṇunnapaccekasacco hoti.

‘‘Kathañcāvuso , bhikkhu samavayasaṭṭhesano hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno kāmesanā pahīnā hoti, bhavesanā pahīnā hoti, brahmacariyesanā paṭippassaddhā. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu samavayasaṭṭhesano hoti.

‘‘Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu anāvilasaṅkappo hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno kāmasaṅkappo pahīno hoti, byāpādasaṅkappo pahīno hoti, vihiṃsāsaṅkappo pahīno hoti. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu anāvilasaṅkappo hoti.

‘‘Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro hoti ? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro hoti.

‘‘Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu suvimuttacitto hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno rāgā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ hoti, dosā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ hoti, mohā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu suvimuttacitto hoti.

‘‘Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu suvimuttapañño hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu ‘rāgo me pahīno ucchinnamūlo tālāvatthukato anabhāvaṃkato āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo’ti pajānāti. ‘Doso me pahīno ucchinnamūlo tālāvatthukato anabhāvaṃkato āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo’ti pajānāti. ‘Moho me pahīno ucchinnamūlo tālāvatthukato anabhāvaṃkato āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo’ti pajānāti. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu suvimuttapañño hoti.

‘‘Dasa asekkhā dhammā – asekkhā sammādiṭṭhi, asekkho sammāsaṅkappo, asekkhā sammāvācā, asekkho sammākammanto, asekkho sammāājīvo, asekkho sammāvāyāmo, asekkhā sammāsati, asekkho sammāsamādhi, asekkhaṃ sammāñāṇaṃ, asekkhā sammāvimutti.

asekkhā dhammā –

‘‘Ime kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena dasa dhammā sammadakkhātā. Tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ na vivaditabbaṃ, yathayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ addhaniyaṃ assa ciraṭṭhitikaṃ, tadassa bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussāna’’nti.
mula_english:
348. “Ten noble abodes (dasa ariyavāsā). Here, friends, a monk has abandoned five factors (pañcaṅgavippahīno hoti), is endowed with six (chaḷaṅgasamannāgato), guards one (ekārakkho), is supported in four (caturāpasseno), has shaken off idiosyncratic truths (paṇunnapaccekasacco), has thoroughly given up searching (samavayasaṭṭhesano), is undisturbed in his resolves (anāvilasaṅkappo), is calmed in his bodily-fabrication (passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro), is well-released in mind (suvimuttacitto), is well-released in discernment (suvimuttapañño).

“And how, friends, has a monk abandoned five factors? Here, friends, a monk’s sensual desire (kāmacchando) is abandoned (pahīno hoti), his ill will (byāpādo) is abandoned, his sloth & torpor (thinamiddhaṃ) is abandoned, his restlessness & anxiety (uddhaccakukuccaṃ) is abandoned, his uncertainty (vicikicchā) is abandoned. This is how a monk has abandoned five factors.

“And how, friends, is a monk endowed with six? Here, friends, a monk, on seeing a form (rūpaṃ) via the eye (cakkhunā), is neither gladdened (sumano) nor saddened (dummano), but remains equanimous (upekkhako), mindful (sato), & alert (sampajāno). On hearing a sound (saddaṃ) via the ear (sotena)… On cognizing an idea (dhammaṃ) via the intellect (manasā), he is neither gladdened nor saddened, but remains equanimous, mindful, & alert. This is how a monk is endowed with six.

“And how, friends, is a monk guarding one? Here, friends, a monk is endowed with an awareness guarded by mindfulness (satārakkhena cetasā samannāgato hoti). This is how a monk is guarding one.

“And how, friends, is a monk supported in four? Here, friends, a monk uses one [factor] with reflection (saṅkhāya), endures one with reflection, avoids one with reflection, dispels one with reflection. This is how a monk is supported in four.

“And how, friends, has a monk shaken off idiosyncratic truths? Here, friends, whatever idiosyncratic truths (puthupaccekasaccāni) there may be among various ascetics (samaṇa) and brahmins (brāhmaṇa), all of those are rejected, shaken off, discarded, spewed out, released, abandoned, relinquished. This is how a monk has shaken off idiosyncratic truths.

“And how, friends, has a monk thoroughly given up searching? Here, friends, a monk has abandoned his search for sensuality (kāmesanā), has abandoned his search for becoming (bhavesanā), and has allayed his search for a holy life (brahmacariyesanā). This is how a monk has thoroughly given up searching.

“And how, friends, is a monk undisturbed in his resolves? Here, friends, a monk's resolve for sensuality (kāmasaṅkappo) is abandoned, his resolve for ill-will (byāpādasaṅkappo) is abandoned, his resolve for harmfulness (vihiṃsāsaṅkappo) is abandoned. This is how a monk is undisturbed in his resolves.

“And how, friends, is a monk calmed in his bodily fabrication (passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro)? Here, friends, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure (sukha) & pain (dukkha)—as with the earlier disappearance of elation (somanassa) & distress (domanassa)—enters & remains in the fourth *jhāna*: purity of equanimity (upekkhā) & mindfulness (sati), neither pleasure nor pain (adukkhamasukhaṃ). This is how a monk is calmed in his bodily fabrication.

“And how, friends, is a monk well-released in mind? Here, friends, a monk’s mind is released from lust (rāgā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ hoti), his mind is released from hate (dosā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ hoti), his mind is released from delusion (mohā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ hoti). This is how a monk is well released in mind.

“And how, friends, is a monk well-released in discernment? Here, friends, a monk discerns, ‘Lust (rāgo) is abandoned in me, its root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising.’ ‘Hate (doso) is abandoned in me, its root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising.’ ‘Delusion (moho) is abandoned in me, its root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising.’ This is how a monk is well-released in discernment.
Ten qualities of one beyond training (*aśaikṣā dharmā*): the right view of one beyond training, (*aśaikṣā samyagdṛṣṭi*), the right resolve of one beyond training (*aśaikṣaḥ samyaksaṃkalpaḥ*), the right speech of one beyond training (*aśaikṣā samyagvācā*), the right action of one beyond training (*aśaikṣo samyakkarmāntaḥ*), the right livelihood of one beyond training (*aśaikṣo samyagājīvaḥ*), the right effort of one beyond training (*aśaikṣā samyagvyāyāmaḥ*), the right mindfulness of one beyond training (*aśaikṣā samyaksmṛtiḥ*), the right concentration of one beyond training (*aśaikṣo samyaksamādhiḥ*), the right knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣaṃ samyagjñānam*), the right release of one beyond training (*aśaikṣā samyagvimuktiḥ*).

Qualities of one beyond training:
"These, friend, are the ten qualities well-proclaimed by that Blessed One—the Knower, the Seer, the Worthy One, the perfectly Awakened One. There all should recite together, without dispute, so that this spiritual life (*brahmacarya*) will endure and last a long time, for the benefit and happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans."
commentary_pali:
348.Ariyavāsāti ariyā eva vasiṃsu vasanti vasissanti etesūti ariyavāsā. Pañcaṅgavippahīnoti pañcahi aṅgehi vippayuttova hutvā khīṇāsavo avasi vasati vasissatīti tasmā ayaṃ pañcaṅgavippahīnatā, ariyassa vāsattā ariyavāsoti vutto. Esa nayo sabbattha.

Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu chaḷaṅgasamannāgato hotīti chaḷaṅgupekkhāya samannāgato hoti. Chaḷaṅgupekkhā nāma keti? Ñāṇādayo. ‘‘Ñāṇa’’nti vutte kiriyato cattāri ñāṇasampayuttacittāni labbhanti. ‘‘Satatavihāro’’ti vutte aṭṭha mahācittāni. ‘‘Rajjanadussanaṃ natthī’’ti vutte dasa cittāni labbhanti. Somanassaṃ āsevanavasena labbhati.

Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu chaḷaṅgasamannāgato hotī

Satārakkhena cetasāti khīṇāsavassa hi tīsu dvāresu sabbakālaṃ sati ārakkhakiccaṃ sādheti . Tenevassa ‘‘carato ca tiṭṭhato ca suttassa ca jāgarassa ca satataṃ samitaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hotī’’ti vuccati.

Puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇānanti bahūnaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ. Ettha ca samaṇāti pabbajjupagatā. Brāhmaṇāti bhovādino. commentary_english:
348. *Ariyavāsā* means those in whom the noble ones have dwelt, do dwell, and will dwell, thus *ariyavāsā*.

*Pañcaṅgavippahīno* means that, having become one who is disconnected from the five constituents, an *arhat* has lived, does live, and will live; therefore, this is *pañcaṅgavippahīnatā*, because of the dwelling of the noble one, it is called *ariyavāso*.

This method applies to all the other cases.

Thus, friends, a *bhikkhu* is endowed with six factors means he is endowed with six factors of equanimity.

What are the six factors of equanimity? They are wisdom and so on.

When “wisdom” is stated, four consciousnesses associated with wisdom are obtained from the action.

When “constant abiding” is stated, eight great consciousnesses [are obtained].

When “there is no attachment or aversion” is stated, ten consciousnesses are obtained.

Joy is obtained by way of cultivation.

Thus, friends, a *bhikkhu* is endowed with six factors.

*Satārakkhena cetasā* means mindfulness constantly fulfills the function of guarding in the three doors for an *arhat*.

Therefore it is said of him, “Whether I am walking or standing or asleep or awake, knowledge and vision are continuously and uninterruptedly present to me.”

*Satārakkhena cetasā*

*Puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇāna* means of many *samaṇa*s and *brāhmaṇa*s.

Here, *samaṇā* means those who have undertaken ordination.

*Brāhmaṇā* means those who use the word “bho” (a term of address).

*Puthupaccekasaccānī* means many individual truths; the meaning is many truths individually grasped thus: “This alone is the true view, this alone is the true view.”

*Nunnānī* means struck down.

*Paṇunnānī* means well struck down.

*Cattānī* means abandoned.

*Vantānī* means vomited.

*Muttānī* means made with bonds cut.

*Pahīnānī* means relinquished.

*Paṭinissaṭṭhānī* means rejected in such a way that they do not rise in the mind again.

All of these are synonyms for the state of having abandoned the grasped-grasping.

*Puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇāna*, *samaṇā*, *brāhmaṇā*, *puthupaccekasaccānī*, *nunnānī*, *paṇunnānī*, *cattānī*, *vantānī*, *muttānī*, *pahīnānī*, *paṭinissaṭṭhānī*

*Samavayasaṭṭhesano* here, *avayā* means not deficient.

*Saṭṭhā* means relinquished.

He whose seeking is rightly not deficient and relinquished is *samavayasaṭṭhesano*. The meaning is: one who has rightly relinquished all seeking.

The accomplishment of the function of the path is described by way of "[his] mind is liberated from passion" and so on.

*Samavayasaṭṭhesano*, *avayā*, *saṭṭhā*, *samavayasaṭṭhesano.*, *rāgā cittaṃ vimutta*

The fruit of retrospection is described by way of "*rāgo* me *pahīno*" and so on.

*Rāgo* *me pahīno*

Description of the Ten Qualities of One Beyond Training

*Asekhā sammādiṭṭhi* and so on, are all qualities associated with the fruition.

Here, wisdom alone is described in the two instances of *sammādiṭṭhi* (right view), and *sammāñāṇa* (right knowledge).

*Sammāvimuttī* (right liberation) is what remains unsaid and is stated by this term.
*Phalasamāpattidhammā saṅgahitāti veditabbā.* should be understood as included in the qualities of fruition attainment.

*Asekhā sammādiṭṭhi sammāvimutti.* "These, friend," etc., should be construed in the same way as stated above.

Thus, the Elder, speaking of sixty questions in terms of six decades, showed the taste of concord.

The exposition of the decade is finished.

The exposition of the resolution of the questions.

mula_pali:
349. Atha kho bhagavā uṭṭhahitvā āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ āmantesi – ‘sādhu sādhu, sāriputta, sādhu kho tvaṃ, sāriputta, bhikkhūnaṃ saṅgītipariyāyaṃ abhāsī’ti. Idamavocāyasmā sāriputto, samanuñño satthā ahosi. Attamanā te bhikkhū āyasmato sāriputtassa bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

Saṅgītisuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ dasamaṃ.
mula_english:
Then the Blessed One, having risen, addressed the Venerable Sāriputta, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta! Excellent indeed, Sāriputta, is the way you have spoken to the monks about the *saṅgīti-pariyāya* (sequence for reciting together)!"

This is what the Venerable Sāriputta said, and the Teacher approved.

The monks were pleased and delighted in the Venerable Sāriputta's words.

The *Saṅgīti Sutta* (Sequence for Recitation Discourse), the tenth, is complete.
commentary_pali:
349. Idha pana ṭhatvā pañhā samodhānetabbā. Imasmiñhi sutte ekakavasena dve pañhā kathitā. Dukavasena sattati. Tikavasena asītisataṃ. Catukkavasena dvesatāni. Pañcakavasena tiṃsasataṃ. Chakkavasena bāttiṃsasataṃ. Sattakavasena aṭṭhanavuti. Aṭṭhakavasena aṭṭhāsīti. Navakavasena catupaṇṇāsa. Dasakavasena samasaṭṭhīti evaṃ sahassaṃ cuddasa pañhā kathitā.

Imañhi suttantaṃ ṭhapetvā tepiṭake buddhavacane añño suttanto evaṃ bahupañhapaṭimaṇḍito natthi. Bhagavā imaṃ suttantaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya sakalaṃ sutvā cintesi – ‘‘dhammasenāpati sāriputto buddhabalaṃ dīpetvā appaṭivattiyaṃ sīhanādaṃ nadati. Sāvakabhāsitoti vutte okappanā na hoti, jinabhāsitoti vutte hoti, tasmā jinabhāsitaṃ katvā devamanussānaṃ okappanaṃ imasmiṃ suttante uppādessāmī’’ti. Tato vuṭṭhāya sādhukāraṃ adāsi. Tena vuttaṃ ‘‘atha kho bhagavā vuṭṭhahitvā āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ āmantesi, sādhu, sādhu, sāriputta, sādhu kho tvaṃ sāriputta, bhikkhūnaṃ saṅgītipariyāyaṃ abhāsī’’ti.

Tattha saṅgītipariyāyanti sāmaggiyā kāraṇaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ‘‘sādhu, kho tvaṃ, sāriputta, mama sabbaññutaññāṇena saṃsanditvā bhikkhūnaṃ sāmaggirasaṃ abhāsī’’ti. Samanuñño satthā ahosīti anumodanena samanuñño ahosi. Ettakena ayaṃ suttanto jinabhāsito nāma jāto. Desanāpariyosāne imaṃ suttantaṃ manasikarontā te bhikkhū arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsūti.

saṅgītipariyāya Samanuñño satthā ahosī

Sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Saṅgītisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
349. Here, after having stood, questions should be brought to a conclusion. In this *sutta*, two questions are spoken of in a singular way.
Seventy in a duality way.
Eighty along with a hundred in a triplicity way.
Two hundreds in a quadruplicity way.
Thirty along with a hundred in a quintuplicity way.
Thirty-two along with a hundred in a sextuplicity way.
Ninety-eight in a septuplicity way.
Eighty-eight in an octuplicity way.
Fifty-four in a nonuplicity way.
Sixty along with a hundred in a decuplicity way. Thus, one thousand four hundred questions are spoken of.

Indeed, setting aside this *suttanta*, in the *Tripiṭaka*, in the Buddha's word, there is no other *suttanta* thus adorned with many questions.
The Blessed One, having heard this entire *suttanta* from the beginning, reflected: "The general of the Dharma, Sāriputta, having illuminated the Buddha's power, roars the lion's roar that cannot be turned back.
If it is said "spoken by a disciple," conviction does not occur; if it is said "spoken by the Victor," it occurs; therefore, having made it spoken by the Victor, I will produce conviction in gods and humans in this *suttanta*."
Then, having risen, he gave applause.
By him it was said: "Then, the Blessed One, having risen, addressed the venerable Sāriputta, 'Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta, excellent, Sāriputta, you have spoken of the Saṅgīti-pariyāya to the monks.'"

There, *saṅgītipariyāya* means the cause of harmony.
This is said: "Excellent, Sāriputta, having harmonized with my all-knowing knowledge, you have spoken of the flavor of harmony to the monks."
*"The Teacher was in accordance"* means he was in accordance with approval.
By this much, this *suttanta* became named "spoken by the Victor."
At the end of the teaching, those monks, attending to this *suttanta*, attained Arhatship.

*Saṅgītipariyāya* *The Teacher was in accordance*
The Saṅgīti Sutta Commentary in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, Dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathā, is finished.

mula_pali:
350. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā campāyaṃ viharati gaggarāya pokkharaṇiyā tīre mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi. Tatra kho āyasmā sāriputto bhikkhū āmantesi – ‘‘āvuso bhikkhave’’ti! ‘‘Āvuso’’ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato sāriputtassa paccassosuṃ. Āyasmā sāriputto etadavoca –

‘‘Dasuttaraṃ pavakkhāmi, dhammaṃ nibbānapattiyā;

Dukkhassantakiriyāya, sabbaganthappamocanaṃ’’.

Eko dhammo
mula_english:
Thus have I heard.

On one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Campā on the banks of the Gaggarā Lake with a large community of monks, approximately five hundred monks in all.

There the venerable Śāriputra addressed the monks: "Friends, monks!" "Friend," those monks replied to the venerable Śāriputra. The venerable Śāriputra said this:

"I will explain the ten ascending qualities, the Dharma leading to the attainment of nirvāṇa,

for the ending of suffering, the complete release from all bonds."

One quality.
commentary_pali:
350.Evaṃme sutanti dasuttarasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ apubbapadavaṇṇanā – āvuso bhikkhaveti sāvakānaṃ ālapanametaṃ. Buddhā hi parisaṃ āmantayamānā ‘bhikkhave’ti vadanti. Sāvakā satthāraṃ uccaṭṭhāne ṭhapessāmāti satthu ālapanena anālapitvā āvusoti ālapanti. Te bhikkhūti te dhammasenāpatiṃ parivāretvā nisinnā bhikkhū. Ke pana te bhikkhūti? Anibaddhavāsā disāgamanīyā bhikkhū. Buddhakāle dve vāre bhikkhū sannipatanti – upakaṭṭhavassūpanāyikakāle ca pavāraṇakāle ca. Upakaṭṭhavassūpanāyikāya dasapi vīsatipi tiṃsampi cattālīsampi paññāsampi bhikkhū vaggā vaggā kammaṭṭhānatthāya āgacchanti. Bhagavā tehi saddhiṃ sammoditvā kasmā, bhikkhave, upakaṭṭhāya vassūpanāyikāya vicarathāti pucchati. Atha te ‘‘bhagavā kammaṭṭhānatthaṃ āgatamha, kammaṭṭhānaṃ no dethā’’ti yācanti.

Satthā tesaṃ cariyavasena rāgacaritassa asubhakammaṭṭhānaṃ deti. Dosacaritassa mettākammaṭṭhānaṃ, mohacaritassa uddeso paripucchā – ‘kālena dhammassavanaṃ, kālena dhammasākacchā, idaṃ tuyhaṃ sappāya’nti ācikkhati. Vitakkacaritassa ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ deti. Saddhācaritassa pasādanīyasuttante buddhasubodhiṃ dhammasudhammataṃ saṅghasuppaṭipattiñca pakāseti. Ñāṇacaritassa aniccatādipaṭisaṃyutte gambhīre suttante katheti. Te kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā sace sappāyaṃ hoti, tattheva vasanti. No ce hoti, sappāyaṃ senāsanaṃ pucchitvā gacchanti. Te tattha vasantā temāsikaṃ paṭipadaṃ gahetvā ghaṭetvā vāyamantā sotāpannāpi honti sakadāgāminopi anāgāminopi arahantopi.

Tato vutthavassā pavāretvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā ‘‘bhagavā ahaṃ tumhākaṃ santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā sotāpattiphalaṃ patto…pe… ahaṃ aggaphalaṃ arahatta’’nti paṭiladdhaguṇaṃ ārocenti. Tattha ime bhikkhū upakaṭṭhāya vassūpanāyikāya āgatā. Evaṃ āgantvā gacchante pana bhikkhū bhagavā aggasāvakānaṃ santikaṃ peseti, yathāha ‘‘apaloketha pana, bhikkhave, sāriputtamoggallāne’’ti. Bhikkhū ca vadanti ‘‘kiṃ nu kho mayaṃ, bhante, apalokema sāriputtamoggallāne’’ti (saṃ. ni. 3.2). Atha ne bhagavā tesaṃ dassane uyyojesi. ‘‘Sevatha, bhikkhave, sāriputtamoggallāne; bhajatha, bhikkhave, sāriputtamoggallāne. Paṇḍitā bhikkhū anuggāhakā sabrahmacārīnaṃ. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, janetā evaṃ sāriputto. Seyyathāpi jātassa āpādetā evaṃ moggallāno. Sāriputto, bhikkhave, sotāpattiphale vineti, moggallāno uttamatthe’’ti (ma. ni. 3.371).

Tadāpi bhagavā imehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ āsayaṃ upaparikkhanto ‘‘ime bhikkhū sāvakavineyyā’’ti addasa. Sāvakavineyyā nāma ye buddhānampi dhammadesanāya bujjhanti sāvakānampi. Buddhavineyyā pana sāvakā bodhetuṃ na sakkonti. Sāvakavineyyabhāvaṃ pana etesaṃ ñatvā katarassa bhikkhuno desanāya bujjhissantīti olokento sāriputtassāti disvā therassa santikaṃ pesesi. Thero te bhikkhū pucchi ‘‘satthu santikaṃ gatattha āvuso’’ti. ‘‘Āma, gatamha satthārā pana amhe tumhākaṃ santikaṃ pesitā’’ti. Tato thero ‘‘ime bhikkhū mayhaṃ desanāya bujjhissanti, kīdisī nu kho tesaṃ desanā vaṭṭatī’’ti cintento ‘‘ime bhikkhū samaggārāmā, sāmaggirasassa dīpikā nesaṃ desanā vaṭṭatī’’ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā tathārūpaṃ desanaṃ desetukāmo dasuttaraṃ pavakkhāmītiādimāha. Tattha dasadhā mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā vibhattoti dasuttaro, ekakato paṭṭhāya yāva dasakā gatotipi dasuttaro, ekekasmiṃ pabbe dasa dasa pañhā visesitātipi dasuttaro, taṃ dasuttaraṃ. Pavakkhāmīti kathessāmi. Dhammanti suttaṃ. Nibbānapattiyāti nibbānapaṭilābhatthāya. Dukkhassantakiriyāyāti sakalassa vaṭṭadukkhassa pariyantakaraṇatthaṃ. Sabbaganthappamocananti abhijjhākāyaganthādīnaṃ sabbaganthānaṃ pamocanaṃ.

Sāvakavineyyā Buddhavineyyā dasuttaraṃ pavakkhāmī dasuttaraṃ. Pavakkhāmī Dhamma Nibbānapattiyā Dukkhassantakiriyāyā Sabbaganthappamocana

Iti thero desanaṃ uccaṃ karonto bhikkhūnaṃ tattha pemaṃ janento evametaṃ uggahetabbaṃ pariyāpuṇitabbaṃ dhāretabbaṃ vācetabbaṃ maññissantīti catūhi padehi vaṇṇaṃ kathesi, ‘‘ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo’’tiādinā nayena tesaṃ tesaṃ suttānaṃ bhagavā viya.

Ekadhammavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
350. Thus have I heard: the Dasuttara Sutta.

Here begins the word-by-word commentary: "Āvuso bhikkhave," this is an address to the disciples. Buddhas, when addressing an assembly, say "bhikkhave". Disciples, thinking "we will place the Teacher in a high position," address the Teacher not with the Teacher's form of address, but with "āvuso".

"Te bhikkhū" means those monks who were sitting surrounding the general of the Dharma.

Who are those monks? Monks who do not have a fixed residence, monks who can come from any direction.

In the Buddha's time, monks would gather on two occasions: at the time for approaching the rains retreat, and at the time for the Pavāraṇā ceremony.

For the approaching rains retreat, groups of ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty monks would come, group by group, for the purpose of [receiving] a meditation subject.

The Blessed One, having greeted them, would ask, "Why, monks, do you wander for the approaching rains retreat?"

Then they would request, "Blessed One, we have come for a meditation subject; give us a meditation subject."

The Teacher would give them an unsuitable meditation subject according to their disposition.

To one of lustful disposition, he would give an impure meditation subject.

To one of hateful disposition, he would give a meditation subject of loving-kindness; to one of deluded disposition, instruction and questioning: "Listening to the Dharma at the right time, discussion of the Dharma at the right time, this is suitable for you," he would say.

To one of discursive disposition, he would give a meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing.

To one of faithful disposition, he would reveal the Buddha's good enlightenment, the Dharma's good nature, and the Sangha's good practice in the Pāsādanīya Suttanta.

To one of wise disposition, he would speak of profound suttas connected with impermanence and so on.

Having taken the meditation subject, if it is suitable, they would stay right there.

If it is not, they would ask about a suitable dwelling and leave.

Staying there, taking up the three-month practice, striving and endeavoring, they would become stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, or arahants.

Then, having completed the rains retreat, having performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, going to the Teacher's presence, they would announce, "Blessed One, having taken a meditation subject in your presence, I have attained the fruit of stream-entry...pe...I have attained the highest fruit, arahantship," they would announce the qualities they had regained.

There, these monks had come for the approaching rains retreat.

When these monks had come and were leaving, the Blessed One sent [them] to the presence of the chief disciples, as he said, "Consult Sāriputta and Moggallāna, monks."

And the monks would say, "What should we consult Sāriputta and Moggallāna about, venerable sir?" (Saṃ. Ni. 3.2).

Then the Blessed One urged them to see them.

"Associate with Sāriputta and Moggallāna, monks; keep company with Sāriputta and Moggallāna.

They are wise monks who assist those living the spiritual life.

Sāriputta is just like one who gives birth, monks.

Moggallāna is just like a wet nurse to the one new-born, monks;

Sāriputta trains others for the fruit of stream-entry, Moggallāna for the supreme goal" (Ma. Ni. 3.
371).

Even then, the Blessed One, after exchanging courteous greetings with these monks, examining the inclinations of those monks, saw that "these monks are capable of being guided by disciples (*sāvakavineyyā*)."

*Sāvakavineyyā* means those who understand the Dharma teaching of the Buddhas and also of the disciples.

However, those capable of being guided by Buddhas (*buddhavineyyā*) are not able to be awakened by disciples.

Knowing their state of being capable of being guided by disciples, considering which monk's teaching they would understand, seeing that it was Sāriputta's, he sent [them] to the elder's presence.

The elder asked those monks, "Have you gone to the Teacher's presence, friends?"

"Yes, we have gone, but the Teacher has sent us to your presence."

Then the elder, thinking, "These monks will understand my teaching; what kind of teaching is suitable for them?" decided, "These monks delight in harmony; a teaching that illuminates the essence of harmony is suitable for them," and desiring to teach such a teaching, he said, beginning with "*dasuttaraṃ pavakkhāmī*."

There, *dasuttara*, because he established the matrix in ten ways and divided [it]; *dasuttara* also because [he] went from the one to the tens; *dasuttara* also because ten questions were distinguished in each section; that *dasuttaraṃ*.

*Pavakkhāmī* means I will tell.

*Dhamma* means discourse (*sutta*).

*Nibbānapattiyā* means for the purpose of attaining *nirvāṇa*.

*Dukkhassantakiriyāyā* means for the purpose of making an end to all the suffering of the cycle [of rebirth] (*vaṭṭa*).

*Sabbaganthappamocana* means the freeing from all bonds (*gantha*), beginning with the bond of covetousness (*abhijjhā*).

*sāvakavineyyā*, *buddhavineyyā*, *dasuttaraṃ pavakkhāmī*, *dasuttaraṃ pavakkhāmī*, *dhamma*, *nibbānapattiyā*, *dukkhassantakiriyāyā*, *sabbaganthappamocana*

Thus, the elder, raising his voice in teaching, generating affection for the monks there, thinking, "They will grasp this, learn it, remember it, recite it," described the qualities with four phrases, like the Blessed One regarding those discourses in the manner beginning with "This is the one way, monks."

Explanation of the One Dharma

mula_pali:
351. ‘‘Eko, āvuso, dhammo bahukāro, eko dhammo bhāvetabbo, eko dhammo pariññeyyo, eko dhammo pahātabbo, eko dhammo hānabhāgiyo, eko dhammo visesabhāgiyo, eko dhammo duppaṭivijjho, eko dhammo uppādetabbo, eko dhammo abhiññeyyo, eko dhammo sacchikātabbo.

(Ka) ‘‘katamo eko dhammo bahukāro? Appamādo kusalesu dhammesu. Ayaṃ eko dhammo bahukāro.

bahukāro?

mula_english:
351. “One *dhamma*, friends, is very helpful. One *dhamma* should be developed. One *dhamma* should be comprehended. One *dhamma* should be abandoned. One *dhamma* is on the side of decline. One *dhamma* is on the side of distinction. One *dhamma* is hard to penetrate. One *dhamma* should be made to arise. One *dhamma* should be directly known. One *dhamma* should be realized.

(ka) “What is the one *dhamma* that is very helpful (*bahukāro*)? It is diligence (*appamāda*) in wholesome qualities (*kusalesu dhammesu*). This one *dhamma* is very helpful.

(kha) “What is the one *dhamma* that should be developed (*bhāvetabbo*)? Mindfulness occupied with the body (*kāyagatāsati*) accompanied by pleasure (*sātasahagatā*). This one *dhamma* should be developed.

(ga) “What is the one *dhamma* that should be comprehended (*pariññeyyo*)? Contact (*phasso*) that has cankers (*sāsavo*) and is connected with clinging (*upādāniyo*). This one *dhamma* should be comprehended.

(gha) “What is the one *dhamma* that should be abandoned (*pahātabbo*)? The conceit ‘I am’ (*asmimāno*). This one *dhamma* should be abandoned.

(ṅa) “What is the one *dhamma* that is on the side of decline (*hānabhāgiyo*)? Unwise attention (*ayoniso manasikāro*). This one *dhamma* is on the side of decline.

(ca) “What is the one *dhamma* that is on the side of distinction (*visesabhāgiyo*)? Wise attention (*yoniso manasikāro*). This one *dhamma* is on the side of distinction.

(cha) “What is the one *dhamma* that is hard to penetrate (*duppaṭivijjho*)? The concentration of mind that is immediately succeeding (*ānantariko cetosamādhi*). This one *dhamma* is hard to penetrate.

(ja) “What is the one *dhamma* that should be made to arise (*uppādetabbo*)? Unshakable knowledge (*akuppaṃ ñāṇaṃ*). This one *dhamma* should be made to arise.

(jha) “What is the one *dhamma* that should be directly known (*abhiññeyyo*)? All beings subsist on nutriment (*sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā*). This one *dhamma* should be directly known.

(ña) “What is the one *dhamma* that should be realized (*sacchikātabbo*)? Unshakable liberation of mind (*akuppā cetovimutti*). This one *dhamma* should be realized.

“Thus, these ten *dhammas* are real, true, actual, not false, not otherwise, rightly awakened to by the Tathāgata.

Two *dhammas*.

commentary_english:
351. (ka) *tatra* **bahukāro**ti *bahūpakāro*: There, *bahukāro* means greatly beneficial.
(kha) **bhāvetabbo**ti *vaḍḍhetabbo*: *bhāvetabbo* means to be developed.
**bhāvetabbo** (ga) **pariññeyyo**ti *tīhi pariññāhi parijānitabbo*: *pariññeyyo* means to be known by way of the three kinds of full knowledge.
**pariññeyyo** (gha) **pahātabbo**ti *pahānānupassanāya pajahitabbo*: *pahātabbo* means to be abandoned by way of contemplating abandonment.
**pahātabbo** (ṅa) **hānabhāgiyo**ti *apāyagāmiparihānāya saṃvattanako*: *hānabhāgiyo* means conducive to the decline of going to unfortunate states of existence.
**hānabhāgiyo** (ca) **visesabhāgiyo**ti *visesagāmivisesāya saṃvattanako*: *visesabhāgiyo* means conducive to a special going to a distinction.
**visesabhāgiyo** (cha) **duppaṭivijjho**ti *duppaccakkhakaro*: *duppaṭivijjho* means difficult to directly realize.
**duppaṭivijjho** (ja) **uppādetabbo**ti *nipphādetabbo*: *uppādetabbo* means to be produced.
**uppādetabbo** (jha) **abhiññeyyo**ti *ñātapariññāya abhijānitabbo*: *abhiññeyyo* means to be thoroughly known by way of knowledge and full knowledge.
**abhiññeyyo** (ña) **sacchikātabbo**ti *paccakkhaṃ kātabbo*: *sacchikātabbo* means to be directly experienced.
**sacchikātabbo** In this way, the meaning should be understood for all the matrices.
Thus, venerable Śāriputra, just as a skilled bamboo worker, having cut a bamboo that is in front of him, having made knots, having made ten parts, making each individual part into a diamond, diamond, splits [it]. Just so, having examined the suitable teaching for those monks, having established the matrix tenfold, dividing each individual passage into individual words, he began to expand the teaching by way of the method that begins with, "Which one quality is greatly beneficial, mindfulness in wholesome qualities?"
There, **appamādo kusalesu dhammesū**ti he spoke of mindfulness, which is universally helpful and beneficial, in wholesome qualities.
Indeed, this mindfulness is greatly beneficial in wholesome qualities by way of the faultless aspect in all of them, such as the fulfillment of ethical conduct, restraint of the senses, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, the seven good qualities, causing the womb of insight to be conceived, the kinds of analytical understanding, the aggregates of the five qualities, namely the aggregate of ethical conduct, and so forth, proper and improper situations, the attainment of great monastic tranquility, the noble truths, the kinds of mindfulness, and so forth, the factors of enlightenment, the kinds of insight-wisdom, and so forth, and the eight kinds of knowledge.
**appamādo kusalesu dhammesū** Because of this, the Blessed One declared, "In as much as there are beings that are footless, and so forth… the *Tathāgata* is declared to be the foremost of them."
Just so, monks, whatever wholesome qualities there are, all of those have mindfulness as their root, mindfulness as their confluence; mindfulness is declared to be the foremost of those qualities." And so forth, by way of the method (Saṃ.
Ni.
5.
139), using comparisons to footprints of elephants, and so forth, the Connected Discourses praises manifold in the section on mindfulness.
Having summarized all of that in one phrase, the elder said, "Mindfulness in wholesome qualities."
In the Dhammapada, the great benefit of mindfulness should be shown by way of the section on mindfulness.
It should also be shown by way of the story of Aśoka -
In the Connected Discourses, in the section on mindfulness, in the Dhammapada (ka) King Aśoka, having heard the verse of the novice Nigrodha, "Mindfulness is the path to the immortal," having been pleased by the novice, made eighty-four thousand monasteries, saying, "Stay, dear one, the Buddha's word of the three baskets has been spoken by you to me."
Thus, the great benefit of mindfulness should be spoken by a monk endowed with strength, having shown it by way of the three baskets.
Whoever, bringing any discourse or verse for the purpose of illuminating mindfulness, should not be spoken to, "You are bringing [it] standing in an improper place; you are a runaway with an improper ford."
Here, the strength and power and measure are for the preacher of the Dharma.
(kha) **kāyagatāsatī**ti *ānāpānaṃ catuiriyāpatho satisampajaññaṃ dvattiṃsākāro catudhātuvavatthānaṃ dasa asubhā nava sivathikā cuṇṇikamanasikāro kesādīsu cattāri rūpajjhānānīti ettha uppannasatiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ*: **kāyagatāsatī** means mindfulness related to the body, that is, mindfulness on inhalation and exhalation, the four postures, mindfulness and clear comprehension, the thirty-two parts [of the body], the four elements analyzed, the ten unattractive objects, the nine charnel grounds, mindfulness directed toward powderiness, the four form *jhānas*, beginning with the hair: in these cases, this is a designation for mindfulness that has arisen.
**sātasahagatā**ti ṭhapetvā catutthajjhānaṃ aññattha sātasahagatā hoti sukhasampayuttā, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ: **sātasahagatā** means excluding the fourth *jhāna*, elsewhere being connected to pleasure is connected to happiness; having this in mind, this is said.
**kāyagatāsatī** **sātasahagatā** (ga) **sāsavo upādāniyo**ti *āsavānañceva upādānānañca paccayabhūto*: **sāsavo upādāniyo** means being the cause of defilements and also of grasping.
iti tebhūmakadhammameva niyameti: Thus, it determines only the qualities of the three realms.
**sāsavo upādāniyo** (gha) **asmimāno**ti *rūpādīsu asmīti māno*: **asmimāno** means the conceit of "I am" in the aggregates and so forth.
*asmimāno*: (ṅa) *ayoniso manasikāro* means unwisely applied thought, which arises through the tendency to consider the impermanent as permanent, and so on, is an ill-directed application of thought.

*ayoniso manasikāro*: (ca) Conversely, *yoniso manasikāro* should be understood as its opposite.

*yoniso manasikāro*: (cha) *ānantariko cetosamādhī*: elsewhere, the immediately succeeding fruition of the path is called *ānantariko cetosamādhi*. Here, however, *ānantariko cetosamādhī* refers to the path immediately succeeding insight, or because of its immediacy to insight, or because it immediately gives its own fruit.

*ānantariko cetosamādhī*: (ja) *akuppaṃ ñāṇa* means elsewhere, the knowledge of fruition is called unshakable knowledge. Here, reflective knowledge is intended.

*akuppaṃ ñāṇa*: (jha) *āhāraṭṭhitikā* means dependent on conditions. *ayaṃ eko dhammo* means the condition by which they endure, this one thing, should be known by the diagnosis as knowledge.

*āhāraṭṭhitikā ayaṃ eko dhammo*: (ña) *akuppā cetovimuttī* means the liberation that is the fruition of Arahatship.

*akuppā cetovimuttī*: In this instance, diagnosis as knowledge has been described with regard to direct knowledge. By diagnosis, the full understanding by scrutinization is meant. By what should be abandoned and what should be directly experienced, the diagnosis as abandoning is meant. *duppaṭivijjho*: Here, the path has been described. *sacchikātabbo*: The fruit has been described; the path is obtained in a single instance, but the fruit is obtained in many instances.

*duppaṭivijjho sacchikātabbo*: *bhūtā* means existing in reality. *tacchā* means truly. *tathā* means having such a nature as has been described. *avitathā* means what has been described does not become otherwise. *anaññathā* means not otherwise than the manner described. *sammā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā* means the *tathāgata*, sitting on the seat of enlightenment, through reason and cause, has himself fully awakened, known, understood, and directly experienced [these things]. By this, the Elder, showing the Jina discourse, "These things are fully awakened by the *tathāgata*, but I am like a scribe reading to your king," generated confidence.

*bhūtā tacchā tathā avitathā anaññathā sammā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā*: The explanation of a single thing is finished.

Explanation of two things
