mula_english:
352. “Two *dharmas*, friends, are very helpful. Two *dharmas* should be developed. Two *dharmas* should be comprehended. Two *dharmas* should be abandoned, two *dharmas* are on the side of decline, two *dharmas* are on the side of distinction, two *dharmas* are hard to penetrate, two *dharmas* should be made to arise, two *dharmas* should be directly known, two *dharmas* should be realized.

(ka) “What are the two *dharmas* that are very helpful? Mindfulness (*smṛti*) and clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*). These two *dharmas* are very helpful.

(kha) “What are the two *dharmas* that should be developed? Serenity (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). These two *dharmas* should be developed.

(ga) “What are the two *dharmas* that should be comprehended? Name (*nāma*) and form (*rūpa*). These two *dharmas* should be comprehended.

(gha) “What are the two *dharmas* that should be abandoned? Ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*). These two *dharmas* should be abandoned.

(ṅa) “What are the two *dharmas* that are on the side of decline? Ungovernability and bad companionship. These two *dharmas* are on the side of decline.

(ca) “What are the two *dharmas* that are on the side of distinction? Governability and good companionship. These two *dharmas* are on the side of distinction.

(cha) “What are the two *dharmas* that are hard to penetrate? The cause and the condition for the defilement of beings, and the cause and the condition for the purification of beings. These two *dharmas* are hard to penetrate.

(ja) “What are the two *dharmas* that should be made to arise? Two knowledges (*jñāna*)—the knowledge of destruction (*kṣaye jñānaṃ*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāde jñānaṃ*). These two *dharmas* should be made to arise.

(jha) “What are the two *dharmas* that should be directly known (*abhijñeyyā*)? Two elements (*dhātu*)—the conditioned element (*saṃkhata dhātu*) and the unconditioned element (*asaṃkhata dhātu*). These two *dharmas* should be directly known.

(ña) “What are the two *dharmas* that should be realized? Knowledge (*vidyā*) and liberation (*vimukti*). These two *dharmas* should be realized.

“Thus, these twenty *dharmas*—true (*bhūta*), genuine (*taccha*), real (*tathā*), not unreal (*avitathā*), not otherwise (*anaññathā*)—have been rightly awakened to by the *Tathāgata*.

Three *dharmas*
commentary_pali:
352. (Ka) ime dve dhammā bahukārāti ime dve satisampajaññā dhammā sīlapūraṇādīsu appamādo viya sabbattha upakārakā hitāvahā.

(Kha) samathoca vipassanā cāti ime dve saṅgītisutte lokiyalokuttarā kathitā. Imasmiṃ dasuttarasutte pubbabhāgā kathitā.

samatho ca vipassanā cā

(Cha) sattānaṃ saṃkilesāya sattānaṃ visuddhiyāti ayoniso manasikāro hetu ceva paccayo ca sattānaṃ saṃkilesāya, yoniso manasikāro visuddhiyā. Tathā dovacassatā pāpamittatā saṃkilesāya; sovacassatā kalyāṇamittatā visuddhiyā. Tathā tīṇi akusalamūlāni; tīṇi kusalamūlāni. Cattāro yogā cattāro visaṃyogā. Pañca cetokhilā pañcindriyāni. Cha agāravā cha gāravā. Satta asaddhammā satta saddhammā. Aṭṭha kusītavatthūni aṭṭha ārambhavatthūni. Nava āghātavatthūni nava āghātappaṭivinayā. Dasa akusalakammapathā dasa kusalakammapathāti evaṃ pabhedā ime dve dhammā duppaṭivijjhāti veditabbā.

sattānaṃ saṃkilesāya sattānaṃ visuddhiyā

(Jha) saṅkhatā dhātūti paccayehi katā pañcakkhandhā. Asaṅkhatā dhātūti paccayehi akataṃ nibbānaṃ.

saṅkhatā dhātū

(Ña) vijjā ca vimutti cāti ettha vijjāti tisso vijjā. Vimuttīti arahattaphalaṃ.

vijjā ca vimutti cā vijjā Vimuttī

Imasmiṃ vāre abhiññādīni ekakasadisāneva, uppādetabbapade pana maggo kathito, sacchikātabbapade phalaṃ.

Dvedhammavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Tayodhammavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
352. (ka) *Ime dve dhammā bahukārā* means these two qualities of mindfulness and clear comprehension (satisampajaññā) are beneficial and conducive to welfare everywhere, like diligence (appamāda) in the fulfillment of morality (sīla), etc.

(kha) *Samatho ca vipassanā cā* means these two, serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), are spoken of in the Saṅgīti Sutta as mundane (lokiya) and supramundane (lokuttara). In this Dasuttara Sutta, their preliminary aspects are discussed.

*Samatho ca vipassanā cā*

(cha) *Sattānaṃ saṃkilesāya sattānaṃ visuddhiyā* means unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāro) is both the cause (hetu) and condition (paccayo) for the defilement (saṃkilesāya) of beings, while wise attention (yoniso manasikāro) is for their purification (visuddhiyā). Similarly, disobedience (dovacassatā) and bad friendship (pāpamittatā) are for defilement; obedience (sovacassatā) and good friendship (kalyāṇamittatā) are for purification. Likewise, the three unwholesome roots (tīṇi akusalamūlāni); the three wholesome roots (tīṇi kusalamūlāni); the four yokes (cattāro yogā); the four unyokings (cattāro visaṃyogā); the five mental blockages (pañca cetokhilā); the five faculties (pañcindriyāni); the six kinds of disrespect (cha agāravā); the six kinds of respect (cha gāravā); the seven unwholesome qualities (satta asaddhammā); the seven wholesome qualities (satta saddhammā); the eight grounds for laziness (aṭṭha kusītavatthūni); the eight grounds for arousing effort (aṭṭha ārambhavatthūni); the nine grounds for resentment (nava āghātavatthūni); the nine ways to overcome resentment (nava āghātappaṭivinayā); the ten unwholesome courses of action (dasa akusalakammapathā); the ten wholesome courses of action (dasa kusalakammapathā). Thus, the distinctions of these two qualities should be understood as difficult to penetrate (duppaṭivijjhāti).

*Sattānaṃ saṃkilesāya sattānaṃ visuddhiyā*

(jha) *Saṅkhatā dhātū* means the conditioned element (saṅkhata dhātu) are the five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā) made by conditions (paccayehi katā). The unconditioned element (asaṅkhatā dhātū) is nirvāṇa (nibbānaṃ) which is unmade by conditions (paccayehi akataṃ).

*Saṅkhatā dhātū*

(ña) *Vijjā ca vimutti cā* means here, *vijjā* is the three kinds of knowledge (tisso vijjā). *Vimuttī* is the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphalaṃ).

*Vijjā ca vimutti cā* *Vijjā* *Vimuttī*

In this section, the higher knowledges (abhiññā), etc., are similar to the single ones, but in the section on what should be produced, the path (maggo) is spoken of, and in the section on what should be realized, the fruit (phalaṃ).

The Dvedhammavaṇṇanā is finished.

Tayodhammavaṇṇanā

mula_pali:
353. ‘‘Tayo dhammā bahukārā, tayo dhammā bhāvetabbā…pe… tayo dhammā sacchikātabbā.

(Ka) ‘‘katame tayo dhammā bahukārā? Sappurisasaṃsevo, saddhammassavanaṃ, dhammānudhammappaṭipatti. Ime tayo dhammā bahukārā.

bahukārā?

(Kha) ‘‘katame tayo dhammā bhāvetabbā? Tayo samādhī – savitakko savicāro samādhi, avitakko vicāramatto samādhi, avitakko avicāro samādhi. Ime tayo dhammā bhāvetabbā.

bhāvetabbā?

(Ga) ‘‘katame tayo dhammā pariññeyyā? Tisso vedanā – sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā. Ime tayo dhammā pariññeyyā.

pariññeyyā?

(Gha) ‘‘katame tayo dhammā pahātabbā? Tisso taṇhā – kāmataṇhā, bhavataṇhā, vibhavataṇhā. Ime tayo dhammā pahātabbā.

pahātabbā?

(Ṅa) ‘‘katame tayo dhammā hānabhāgiyā? Tīṇi akusalamūlāni – lobho akusalamūlaṃ, doso akusalamūlaṃ, moho akusalamūlaṃ. Ime tayo dhammā hānabhāgiyā.

hānabhāgiyā?

(Ca) ‘‘katame tayo dhammā visesabhāgiyā? Tīṇi kusalamūlāni – alobho kusalamūlaṃ, adoso kusalamūlaṃ, amoho kusalamūlaṃ. Ime tayo dhammā visesabhāgiyā.

visesabhāgiyā?

(Cha) ‘‘katame tayo dhammā duppaṭivijjhā? Tisso nissaraṇiyā dhātuyo – kāmānametaṃ nissaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ nekkhammaṃ, rūpānametaṃ nissaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ arūpaṃ, yaṃ kho pana kiñci bhūtaṃ saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppannaṃ, nirodho tassa nissaraṇaṃ. Ime tayo dhammā duppaṭivijjhā.

duppaṭivijjhā?

(Ja) ‘‘katame tayo dhammā uppādetabbā? Tīṇi ñāṇāni – atītaṃse ñāṇaṃ, anāgataṃse ñāṇaṃ, paccuppannaṃse ñāṇaṃ. Ime tayo dhammā uppādetabbā.

uppādetabbā?

(Jha) ‘‘katame tayo dhammā abhiññeyyā? Tisso dhātuyo – kāmadhātu, rūpadhātu, arūpadhātu. Ime tayo dhammā abhiññeyyā.

abhiññeyyā?

(Ña) ‘‘katame tayo dhammā sacchikātabbā? Tisso vijjā – pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ vijjā, sattānaṃ cutūpapāte ñāṇaṃ vijjā, āsavānaṃ khaye ñāṇaṃ vijjā. Ime tayo dhammā sacchikātabbā.

sacchikātabbā?

‘‘Iti ime tiṃsa dhammā bhūtā tacchā tathā avitathā anaññathā sammā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā.

Cattāro dhammā
mula_english:
“Three dhammas, friends, are very helpful. Three dhammas should be developed…pe… Three dhammas should be realized.”

(ka) “Which three *dharmas* are very helpful? Association with good people ( *satpuruṣa*), hearing the good *dharma* ( *saddharma*), and practicing the *dharma* in accordance with the *dharma*. These three *dharmas* are very helpful."

(kha) "Which three *dharmas* should be developed? Three kinds of concentration (*samādhi*): concentration with initial application and sustained application of thought (*savitakko savicāro samādhi*), concentration without initial application but with sustained application of thought (*avitakko vicāramatto samādhi*), concentration without initial application and without sustained application of thought (*avitakko avicāro samādhi*). These three *dharmas* should be developed."

(ga) "Which three *dharmas* should be fully understood? Three kinds of feeling (*vedanā*): pleasant feeling (*sukhā vedanā*), painful feeling (*duḥkhā vedanā*), neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*adukkhamasukhā vedanā*). These three *dharmas* should be fully understood."

(gha) "Which three *dharmas* should be abandoned? Three kinds of craving (*taṇhā*): craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmataṇhā*), craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*), craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*). These three *dharmas* should be abandoned."

(ṅa) "Which three *dharmas* are on the side of decline? Three unwholesome roots (*akusalamūlāni*): greed (*lobho*), an unwholesome root; hatred (*doso*), an unwholesome root; delusion (*moho*), an unwholesome root. These three *dharmas* are on the side of decline."

(ca) "Which three *dharmas* are on the side of distinction? Three wholesome roots (*kusalamūlāni*): non-greed (*alobho*) is a wholesome root; non-hatred (*adoso*) is a wholesome root; non-delusion (*amoho*) is a wholesome root. These three *dharmas* are on the side of distinction."

(cha) "Which three *dharmas* are hard to penetrate? Three liberating elements (*nissaraṇiyā dhātuyo*): the liberation from sense pleasures is renunciation (*nekkhammaṃ*); the liberation from form is the formless (*arūpaṃ*); and whatever is conditioned (*saṅkhataṃ*), created (*bhūtaṃ*), dependently arisen (*paṭiccasamuppannaṃ*), its cessation (*nirodho*) is the liberation. These three *dharmas* are hard to penetrate."

(ja) "Which three *dharmas* should be made to arise? Three knowledges (*ñāṇāni*): knowledge of the past (*atītaṃse ñāṇaṃ*), knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃse ñāṇaṃ*), knowledge of the present (*paccuppannaṃse ñāṇaṃ*). These three *dharmas* should be made to arise."

(jha) "Which three *dharmas* should be directly known? Three realms (*dhātuyo*): the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the formless realm (*arūpadhātu*). These three *dharmas* should be directly known."

(ña) "Which three *dharmas* should be realized? Three knowledges (*tisso vijjā*): the knowledge of remembering past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ*) is knowledge; the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings (*sattānaṃ cutūpapāte ñāṇaṃ*) is knowledge; the knowledge of the destruction of the *āsavas* (*āsavānaṃ khaye ñāṇaṃ*) is knowledge. These three *dharmas* should be realized."

"Thus, these thirty *dharmas*—true, genuine, real, not unreal, not otherwise—have been rightly awakened to by the *Tathāgata*."

Four *dharmas*
commentary_pali:
353. (Cha) kāmānametaṃ nissaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ nekkhammanti ettha nekkhammanti anāgāmimaggo adhippeto. So hi sabbaso kāmānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ. Rūpānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ āruppanti ettha āruppepi arahattamaggo. Puna uppattinivāraṇato sabbaso rūpānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ nāma. Nirodho tassanissaraṇanti idha arahattaphalaṃ nirodhoti adhippetaṃ. Arahattaphalena hi nibbāne diṭṭhe puna āyatiṃ sabbasaṅkhārā na hontīti arahattaṃ saṅkhatanirodhassa paccayattā nirodhoti vuttaṃ.

(Ja) atītaṃse ñāṇanti atītaṃsārammaṇaṃ ñāṇaṃ itaresupi eseva nayo.

atītaṃse ñāṇa

Imasmimpi vāre abhiññādayo ekakasadisāva. Duppaṭivijjhapade pana maggo kathito, sacchikātabbe phalaṃ.

Tayodhammavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Cattārodhammavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
(cha) "kāmānametaṃ nissaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ nekkhamma" here, "nekkhamma" means the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
For that is utterly the escape from desires (*kāma*).
"rūpānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ āruppa" here, even in the formless realms (*āruppa*), it is the path of *arhatship*.
Since it prevents further rebirth, it is called the utter escape from forms (*rūpa*).
"nirodho tassa nissaraṇaṃ" here, *nirodha* means the fruit of *arhatship*.
For when *nirvāṇa* is seen by the fruit of *arhatship*, all conditioned things (*saṅkhārā*) do not arise again in the future. Therefore, *arhatship* is said to be *nirodha* because it is the cause of the cessation of conditioned things.

(ja) "atītaṃse ñāṇa" means knowledge (*ñāṇa*) with a past object. The same method applies to the others as well.

"atītaṃse ñāṇa" in this instance as well, the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) etc. are similar to being alone.
However, in the difficult-to-penetrate state, the path is described, and the fruit is to be realized.

The explanation of the three teachings is finished.

Explanation of the four teachings

mula_pali:
354. ‘‘Cattāro dhammā bahukārā, cattāro dhammā bhāvetabbā…pe… cattāro dhammā sacchikātabbā.

(Ka) ‘‘katame cattāro dhammā bahukārā? Cattāri cakkāni – patirūpadesavāso, sappurisūpanissayo sappurisupassayo (syā. kaṃ.), attasammāpaṇidhi, pubbe ca katapuññatā. Ime cattāro dhammā bahukārā.

bahukārā? sappurisupassayo (syā. kaṃ.)

(Kha) ‘‘katame cattāro dhammā bhāvetabbā? Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā – idhāvuso, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Vedanāsu…pe… citte… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ime cattāro dhammā bhāvetabbā.

bhāvetabbā?

(Ga) ‘‘katame cattāro dhammā pariññeyyā? Cattāro āhārā – kabaḷīkāro kavaḷīkāro (syā. kaṃ.) āhāro oḷāriko vā sukhumo vā, phasso dutiyo, manosañcetanā tatiyā, viññāṇaṃ catutthaṃ. Ime cattāro dhammā pariññeyyā.

pariññeyyā? kavaḷīkāro (syā. kaṃ.)

(Gha) ‘‘katame cattāro dhammā pahātabbā? Cattāro oghā – kāmogho, bhavogho, diṭṭhogho, avijjogho. Ime cattāro dhammā pahātabbā.

pahātabbā?

(Ṅa) ‘‘katame cattāro dhammā hānabhāgiyā? Cattāro yogā – kāmayogo, bhavayogo, diṭṭhiyogo, avijjāyogo. Ime cattāro dhammā hānabhāgiyā.

hānabhāgiyā?

(Ca) ‘‘katame cattāro dhammā visesabhāgiyā? Cattāro visaññogā – kāmayogavisaṃyogo, bhavayogavisaṃyogo, diṭṭhiyogavisaṃyogo, avijjāyogavisaṃyogo. Ime cattāro dhammā visesabhāgiyā.

visesabhāgiyā?

(Cha) ‘‘katame cattāro dhammā duppaṭivijjhā? Cattāro samādhī – hānabhāgiyo samādhi, ṭhitibhāgiyo samādhi, visesabhāgiyo samādhi, nibbedhabhāgiyo samādhi. Ime cattāro dhammā duppaṭivijjhā.

duppaṭivijjhā?

(Ja) ‘‘katame cattāro dhammā uppādetabbā? Cattāri ñāṇāni – dhamme ñāṇaṃ, anvaye ñāṇaṃ, pariye ñāṇaṃ, sammutiyā ñāṇaṃ. Ime cattāro dhammā uppādetabbā.

uppādetabbā?

(Jha) ‘‘katame cattāro dhammā abhiññeyyā? Cattāri ariyasaccāni – dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhasamudayaṃ dukkhasamudayo (syā. kaṃ.) ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhanirodhaṃ dukkhanirodho (syā. kaṃ.) ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ. Ime cattāro dhammā abhiññeyyā.

abhiññeyyā? dukkhasamudayo (syā. kaṃ.) dukkhanirodho (syā. kaṃ.)

(Ña) ‘‘katame cattāro dhammā sacchikātabbā? Cattāri sāmaññaphalāni – sotāpattiphalaṃ, sakadāgāmiphalaṃ, anāgāmiphalaṃ, arahattaphalaṃ . Ime cattāro dhammā sacchikātabbā.

sacchikātabbā?

‘‘Iti ime cattārīsadhammā bhūtā tacchā tathā avitathā anaññathā sammā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā.

Pañca dhammā
mula_english:
354. “Four *dhammas*, friends, are very helpful. Four *dhammas* should be developed… Four *dhammas* should be directly known.

(a) “Which four *dhammas* are very helpful (*bahukārā*)? The four wheels: living in a suitable region, reliance on noble persons (*sappurisūpanissayo*), setting oneself in the right direction, and past merit. These four *dhammas* are very helpful.

(b) “Which four *dhammas* should be developed (*bhāvetabbā*)? The four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhānā*): Here, monks, a monk abides contemplating body as body, ardent, clearly aware and mindful, having put aside hankering and fretting for the world; he abides contemplating feelings… mind… mind-objects as mind-objects, ardent, clearly aware and mindful, having put aside hankering and fretting for the world. These four *dhammas* should be developed.

(c) “Which four *dhammas* should be fully understood (*pariññeyyā*)? The four nutriments (*āhārā*): edible food (*kabaḷīkāro āhāro*), gross (*oḷāriko*) or subtle, contact as the second, mental volition as the third, and consciousness as the fourth. These four *dhammas* should be fully understood.

(d) “Which four *dhammas* should be abandoned (*pahātabbā*)? The four floods (*oghā*): the flood of sensuality (*kāmogho*), the flood of becoming (*bhavogho*), the flood of views (*diṭṭhogho*), the flood of ignorance (*avijjogho*). These four *dhammas* should be abandoned.

(e) “Which four *dhammas* are on the side of decline (*hānabhāgiyā*)? The four bonds (*yogā*): the bond of sensuality (*kāmayogo*), the bond of becoming (*bhavayogo*), the bond of views (*diṭṭhiyogo*), the bond of ignorance (*avijjāyogo*). These four *dhammas* are on the side of decline.

(f) “Which four *dhammas* are on the side of distinction (*visesabhāgiyā*)? The four detachments (*visaññogā*): detachment from the bond of sensuality (*kāmayogavisaṃyogo*), detachment from the bond of becoming (*bhavayogavisaṃyogo*), detachment from the bond of views (*diṭṭhiyogavisaṃyogo*), detachment from the bond of ignorance (*avijjāyogavisaṃyogo*). These four *dhammas* are on the side of distinction.

(g) “Which four *dhammas* are hard to penetrate (*duppaṭivijjhā*)? The four concentrations (*samādhī*): concentration on the side of decline (*hānabhāgiyo samādhi*), concentration on the side of stability (*ṭhitibhāgiyo samādhi*), concentration on the side of distinction (*visesabhāgiyo samādhi*), concentration on the side of penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiyo samādhi*). These four *dhammas* are hard to penetrate.

(h) “Which four *dhammas* should be made to arise (*uppādetabbā*)? The four knowledges (*ñāṇāni*): knowledge of the Dhamma (*dhamme ñāṇaṃ*), knowledge of inference (*anvaye ñāṇaṃ*), knowledge of language (*pariye ñāṇaṃ*), knowledge of convention (*sammutiyā ñāṇaṃ*). These four *dhammas* should be made to arise.

(i) “Which four *dhammas* should be directly known (*abhiññeyyā*)? The four Noble Truths (*ariyasaccāni*): the noble truth of suffering (*dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ*), the noble truth of the origin of suffering (*dukkhasamudayaṃ ariyasaccaṃ*), the noble truth of the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ*), the noble truth of the path to the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodhagāminīpaṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ*). These four *dhammas* should be directly known.
The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering (dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ). These four *dharmas* should be directly known (ime cattāro dhammā abhiññeyyā).

Which four *dharmas* should be realized (sacchikātabbā)? The four fruits of the contemplative life (cattāri sāmaññaphalāni): the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphalaṃ), the fruit of once-returning (sakadāgāmiphalaṃ), the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphalaṃ), the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphalaṃ). These four *dharmas* should be realized (ime cattāro dhammā sacchikātabbā).

Thus, these forty *dharmas*—true, genuine, real, not unreal, not otherwise—have been rightly awakened to by the *Tathāgata*.

Five *dharmas*.
commentary_pali:
354. (Ka) cattāri cakkānīti ettha cakkaṃ nāma dārucakkaṃ, ratanacakkaṃ, dhammacakkaṃ, iriyāpathacakkaṃ, sampatticakkanti pañcavidhaṃ. Tattha ‘‘yaṃ panidaṃ samma, rathakāra, cakkaṃ chahi māsehi niṭṭhitaṃ, chārattūnehī’’ti (a. ni. 3.15) idaṃ dārucakkaṃ. ‘‘Pitarā pavattitaṃ cakkaṃ anuppavattetī’’ti (a. ni. 5.132) idaṃ ratanacakkaṃ. ‘‘Pavattitaṃ cakka’’nti (ma. ni. 2.399) idaṃ dhammacakkaṃ. ‘‘Catucakkaṃ navadvāra’’nti (saṃ. ni. 1.29) idaṃ iriyāpathacakkaṃ. ‘‘Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, cakkāni, yehi samannāgatānaṃ devamanussānaṃ catucakkaṃ pavattatī’’ti (a. ni. 4.31) idaṃ sampatticakkaṃ. Idhāpi etadeva adhippetaṃ.

Patirūpadesavāsoti yattha catasso parisā sandissanti, evarūpe anucchavike dese vāso. Sappurisūpanissayoti buddhādīnaṃ sappurisānaṃ avassayanaṃ sevanaṃ bhajanaṃ. Attasammāpaṇidhīti attano sammā ṭhapanaṃ, sace pana pubbe assaddhādīhi samannāgato hoti, tāni pahāya saddhādīsu patiṭṭhāpanaṃ. Pubbe ca katapuññatāti pubbe upacitakusalatā. Idamevettha pamāṇaṃ. Yena hi ñāṇasampayuttacittena kusalaṃ kataṃ hoti, tadeva kusalaṃ taṃ purisaṃ patirūpadese upaneti, sappurise bhajāpesi . So eva ca puggalo attānaṃ sammā ṭhapeti. Catūsu āhāresu paṭhamo lokiyova. Sesā pana tayo saṅgītisutte lokiyalokuttaramissakā kathitā. Idha pubbabhāge lokiyā.

Patirūpadesavāso Sappurisūpanissayo Attasammāpaṇidhī Pubbe ca katapuññatā

(Ca) kāmayogavisaṃyogādayo anāgāmimaggādivasena veditabbā.

kāmayogavisaṃyogā

(Cha) hānabhāgiyādīsu paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhī kāmasahagatā saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti hānabhāgiyo samādhi. Tadanudhammatā sati santiṭṭhati ṭhitibhāgiyo samādhi. Vitakkasahagatā saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti visesabhāgiyo samādhi. Nibbidāsahagatā saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti virāgūpasañhito nibbedhabhāgiyo samādhīti iminā nayena sabbasamāpattiyo vitthāretvā attho veditabbo. Visuddhimagge panassa vinicchayakathā kathitāva.

hānabhāgiyā hānabhāgiyo ṭhitibhāgiyo visesabhāgiyo nibbedhabhāgiyo

Imasmimpi vāre abhiññādīni ekakasadisāneva. Abhiññāpade panettha maggo kathito. Sacchikātabbapade phalaṃ.

Cattārodhammavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Pañcadhammavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
354. (ka) The term *cattāri cakkānī* ("four wheels") refers to five kinds of *cakka* (wheel): a wooden wheel (*dārucakkaṃ*), a jewel wheel (*ratanacakkaṃ*), the wheel of the Dharma (*dhammacakkaṃ*), the wheel of deportment (*iriyāpathacakkaṃ*), and the wheel of prosperity (*sampatticakkaṃ*).

Here, the wooden wheel (*dārucakkaṃ*) is that which is mentioned: “That wheel, friend Samma, made by a wheelwright, is finished in six months less six nights" (A. Ni. 3.15).

The jewel wheel (*ratanacakkaṃ*) is that which is mentioned: "He sets rolling the wheel that was set rolling by his father" (A. Ni. 5.132).

The wheel of the Dharma (*dhammacakkaṃ*) is that which is mentioned: "The wheel that was set rolling" (M. Ni. 2.399).

The wheel of deportment (*iriyāpathacakkaṃ*) is that which is mentioned: "Four-wheeled, with nine doors" (Saṃ. Ni. 1.29).

The wheel of prosperity (*sampatticakkaṃ*) is that which is mentioned: "These four wheels, monks, bring about the prosperity of gods and humans who possess them" (A. Ni. 4.31). Here also, this alone is intended.

Living in a suitable location (*patirūpadesavāso*) means living in a suitable and appropriate place where the four assemblies are found.

Reliance on good people (*sappurisūpanissayo*) means resorting to, attending on, and cultivating good people such as the Buddhas.

Right self-direction (*attasammāpaṇidhī*) means rightly establishing oneself; but if one formerly possessed lack of faith, etc., it means abandoning those and establishing oneself in faith, etc.

Having done meritorious deeds in the past (*pubbe ca katapuññatā*) means past accumulation of wholesome qualities.

This alone is the measure here. For, the wholesome deed that was done with a mind conjoined with knowledge leads that person to a suitable location, causes him to cultivate good people. That very person establishes himself rightly.

Among the four nutriments (*āhāra*), the first is only mundane (*lokiya*). But the remaining three are said in the Saṅgīti Sutta to be a mixture of mundane and supramundane (*lokiyalokuttaramissakā*). Here, in the former part, they are mundane.

Living in a suitable location, reliance on good people, right self-direction, and having done meritorious deeds in the past.

(ca) Disconnection from sense pleasures (*kāmayogavisaṃyogā*) and so on should be understood as the path of a non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*), etc.
The attainment of the first *jhāna* in those that are characterized by detachment from the union of sensual pleasures (cha), perceptions and attention accompanied by sensuality arise, [*hānabhāgiyo*] *samādhi*.

Mindfulness is established in accordance with that subsequent teaching, [*ṭhitibhāgiyo*] *samādhi*.

Perceptions and attention accompanied by thought arise, [*visesabhāgiyo*] *samādhi*.

Perceptions and attention accompanied by disgust arise, associated with detachment, [*nibbedhabhāgiyo*] *samādhi*. In this way, the meaning should be understood by expanding all attainments (*samāpattiyo*).

But in the *Visuddhimagga*, his decisive speech has been spoken.

[*hānabhāgiyā*], [*hānabhāgiyo*], [*ṭhitibhāgiyo*], [*visesabhāgiyo*], [*nibbedhabhāgiyo*], in this instance also, the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) etc. are just like single instances.

Herein, in the place of higher knowledge (*abhiññāpade*), the path (*maggo*) is spoken.

In the place of what should be directly experienced (*sacchikātabbapade*), [there is] the fruit (*phalaṃ*).

The four descriptions of the Dharma are completed.

The five descriptions of the Dharma.

mula_pali:
355. ‘‘Pañca dhammā bahukārā…pe… pañca dhammā sacchikātabbā.

(Ka) ‘‘katame pañca dhammā bahukārā? Pañca padhāniyaṅgāni – idhāvuso, bhikkhu saddho hoti, saddahati tathāgatassa bodhiṃ – ‘itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussānaṃ buddho bhagavā’ti. Appābādho hoti appātaṅko samavepākiniyā gahaṇiyā samannāgato nātisītāya nāccuṇhāya majjhimāya padhānakkhamāya. Asaṭho hoti amāyāvī yathābhūtamattānaṃ āvīkattā satthari vā viññūsu vā sabrahmacārīsu. Āraddhavīriyo viharati akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampadāya, thāmavā daḷhaparakkamo anikkhittadhuro kusalesu dhammesu. Paññavā hoti udayatthagāminiyā paññāya samannāgato ariyāya nibbedhikāya sammā dukkhakkhayagāminiyā. Ime pañca dhammā bahukārā.

bahukārā?

(Kha) ‘‘katame pañca dhammā bhāvetabbā? Pañcaṅgiko sammāsamādhi – pītipharaṇatā, sukhapharaṇatā, cetopharaṇatā , ālokapharaṇatā, paccavekkhaṇanimittaṃ paccavekkhaṇānimittaṃ (syā. kaṃ.). Ime pañca dhammā bhāvetabbā.

bhāvetabbā? paccavekkhaṇānimittaṃ (syā. kaṃ.)

(Ga) ‘‘katame pañca dhammā pariññeyyā? Pañcupādānakkhandhā seyyathīdaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) – rūpupādānakkhandho, vedanupādānakkhandho, saññupādānakkhandho, saṅkhārupādānakkhandho viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Ime pañca dhammā pariññeyyā.

pariññeyyā? seyyathīdaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.)

(Gha) ‘‘katame pañca dhammā pahātabbā? Pañca nīvaraṇāni – kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ, byāpādanīvaraṇaṃ, thinamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ, uddhaccakukuccanīvaraṇaṃ, vicikicchānīvaraṇaṃ. Ime pañca dhammā pahātabbā.

pahātabbā?

(Ṅa) ‘‘katame pañca dhammā hānabhāgiyā? Pañca cetokhilā – idhāvuso, bhikkhu satthari kaṅkhati vicikicchati nādhimuccati na sampasīdati. Yo so, āvuso, bhikkhu satthari kaṅkhati vicikicchati nādhimuccati na sampasīdati, tassa cittaṃ na namati ātappāya anuyogāya sātaccāya padhānāya. Yassa cittaṃ na namati ātappāya anuyogāya sātaccāya padhānāya . Ayaṃ paṭhamo cetokhilo. Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu dhamme kaṅkhati vicikicchati…pe… saṅghe kaṅkhati vicikicchati…pe… sikkhāya kaṅkhati vicikicchati…pe… sabrahmacārīsu kupito hoti anattamano āhatacitto khilajāto, yo so, āvuso, bhikkhu sabrahmacārīsu kupito hoti anattamano āhatacitto khilajāto, tassa cittaṃ na namati ātappāya anuyogāya sātaccāya padhānāya. Yassa cittaṃ na namati ātappāya anuyogāya sātaccāya padhānāya. Ayaṃ pañcamo cetokhilo. Ime pañca dhammā hānabhāgiyā.

hānabhāgiyā?

(Ca) ‘‘katame pañca dhammā visesabhāgiyā? Pañcindriyāni – saddhindriyaṃ, vīriyindriyaṃ, satindriyaṃ, samādhindriyaṃ, paññindriyaṃ. Ime pañca dhammā visesabhāgiyā.

visesabhāgiyā?

(Cha) ‘‘katame pañca dhammā duppaṭivijjhā? Pañca nissaraṇiyā dhātuyo – idhāvuso, bhikkhuno kāme manasikaroto kāmesu cittaṃ na pakkhandati na pasīdati na santiṭṭhati na vimuccati. Nekkhammaṃ kho panassa manasikaroto nekkhamme cittaṃ pakkhandati pasīdati santiṭṭhati vimuccati. Tassa taṃ cittaṃ sugataṃ subhāvitaṃ suvuṭṭhitaṃ suvimuttaṃ visaṃyuttaṃ kāmehi. Ye ca kāmapaccayā uppajjanti āsavā vighātā pariḷāhā, mutto so tehi. Na so taṃ vedanaṃ vedeti. Idamakkhātaṃ kāmānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ.

duppaṭivijjhā?

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno byāpādaṃ manasikaroto byāpāde cittaṃ na pakkhandati na pasīdati na santiṭṭhati na vimuccati. Abyāpādaṃ kho panassa manasikaroto abyāpāde cittaṃ pakkhandati pasīdati santiṭṭhati vimuccati. Tassa taṃ cittaṃ sugataṃ subhāvitaṃ suvuṭṭhitaṃ suvimuttaṃ visaṃyuttaṃ byāpādena. Ye ca byāpādapaccayā uppajjanti āsavā vighātā pariḷāhā, mutto so tehi. Na so taṃ vedanaṃ vedeti. Idamakkhātaṃ byāpādassa nissaraṇaṃ.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno vihesaṃ manasikaroto vihesāya cittaṃ na pakkhandati na pasīdati na santiṭṭhati na vimuccati. Avihesaṃ kho panassa manasikaroto avihesāya cittaṃ pakkhandati pasīdati santiṭṭhati vimuccati . Tassa taṃ cittaṃ sugataṃ subhāvitaṃ suvuṭṭhitaṃ suvimuttaṃ visaṃyuttaṃ vihesāya. Ye ca vihesāpaccayā uppajjanti āsavā vighātā pariḷāhā, mutto so tehi. Na so taṃ vedanaṃ vedeti. Idamakkhātaṃ vihesāya nissaraṇaṃ.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno rūpe manasikaroto rūpesu cittaṃ na pakkhandati na pasīdati na santiṭṭhati na vimuccati. Arūpaṃ kho panassa manasikaroto arūpe cittaṃ pakkhandati pasīdati santiṭṭhati vimuccati. Tassa taṃ cittaṃ sugataṃ subhāvitaṃ suvuṭṭhitaṃ suvimuttaṃ visaṃyuttaṃ rūpehi. Ye ca rūpapaccayā uppajjanti āsavā vighātā pariḷāhā, mutto so tehi. Na so taṃ vedanaṃ vedeti. Idamakkhātaṃ rūpānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno sakkāyaṃ manasikaroto sakkāye cittaṃ na pakkhandati na pasīdati na santiṭṭhati na vimuccati. Sakkāyanirodhaṃ kho panassa manasikaroto sakkāyanirodhe cittaṃ pakkhandati pasīdati santiṭṭhati vimuccati. Tassa taṃ cittaṃ sugataṃ subhāvitaṃ suvuṭṭhitaṃ suvimuttaṃ visaṃyuttaṃ sakkāyena. Ye ca sakkāyapaccayā uppajjanti āsavā vighātā pariḷāhā, mutto so tehi. Na so taṃ vedanaṃ vedeti. Idamakkhātaṃ sakkāyassa nissaraṇaṃ. Ime pañca dhammā duppaṭivijjhā.

(Ja) ‘‘katame pañca dhammā uppādetabbā? Pañca ñāṇiko sammāsamādhi – ‘ayaṃ samādhi paccuppannasukho ceva āyatiñca sukhavipāko’ti paccattaṃyeva ñāṇaṃ uppajjati. ‘Ayaṃ samādhi ariyo nirāmiso’ti paccattaññeva ñāṇaṃ uppajjati. ‘Ayaṃ samādhi akāpurisasevito’ti paccattaṃyeva ñāṇaṃ uppajjati. ‘Ayaṃ samādhi santo paṇīto paṭippassaddhaladdho ekodibhāvādhigato, na sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāritagato’ti na ca sasaṅkhāraniggayha vāritavatoti (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), na sasaṅkhāraniggayhavārivāvato (ka.), na sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāriyādhigato (?) paccattaṃyeva ñāṇaṃ uppajjati. ‘So kho panāhaṃ imaṃ samādhiṃ satova samāpajjāmi sato vuṭṭhahāmī’ti paccattaṃyeva ñāṇaṃ uppajjati. Ime pañca dhammā uppādetabbā.

uppādetabbā? na ca sasaṅkhāraniggayha vāritavatoti (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), na sasaṅkhāraniggayhavārivāvato (ka.), na sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāriyādhigato (?)

(Jha) ‘‘katame pañca dhammā abhiññeyyā? Pañca vimuttāyatanāni – idhāvuso, bhikkhuno satthā dhammaṃ deseti aññataro vā garuṭṭhāniyo sabrahmacārī. Yathā yathā, āvuso, bhikkhuno satthā dhammaṃ deseti, aññataro vā garuṭṭhāniyo sabrahmacārī, tathā tathā so bhikkhu (syā. kaṃ.) tasmiṃ dhamme atthappaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti dhammapaṭisaṃvedī ca. Tassa atthappaṭisaṃvedino dhammapaṭisaṃvedino pāmojjaṃ jāyati, pamuditassa pīti jāyati, pītimanassa kāyo passambhati, passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedeti, sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Idaṃ paṭhamaṃ vimuttāyatanaṃ.

abhiññeyyā? bhikkhu (syā. kaṃ.)

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno na heva kho satthā dhammaṃ deseti, aññataro vā garuṭṭhāniyo sabrahmacārī, api ca kho yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena paresaṃ deseti yathā yathā, āvuso, bhikkhu yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena paresaṃ deseti. Tathā tathā so tasmiṃ dhamme atthappaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti dhammapaṭisaṃvedī ca. Tassa atthappaṭisaṃvedino dhammapaṭisaṃvedino pāmojjaṃ jāyati, pamuditassa pīti jāyati, pītimanassa kāyo passambhati, passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedeti, sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Idaṃ dutiyaṃ vimuttāyatanaṃ.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno na heva kho satthā dhammaṃ deseti, aññataro vā garuṭṭhāniyo sabrahmacārī, nāpi yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena paresaṃ deseti. Api ca kho, yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena sajjhāyaṃ karoti. Yathā yathā, āvuso, bhikkhu yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena sajjhāyaṃ karoti tathā tathā so tasmiṃ dhamme atthappaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti dhammapaṭisaṃvedī ca. Tassa atthappaṭisaṃvedino dhammapaṭisaṃvedino pāmojjaṃ jāyati, pamuditassa pīti jāyati, pītimanassa kāyo passambhati, passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedeti, sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Idaṃ tatiyaṃ vimuttāyatanaṃ.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno na heva kho satthā dhammaṃ deseti, aññataro vā garuṭṭhāniyo sabrahmacārī, nāpi yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena paresaṃ deseti, nāpi yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena sajjhāyaṃ karoti. Api ca kho, yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ cetasā anuvitakketi anuvicāreti manasānupekkhati. Yathā yathā , āvuso , bhikkhu yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ cetasā anuvitakketi anuvicāreti manasānupekkhati tathā tathā so tasmiṃ dhamme atthappaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti dhammapaṭisaṃvedī ca. Tassa atthappaṭisaṃvedino dhammapaṭisaṃvedino pāmojjaṃ jāyati, pamuditassa pīti jāyati, pītimanassa kāyo passambhati, passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedeti, sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Idaṃ catutthaṃ vimuttāyatanaṃ.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno na heva kho satthā dhammaṃ deseti, aññataro vā garuṭṭhāniyo sabrahmacārī, nāpi yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena paresaṃ deseti, nāpi yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena sajjhāyaṃ karoti, nāpi yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ cetasā anuvitakketi anuvicāreti manasānupekkhati; api ca khvassa aññataraṃ samādhinimittaṃ suggahitaṃ hoti sumanasikataṃ sūpadhāritaṃ suppaṭividdhaṃ paññāya. Yathā yathā, āvuso, bhikkhuno aññataraṃ samādhinimittaṃ suggahitaṃ hoti sumanasikataṃ sūpadhāritaṃ suppaṭividdhaṃ paññāya tathā tathā so tasmiṃ dhamme atthappaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti dhammappaṭisaṃvedī ca. Tassa atthappaṭisaṃvedino dhammappaṭisaṃvedino pāmojjaṃ jāyati, pamuditassa pīti jāyati, pītimanassa kāyo passambhati, passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedeti, sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Idaṃ pañcamaṃ vimuttāyatanaṃ. Ime pañca dhammā abhiññeyyā.

(Ña) ‘‘katame pañca dhammā sacchikātabbā? Pañca dhammakkhandhā – sīlakkhandho , samādhikkhandho, paññākkhandho, vimuttikkhandho, vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandho. Ime pañca dhammā sacchikātabbā.

sacchikātabbā?

‘‘Iti ime paññāsa dhammā bhūtā tacchā tathā avitathā anaññathā sammā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā.

Cha dhammā
mula_english:
355. “Five *dhammas*, friends, are very helpful… and so on … five *dhammas* should be realized.

(a) “What five *dhammas* are very helpful (bahukārā)? The five factors of striving (pañca padhāniyaṅgāni): Here, friends, a bhikkhu has faith (saddho hoti), he trusts in the Tathāgata’s awakening (Tathāgatassa bodhiṃ): ‘Indeed, the Blessed One is an *arahaṃ*, a *sammāsambuddho*, accomplished in knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇasampanno*), well-gone (*sugato*), knower of the world (*lokavidū*), unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed (*anuttaro purisadammasārathi*), teacher of gods and humans (*satthā devamanussānaṃ*), awakened (*buddho*), blessed (*bhagavā*)’.

He is free from illness & discomfort (appābādho hoti appātaṅko), endowed with good digestion—not too cold, not too hot, of moderate strength—fit for exertion (samavepākiniyā gahaṇiyā samannāgato nātisītāya nāccuṇhāya majjhimāya padhānakkhamāya).

“He is neither fraudulent nor deceitful (asaṭho hoti amāyāvī). He declares himself to the Teacher or to his observant companions in the holy life in line with what he actually is (yathābhūtamattānaṃ āvīkattā satthari vā viññūsu vā sabrahmacārīsu).

“He is energetic in abandoning unwholesome states and in undertaking wholesome states (āraddhavīriyo viharati akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampadāya); he is steadfast, firm in striving, not remiss in developing wholesome states (thāmavā daḷhaparakkamo anikkhittadhuro kusalesu dhammesu).

“He is wise (paññavā hoti); he possesses wisdom regarding rise and disappearance that is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering (udayatthagāminiyā paññāya samannāgato ariyāya nibbedhikāya sammā dukkhakkhayagāminiyā). These five *dhammas* are very helpful.

(b) “What five *dhammas* should be developed (bhāvetabbā)? The five-factored right concentration (pañcaṅgiko sammāsamādhi): the pervading of joy (pītipharaṇatā), the pervading of pleasure (sukhapharaṇatā), the pervading of mind (cetopharaṇatā), the pervading of light (ālokapharaṇatā), the attribute of retrospecting (paccavekkhaṇanimittaṃ). These five *dhammas* should be developed.

(c) “What five *dhammas* should be comprehended (pariññeyyā)? The five aggregates subject to clinging (pañcupādānakkhandhā): the form clinging-aggregate (rūpupādānakkhandho), the feeling clinging-aggregate (vedanupādānakkhandho), the perception clinging-aggregate (saññupādānakkhandho), the fabrication clinging-aggregate (saṅkhārupādānakkhandho), the consciousness clinging-aggregate (viññāṇupādānakkhandho). These five *dhammas* should be comprehended.

(d) “What five *dhammas* should be abandoned (pahātabbā)? The five hindrances (pañca nīvaraṇāni): the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ), the hindrance of ill-will (byāpādanīvaraṇaṃ), the hindrance of sloth and torpor (thinamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ), the hindrance of restlessness and remorse (uddhaccakukuccanīvaraṇaṃ), the hindrance of doubt (vicikicchānīvaraṇaṃ). These five *dhammas* should be abandoned.

(e) “What five *dhammas* are on the side of decline (hānabhāgiyā)? The five mental blockages (pañca cetokhilā): Here, friends, a *bhikkhu* is doubtful, uncertain, indecisive about the Teacher (satthari kaṅkhati vicikicchati nādhimuccati na sampasīdati). When a *bhikkhu* is doubtful, uncertain, indecisive about the Teacher and is not confident in him, then his mind doesn’t tend toward ardency, commitment, perseverance, or exertion (tassa cittaṃ na namati ātappāya anuyogāya sātaccāya padhānāya). When one’s mind doesn’t tend toward ardency, commitment, perseverance, or exertion. This is the first mental blockage (ayaṃ paṭhamo cetokhilo). “Furthermore, friends, a *bhikkhu* is doubtful, uncertain, indecisive about the Dhamma… about the Sangha… about the training… “There is the case where a monk is angered & unhappy with his fellows in the holy life, his mind rigid & hostile (sabrahmacārīsu kupito hoti anattamano āhatacitto khilajāto). When a *bhikkhu* is angered & unhappy with his fellows in the holy life, his mind rigid & hostile, then his mind doesn’t tend toward ardency, commitment, perseverance, or exertion (tassa cittaṃ na namati ātappāya anuyogāya sātaccāya padhānāya). When one’s mind doesn’t tend toward ardency, commitment, perseverance, or exertion.
This is the fifth mental blockage.
These five *dhammas* are on the side of decline.

hānabhāgiyā?

(ca) “Which are the five *dhammas* on the side of distinction (*viśeṣabhāgīya*)? The five faculties (*pañcindriyāṇi*): the faculty of faith (*śraddhindriyaṃ*), the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriyaṃ*), the faculty of mindfulness (*satindriyaṃ*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriyaṃ*), and the faculty of wisdom (*prajñindriyaṃ*).
These five *dhammas* are on the side of distinction (*viśeṣabhāgīya*).

visesabhāgiyā? (cha) “Which are the five *dhammas* that are hard to penetrate (*duppaṭivijjhā*)? The five liberating elements (*pañca nissaraṇiyā dhātuyo*): Here, *āvuso*, when a *bhikkhu* attends to sensual pleasures (*kāma*), his mind does not leap up at sensual pleasures, does not grow confident, steadfast, or released in sensual pleasures.
But when attending to renunciation (*naikṣammya*), his mind leaps up at renunciation, grows confident, steadfast, and released in renunciation.
When his mind is rightly-gone (*sugataṃ*), rightly developed (*subhāvitaṃ*), has rightly risen above (*suvuṭṭhitaṃ*), gained release (*suvimuttaṃ*), and become disjoined (*visaṃyuttaṃ*) from sensual pleasures (*kāmehi*),
then whatever effluents (*āsava*), torments (*vighāta*), and fevers (*pariḷāha*) there are that arise in dependence on sensual pleasures, he is released (*mutto*) from them.
He doesn’t experience that feeling (*vedanā*).
This is expounded as the escape (*nissaraṇaṃ*) from sensual pleasures (*kāma*).

duppaṭivijjhā? “And further, *āvuso*, when a *bhikkhu* attends to ill will (*byāpāda*), his mind does not leap up at ill will, does not grow confident, steadfast, or released in ill will.
But when attending to non-ill will (*abyāpāda*), his mind leaps up at non-ill will, grows confident, steadfast, and released in non-ill will.
When his mind is rightly-gone (*sugataṃ*), rightly developed (*subhāvitaṃ*), has rightly risen above (*suvuṭṭhitaṃ*), gained release (*suvimuttaṃ*), and become disjoined (*visaṃyuttaṃ*) from ill will (*byāpāda*),
then whatever effluents (*āsava*), torments (*vighāta*), and fevers (*pariḷāha*) there are that arise in dependence on ill will (*byāpāda*), he is released (*mutto*) from them.
He doesn’t experience that feeling (*vedanā*).
This is expounded as the escape (*nissaraṇaṃ*) from ill will (*byāpāda*).

“And further, *āvuso*, when a *bhikkhu* attends to harmfulness (*vihesā*), his mind does not leap up at harmfulness, does not grow confident, steadfast, or released in harmfulness.
But when attending to harmlessness (*avihesā*), his mind leaps up at harmlessness, grows confident, steadfast, and released in harmlessness.
When his mind is rightly-gone (*sugataṃ*), rightly developed (*subhāvitaṃ*), has rightly risen above (*suvuṭṭhitaṃ*), gained release (*suvimuttaṃ*), and become disjoined (*visaṃyuttaṃ*) from harmfulness (*vihesā*),
then whatever effluents (*āsava*), torments (*vighāta*), and fevers (*pariḷāha*) there are that arise in dependence on harmfulness (*vihesā*), he is released (*mutto*) from them.
He doesn’t experience that feeling (*vedanā*).
This is expounded as the escape (*nissaraṇaṃ*) from harmfulness (*vihesā*).

“And further, *āvuso*, when a *bhikkhu* attends to forms (*rūpa*), his mind does not leap up at forms, does not grow confident, steadfast, or released in forms.
But when attending to the formless (*arūpa*), his mind leaps up at the formless, grows confident, steadfast, and released in the formless.
When his mind is rightly-gone (*sugataṃ*), rightly developed (*subhāvitaṃ*), has rightly risen above (*suvuṭṭhitaṃ*), gained release (*suvimuttaṃ*), and become disjoined (*visaṃyuttaṃ*) from forms (*rūpehi*),
then whatever effluents (*āsava*), torments (*vighāta*), and fevers (*pariḷāha*) there are that arise in dependence on forms (*rūpa*), he is released (*mutto*) from them.
He doesn’t experience that feeling (*vedanā*).
This is expounded as the escape (*nissaraṇaṃ*) from forms (*rūpa*).

“And further, *āvuso*, when a *bhikkhu* attends to self-identification (*sakkāya*), his mind does not leap up at self-identification, does not grow confident, steadfast, or released in self-identification.
But when attending to the cessation of self-identification (*sakkāyanirodhaṃ*), his mind leaps up at the cessation of self-identification, grows confident, steadfast, and released in the cessation of self-identification.
When his mind is rightly-gone (*sugataṃ*), rightly developed (*subhāvitaṃ*), has rightly risen above (*suvuṭṭhitaṃ*), gained release (*suvimuttaṃ*), and become disjoined (*visaṃyuttaṃ*) from self-identification (*sakkāya*).
And then whatever *āsavas* (effluents), torments, and fevers there are that arise in dependence on *sakkāya* (self-identification), he is released from them.
He doesn’t experience that feeling.
This is expounded as the escape from self-identification (*sakkāyassa nissaraṇaṃ*).
These five *dharmas* are hard to penetrate (*duppaṭivijjhā*).

“Which five *dharmas* should be made to arise (*uppādetabbā*)? The five kinds of right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*) with knowledges (*ñāṇiko*) – ‘This concentration (*samādhi*) is blissful in the present and will result in bliss in the future,’ the knowledge (*ñāṇaṃ*) arises right within oneself (*paccattaṃyeva*).
‘This concentration (*samādhi*) is noble (*ariyo*) and not connected with the baits of the flesh (*nirāmiso*)’ the knowledge (*ñāṇaṃ*) arises right within oneself (*paccattaññeva*).
‘This concentration (*samādhi*) is not obtained by base people (*akāpurisasevito*)’ the knowledge (*ñāṇaṃ*) arises right within oneself (*paccattaṃyeva*).
‘This concentration (*samādhi*) is peaceful (*santo*), exquisite (*paṇīto*), the acquiring of calm (*paṭippassaddhaladdho*), the attainment of unification (*ekodibhāvādhigato*), not kept in place by the fabrications of forceful restraint (*na sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāritagato*)’ the knowledge (*ñāṇaṃ*) arises right within oneself (*paccattaṃyeva*).
‘I enter into this concentration (*samādhi*) mindfully (*satova*), and mindfully I emerge from it (*sato vuṭṭhahāmī*)’ the knowledge (*ñāṇaṃ*) arises right within oneself (*paccattaṃyeva*).
These five *dharmas* should be made to arise (*uppādetabbā*).

“Which five *dharmas* should be completely known (*abhiññeyyā*)? The five bases for deliverance (*pañca vimuttāyatanāni*) – Here, Āvuso, the Teacher (*satthā*) teaches the *dhamma* to the monk (*bhikkhuno*), or a fellow person leading the holy life (*sabrahmacārī*) who is in a position worthy of respect (*garuṭṭhāniyo*).
In whatever way, Āvuso, the Teacher (*satthā*) teaches the *dhamma* to the monk (*bhikkhuno*), or a fellow person leading the holy life (*sabrahmacārī*) who is in a position worthy of respect (*garuṭṭhāniyo*), in just that way the monk is sensitive to the meaning (*atthappaṭisaṃvedī*) and sensitive to the *dhamma*.
In him—sensitive to the meaning (*atthappaṭisaṃvedino*), sensitive to the *dhamma*—joy (*pāmojjaṃ*) is born, when he is joyful (*pamuditassa*) rapture (*pīti*) is born, when his mind is filled with rapture (*pītimanassa*) his body (*kāyo*) grows calm (*passambhati*), when the body is calm (*passaddhakāyo*) he feels pleasure (*sukhaṃ vedeti*), feeling pleasure (*sukhino*) the mind (*cittaṃ*) becomes concentrated (*samādhiyati*).
This is the first opening to release (*idaṃ paṭhamaṃ vimuttāyatanaṃ*).

“And further, Āvuso, it’s not that the Teacher (*satthā*) teaches the *dhamma* to the monk (*bhikkhuno*), or a fellow person leading the holy life (*sabrahmacārī*) who is in a position worthy of respect (*garuṭṭhāniyo*), but the monk teaches the *dhamma* as he has heard it (*yathāsutaṃ*) and as he has learned it (*yathāpariyattaṃ*) to others in detail (*vitthārena*). In whatever way, Āvuso, the monk teaches the *dhamma* as he has heard it (*yathāsutaṃ*) and as he has learned it (*yathāpariyattaṃ*) to others in detail (*vitthārena*),
in just that way the monk is sensitive to the meaning (*atthappaṭisaṃvedī*) and sensitive to the *dhamma*.
In him—sensitive to the meaning (*atthappaṭisaṃvedino*), sensitive to the *dhamma*—joy (*pāmojjaṃ*) is born, when he is joyful (*pamuditassa*) rapture (*pīti*) is born, when his mind is filled with rapture (*pītimanassa*) his body (*kāyo*) grows calm (*passambhati*), when the body is calm (*passaddhakāyo*) he feels pleasure (*sukhaṃ vedeti*), feeling pleasure (*sukhino*) the mind (*cittaṃ*) becomes concentrated (*samādhiyati*).
This is the second opening to release (*idaṃ dutiyaṃ vimuttāyatanaṃ*).
“And further, Āvuso, it's not that the Teacher ( *śāstā*) teaches the *dhamma* to the monk, nor a fellow person worthy of respect in the holy life. Nor does he teach the *dhamma* to others in detail, as he has heard it, as he has learned it.

But he recites the *dhamma* in detail, as he has heard it, as he has learned it.

In whatever way, Āvuso, the monk recites the *dhamma* in detail, as he has heard it, as he has learned it, in just that way he is sensitive to the meaning (*arthappaṭisaṃvedī*) and the *dhamma* (*dhammappaṭisaṃvedī*) with regard to that *dhamma*.

In him—sensitive to the meaning, sensitive to the *dhamma*—joy (*pāmojja*) is born. When he is joyful, rapture (*pīti*) is born. When his mind is filled with rapture, his body becomes tranquil; tranquil in body, he experiences happiness (*sukha*); being happy, his mind becomes concentrated (*samādhiyati*).

This is the third opening to release (*vimuttāyatana*).

“And further, Āvuso, it's not that the Teacher teaches the *dhamma* to the monk, nor a fellow person worthy of respect in the holy life. Nor does he teach the *dhamma* to others in detail, as he has heard it, as he has learned it; nor does he recite the *dhamma* in detail, as he has heard it, as he has learned it.

But in his awareness, he directs his thoughts to the *dhamma* in detail, as he has heard it, as he has learned it; he evaluates it, & mentally examines it.

In whatever way, Āvuso, the monk, in his awareness, directs his thoughts to the *dhamma* in detail, as he has heard it, as he has learned it, evaluates it, & mentally examines it, in just that way he is sensitive to the meaning and the *dhamma* with regard to that *dhamma*.

In him—sensitive to the meaning, sensitive to the *dhamma*—joy is born. When he is joyful, rapture is born. When his mind is filled with rapture, his body becomes tranquil; tranquil in body, he experiences happiness; being happy, his mind becomes concentrated.

This is the fourth opening to release.

“And further, Āvuso, it's not that the Teacher teaches the *dhamma* to the monk, nor a fellow person worthy of respect in the holy life. Nor does he teach the *dhamma* to others in detail, as he has heard it, as he has learned it; nor does he recite the *dhamma* in detail, as he has heard it, as he has learned it; nor does he, in his awareness, direct his thoughts to the *dhamma* in detail, as he has heard it, as he has learned it, evaluate it, or mentally examine it. But he has well grasped a certain theme of concentration (*samādhinimitta*), has attended to it well, sustained it well, has penetrated it well with discernment (*paññāya*).

In whatever way, Āvuso, the monk has well grasped a certain theme of concentration, has attended to it well, sustained it well, has penetrated it well with discernment, in just that way he is sensitive to the meaning and the *dhamma* with regard to that *dhamma*.

In him—sensitive to the meaning, sensitive to the *dhamma*—joy is born. When he is joyful, rapture is born. When his mind is filled with rapture, his body becomes tranquil; tranquil in body, he experiences happiness; being happy, his mind becomes concentrated.

This is the fifth opening to release.

These five *dhammas* should be directly known (*abhiññeyyā*).

(Question:) “Which five *dhammas* should be realized (*sacchikātabbā*)?” The five aggregates of *dhamma* (*dhammakkhandhā*): the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*), the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*), the aggregate of discernment (*paññākkhandha*), the aggregate of release (*vimuttikkhandha*), the aggregate of knowledge & vision of release (*vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandha*).

These five *dhammas* should be realized (*sacchikātabbā*).

(Statement:) “Thus, these fifty *dhammas*—true (*bhūtā*), genuine (*tacchā*), real (*tathā*), not unreal (*avitathā*), not otherwise (*anaññathā*)—have been rightly awakened to (*abhisambuddhā*) by the *Tathāgata*.

Six *dhammas*

355. (Kha) pītipharaṇatādīsu pītiṃ pharamānā uppajjatīti dvīsu jhānesu paññā pītipharaṇatā nāma. Sukhaṃ pharamānaṃ uppajjatīti tīsu jhānesu paññā sukhapharaṇatā nāma. Paresaṃ ceto pharamānā uppajjatīti cetopariyapaññā cetopharaṇatā nāma. Ālokapharaṇe uppajjatīti dibbacakkhupaññā ālokapharaṇatā nāma. Paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ paccavekkhaṇanimittaṃ nāma. Vuttampi cetaṃ ‘‘dvīsu jhānesu paññā pītipharaṇatā, tīsu jhānesu paññā sukhapharaṇatā. Paracitte paññā cetopharaṇatā, dibbacakkhu ālokapharaṇatā. Tamhā tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhitassa paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ paccavekkhaṇanimitta’’nti (vibha. 804).

Tattha pītipharaṇatā sukhapharaṇatā dve pādā viya. Cetopharaṇatā ālokapharaṇatā dve hatthā viya. Abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ majjhimakāyo viya . Paccavekkhaṇanimittaṃ sīsaṃ viya. Iti āyasmā sāriputtatthero pañcaṅgikaṃ sammāsamādhiṃ aṅgapaccaṅgasampannaṃ purisaṃ katvā dassesi.

(Ja) ayaṃ samādhi paccuppannasukho ce vātiādīsu arahattaphalasamādhi adhippeto. So hi appitappitakkhaṇe sukhattā paccuppannasukho. Purimo purimo pacchimassa pacchimassa samādhisukhassa paccayattā āyatiṃ sukhavipāko.

ayaṃ samādhi paccuppannasukho ce vā paccuppannasukho. sukhavipāko.

Kilesehi ārakattā ariyo. Kāmāmisavaṭṭāmisalokāmisānaṃ abhāvā nirāmiso. Buddhādīhi mahāpurisehi sevitattā akāpurisasevito. Aṅgasantatāya ārammaṇasantatāya sabbakilesadarathasantatāya ca santo. Atappanīyaṭṭhena paṇīto. Kilesapaṭippassaddhiyā laddhattā kilesapaṭippassaddhibhāvaṃ vā laddhattā paṭippassaddhaladdho. Paṭippassaddhaṃ paṭippassaddhīti hi idaṃ atthato ekaṃ. Paṭippassaddhakilesena vā arahatā laddhattā paṭippassaddhaladdho. Ekodibhāvena adhigatattā ekodibhāvameva vā adhigatattā ekodibhāvādhigato. Appaguṇasāsavasamādhi viya sasaṅkhārena sappayogena cittena paccanīkadhamme niggayha kilese vāretvā anadhigatattā nasasaṅkhāraniggayhavāritagato. Tañca samādhiṃ samāpajjanto tato vā vuṭṭhahanto sativepullapattattā. Satova samāpajjati sato vuṭṭhahati. Yathāparicchinnakālavasena vā sato samāpajjati sato vuṭṭhahati. Tasmā yadettha ‘‘ayaṃ samādhi paccuppannasukho ceva āyatiñca sukhavipāko’’ti evaṃ paccavekkhamānassa paccattaṃyeva aparappaccayaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppajjati, taṃ ekamaṅgaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Evamimehi pañcahi paccavekkhaṇañāṇehi ayaṃ samādhi ‘‘pañcañāṇiko sammāsamādhī’’ti vutto.

commentary_english:
355. (kha) In the case of *pītipharaṇatā* etc., wisdom (*paññā*) in the two *jhānas* arises spreading joy (*pītiṃ pharamānā*), hence it is called *pītipharaṇatā*. Wisdom (*paññā*) in the three *jhānas* arises spreading happiness (*sukhaṃ pharamānaṃ*), hence it is called *sukhapharaṇatā*. The wisdom that considers the minds of others (*cetopariyapaññā*) arises spreading mind (*paresaṃ ceto pharamānā*), hence it is called *cetopharaṇatā*. The divine-eye wisdom (*dibbacakkhupaññā*) arises spreading light (*ālokapharaṇe*), hence it is called *ālokapharaṇatā*. Reviewing-knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ*) is called *paccavekkhaṇanimittaṃ*.

And this was said: “Wisdom in the two *jhānas* is *pītipharaṇatā*, wisdom in the three *jhānas* is *sukhapharaṇatā*. Wisdom concerning the minds of others is *cetopharaṇatā*, the divine eye is *ālokapharaṇatā*. For one rising from that samādhi, reviewing-knowledge is *paccavekkhaṇanimitta*” (Vibha. 804).

There, *pītipharaṇatā* and *sukhapharaṇatā* are like two feet. *Cetopharaṇatā* and *ālokapharaṇatā* are like two hands. The *jhāna* that produces the higher knowledges (*abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ*) is like the central body. Reviewing-knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇanimittaṃ*) is like the head. Thus, venerable Sāriputta showed right-concentration (*sammāsamādhiṃ*) with five factors (*pañcaṅgikaṃ*), making it a person complete with limbs and parts.

(ja) In "*ayaṃ samādhi paccuppannasukho ce vā*" etc., the *samādhi* of the fruit of arahantship is intended. For, being pleasant at the moment of application, it is *paccuppannasukho* (present happiness). The preceding is a condition for the subsequent *samādhi*-happiness, hence in the future it is *sukhavipāko* (happiness-result).

*ayaṃ samādhi paccuppannasukho ce vā* *paccuppannasukho*. *sukhavipāko*.

Being far from defilements, it is *ariyo* (noble). Because of the absence of sensual pleasures (*kāmāmisa*), round pleasures (*vaṭṭāmisa*), and worldly pleasures (*lokāmisa*), it is *nirāmiso* (unworldly). Because it is cultivated by great beings such as the Buddha etc., it is *akāpurisasevito* (cultivated by non-base persons). By the continuity of factors, the continuity of object, and the continuity of the cutting off of all defilements, it is *santo* (peaceful). By way of being not needing to be heated, it is *paṇīto* (excellent). Having been obtained by the calming of defilements, or by having obtained the state of calming defilements, it is *paṭippassaddhaladdho* (obtained through calming). For *paṭippassaddhaṃ* and *paṭippassaddhī* are, in meaning, one. Or, having been obtained by the Arahant through calmed defilements, it is *paṭippassaddhaladdho*. Having been attained by way of one-pointedness, or having attained one-pointedness itself, it is *ekodibhāvādhigato* (attained through one-pointedness). Unlike the *samādhi* with qualities and *āsavas*, by suppressing opposing states with effort and exertion of mind, warding off defilements, and not being attained, it is *nasasaṅkhāraniggayhavāritagato*. And while entering into that *samādhi* or rising from it, being one who has obtained abundance of mindfulness, one enters mindfully (*sato samāpajjati*) and rises mindfully (*sato vuṭṭhahati*). Or, according to the defined time, one enters mindfully and rises mindfully. Therefore, the knowledge that arises in oneself without depending on another, while reviewing in this way: “This *samādhi* is both present happiness and has a happiness-result in the future,” that is one factor.
So with the rest.

Thus, this *samādhi* is called "right *samādhi* with five knowledges" because of these five knowledges of reflection.

Noble.
Without sensual pleasures.
Not practiced by inferior persons.
Peaceful.
Excellent.
Attained through tranquility.
Realized through unification of mind.
Whose progress is stopped by the restraint of the breath.
He enters mindfully, and he emerges mindfully.

Cha nissaraṇiyā dhātuyo – idhāvuso, bhikkhu evaṃ vadeyya – ‘mettā hi kho me, cetovimutti bhāvitā bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā, atha ca pana me byāpādo cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī’ti. So ‘mā hevaṃ’ tissa vacanīyo ‘māyasmā evaṃ avaca, mā bhagavantaṃ abbhācikkhi. Na hi sādhu bhagavato abbhakkhānaṃ, na hi bhagavā evaṃ vadeyya. Aṭṭhānametaṃ āvuso anavakāso yaṃ mettāya cetovimuttiyā bhāvitāya bahulīkatāya yānīkatāya vatthukatāya anuṭṭhitāya paricitāya susamāraddhāya. Atha ca panassa byāpādo cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassatīti, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Nissaraṇaṃ hetaṃ, āvuso, byāpādassa, yadidaṃ mettācetovimuttī’ti.

duppaṭivijjhā?

‘‘Idha panāvuso, bhikkhu evaṃ vadeyya – ‘karuṇā hi kho me cetovimutti bhāvitā bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā. Atha ca pana me vihesā cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī’ti. So – ‘mā hevaṃ’ tissa vacanīyo, ‘māyasmā evaṃ avaca, mā bhagavantaṃ abbhācikkhi…pe… nissaraṇaṃ hetaṃ, āvuso, vihesāya, yadidaṃ karuṇācetovimuttī’ti.

‘‘Idha panāvuso, bhikkhu evaṃ vadeyya – ‘muditā hi kho me cetovimutti bhāvitā…pe… atha ca pana me arati cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī’ti. So – ‘mā hevaṃ’ tissa vacanīyo ‘māyasmā evaṃ avaca…pe… nissaraṇaṃ hetaṃ, āvuso aratiyā, yadidaṃ muditācetovimuttī’ti.

‘‘Idha panāvuso, bhikkhu evaṃ vadeyya – ‘upekkhā hi kho me cetovimutti bhāvitā…pe… atha ca pana me rāgo cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī’ti. So – ‘mā hevaṃ’ tissa vacanīyo ‘māyasmā evaṃ avaca…pe… nissaraṇaṃ hetaṃ, āvuso, rāgassa yadidaṃ upekkhācetovimuttī’ti.

‘‘Idha panāvuso, bhikkhu evaṃ vadeyya – ‘animittā hi kho me cetovimutti bhāvitā…pe… atha ca pana me nimittānusāri viññāṇaṃ hotī’ti. So – ‘mā hevaṃ’ tissa vacanīyo ‘māyasmā evaṃ avaca…pe… nissaraṇaṃ hetaṃ, āvuso, sabbanimittānaṃ yadidaṃ animittā cetovimuttī’ti.

‘‘Idha panāvuso, bhikkhu evaṃ vadeyya – ‘asmīti kho me vigataṃ, ayamahamasmīti na samanupassāmi, atha ca pana me vicikicchākathaṃkathāsallaṃ cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī’ti. So – ‘mā hevaṃ’ tissa vacanīyo ‘māyasmā evaṃ avaca, mā bhagavantaṃ abbhācikkhi, na hi sādhu bhagavato abbhakkhānaṃ, na hi bhagavā evaṃ vadeyya. Aṭṭhānametaṃ, āvuso, anavakāso yaṃ asmīti vigate ayamahamasmīti asamanupassato. Atha ca panassa vicikicchākathaṃkathāsallaṃ cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassati, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Nissaraṇaṃ hetaṃ, āvuso, vicikicchākathaṃkathāsallassa, yadidaṃ asmimānasamugghāṭo’ti. Ime cha dhammā duppaṭivijjhā.

(Ja) ‘‘katame cha dhammā uppādetabbā? Cha satatavihārā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā neva sumano hoti na dummano, upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno. Sotena saddaṃ sutvā…pe… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya neva sumano hoti na dummano, upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno. Ime cha dhammā uppādetabbā.

uppādetabbā?

(Jha) ‘‘katame cha dhammā abhiññeyyā? Cha anuttariyāni – dassanānuttariyaṃ, savanānuttariyaṃ, lābhānuttariyaṃ, sikkhānuttariyaṃ, pāricariyānuttariyaṃ, anussatānuttariyaṃ. Ime cha dhammā abhiññeyyā.

abhiññeyyā?

(Ña) ‘‘katame cha dhammā sacchikātabbā? Cha abhiññā – idhāvuso, bhikkhu anekavihitaṃ iddhividhaṃ paccanubhoti – ekopi hutvā bahudhā hoti , bahudhāpi hutvā eko hoti. Āvibhāvaṃ tirobhāvaṃ. Tirokuṭṭaṃ tiropākāraṃ tiropabbataṃ asajjamāno gacchati seyyathāpi ākāse . Pathaviyāpi ummujjanimujjaṃ karoti seyyathāpi udake. Udakepi abhijjamāne gacchati seyyathāpi pathaviyaṃ. Ākāsepi pallaṅkena kamati seyyathāpi pakkhī sakuṇo. Imepi candimasūriye evaṃmahiddhike evaṃmahānubhāve pāṇinā parāmasati parimajjati. Yāva brahmalokāpi kāyena vasaṃ vatteti.

sacchikātabbā?

‘‘Dibbāya sotadhātuyā visuddhāya atikkantamānusikāya ubho sadde suṇāti dibbe ca mānuse ca, ye dūre santike ca.

‘‘Parasattānaṃ parapuggalānaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāti jānāti (syā. kaṃ.), sarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ sarāgaṃ cittanti pajānāti …pe… avimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ avimuttaṃ cittanti pajānāti.

jānāti (syā. kaṃ.)

‘‘So anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, seyyathidaṃ ekampi jātiṃ…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati.

‘‘Dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāti …pe…

‘‘Āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati. Ime cha dhammā sacchikātabbā.

‘‘Iti ime saṭṭhi dhammā bhūtā tacchā tathā avitathā anaññathā sammā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā.

Satta dhammā
mula_english:
356. “Six *dhammas*, friends, are very helpful… Six *dhammas* should be directly known. (a) “What are the six helpful *dhammas*? Six memorable qualities. Here, friends, a *bhikṣu*’s acts of loving-kindness are present with his fellows in the holy life, both openly and in private. This quality, too, is memorable, creates love and respect, and conduces to helpfulness, to non-dispute, to concord, and to unity. “Furthermore, friends, a *bhikṣu*’s verbal acts of loving-kindness…conduce to unity. “Furthermore, friends, a *bhikṣu*’s mental acts of loving-kindness…conduce to unity. “Furthermore, friends, a *bhikṣu* who shares without reservation any lawful gains he has gained righteously—even what is just enough to fill a bowl—with his virtuous fellows in the holy life. This quality, too, is memorable…conduces to unity. “Furthermore, friends, a *bhikṣu* dwells both in public and in private possessing in common with his companions in the holy life those virtues that are unbroken, untorn, unblotched, unmottled, liberating, commended by the wise, not misapprehended, and conducive to concentration. This quality, too, is memorable…conduces to unity. “Furthermore, friends, with reference to the view that is noble, leading outward, that leads those who act in accordance with it to the right ending of suffering & stress—the monk dwells with his view in tune with that of his companions in the holy life, to their faces & behind their backs. This, too, is a condition that is conducive to amiability, that engenders feelings of endearment, engenders feelings of respect, leading to a sense of fellowship, a lack of disputes, harmony, & a state of unity. These six *dhammas* are very helpful. (b) “What are the six *dhammas* that should be developed (*bhāvetabbā*)? Six recollections: recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati), recollection of the Dhamma (dhammānussati), recollection of the Sangha (saṃghānussati), recollection of virtue (sīlānussati), recollection of generosity (cāgānussati), recollection of the deities (devatānussati). These six *dhammas* should be developed. (c) “What are the six *dhammas* that should be fully understood (*pariññeyyā*)? Six internal sense bases (*ajjhattikāni āyatanāni*): the eye-base (cakkhāyatanaṃ), the ear-base (sotāyatanaṃ), the nose-base (ghānāyatanaṃ), the tongue-base (jivhāyatanaṃ), the body-base (kāyāyatanaṃ), and the mind-base (manāyatanaṃ). These six *dhammas* should be fully understood. (d) “What are the six *dhammas* that should be abandoned (*pahātabbā*)? Six kinds of craving (*taṇhākāyā*): craving for sights (*rūpataṇhā*), craving for sounds (*saddataṇhā*), craving for smells (*gandhataṇhā*), craving for tastes (*rasataṇhā*), craving for tactile objects (*phoṭṭhabbataṇhā*), and craving for mental objects (*dhammataṇhā*). These six *dhammas* should be abandoned. (e) “What are the six *dhammas* on the side of decline (*hānabhāgiyā*)? Six kinds of disrespect (*agāravā*): Here, friends, a *bhikṣu* dwells without respect or deference for the Teacher (*satthari agāravo viharati appatisso*)…for the Dhamma (*dhamme*)…for the Saṅgha (*saṃghe*)…for the training (*sikkhāya*)…for heedfulness (*appamāde*)…for welcoming manners (*paṭisanthāre agāravo viharati appatisso*). These six *dhammas* are on the side of decline. (f) “What are the six *dhammas* on the side of distinction (*visesabhāgiyā*)? Six kinds of respect (*gāravā*): Here, friends, a *bhikṣu* dwells with respect and deference for the Teacher (*satthari sagāravo viharati sappatisso*)…for the Dhamma (*dhamme*)…for the Saṅgha (*saṃghe*)…for the training (*sikkhāya*)…for heedfulness (*appamāde*)…for welcoming manners (*paṭisanthāre sagāravo viharati sappatisso*). These six *dhammas* are on the side of distinction. (g) “What are the six *dhammas* that are hard to penetrate (*duppaṭivijjhā*)? Six liberating elements (*nissaraṇiyā dhātuyo*): Here, friends, a *bhikṣu* might say this: ‘I have developed, cultivated, made much of, made the vehicle, made the foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken loving-kindness as the liberation of mind (*mettā cetovimutti bhāvitā bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā*), and yet ill-will (*byāpādo*) still keeps overpowering my mind (*cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī*).’ He should be told, ‘Don’t say that. You shouldn’t speak in that way. Don’t misrepresent the Blessed One (*mā bhagavantaṃ abbhācikkhi*). It’s not right to misrepresent the Blessed One (*na hi sādhu bhagavato abbhakkhānaṃ*), and the Blessed One wouldn’t say that (*na hi bhagavā evaṃ vadeyya*). It’s impossible, there is no way that—when goodwill as the liberation of mind (*mettāya cetovimuttiyā*) has been developed, pursued, handed the reins, taken as a basis, steadied, consolidated, & well-undertaken—ill will (*byāpādo*) would still keep overpowering the mind (*cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassati*). That possibility doesn’t exist (*netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati*). For this is the escape from ill will: goodwill as an awareness-release (*nissaraṇaṃ hetaṃ, āvuso, byāpādassa, yadidaṃ mettācetovimuttī*)’." """Are these difficult to penetrate?""" “And further, there is the case where a monk might say, ‘Although compassion (karuṇā) has been developed, pursued, handed the reins, taken as a basis, steadied, consolidated, & well-undertaken by me as my awareness-release (cetovimutti), still harmfulness (vihesā) keeps overpowering my mind.’ He should be told, ‘Don’t say that. You shouldn’t speak in that way. Don’t misrepresent the Blessed One, for it’s not right to misrepresent the Blessed One, and the Blessed One wouldn’t say that. It’s impossible, there is no way that—when compassion as an awareness-release has been developed, pursued, handed the reins, taken as a basis, steadied, consolidated, & well undertaken—harmfulness would still keep overpowering the mind. That possibility doesn’t exist, for this is the escape from harmfulness: compassion as an awareness-release (karuṇā-cetovimutti).’ “And further, there is the case where a monk might say, ‘Although empathetic joy (muditā) has been developed, pursued, handed the reins, taken as a basis, steadied, consolidated, & well undertaken by me as my awareness-release, still resentment (arati) keeps overpowering my mind.’ He should be told, ‘Don’t say that. You shouldn’t speak in that way. Don’t misrepresent the Blessed One, for it’s not right to misrepresent the Blessed One, and the Blessed One wouldn’t say that. It’s impossible, there is no way that—when empathetic joy as an awareness release (muditā-cetovimutti) has been developed, pursued, handed the reins, taken as a basis, steadied, consolidated, & well undertaken—resentment would still keep overpowering the mind. That possibility doesn’t exist, for this is the escape from resentment: empathetic joy as an awareness-release.’ “And further, there is the case where a monk might say, ‘Although equanimity (upekkhā) has been developed, pursued, handed the reins, taken as a basis, steadied, consolidated, & well undertaken by me as my awareness-release, still passion (rāga) keeps overpowering my mind.’ He should be told, ‘Don’t say that. You shouldn’t speak in that way. Don’t misrepresent the Blessed One, for it’s not right to misrepresent the Blessed One, and the Blessed One wouldn’t say that. It’s impossible, there is no way that—when equanimity as an awareness-release (upekkhā-cetovimutti) has been developed, pursued, handed the reins, taken as a basis, steadied, consolidated, & well undertaken—passion would still keep overpowering the mind. That possibility doesn’t exist, for this is the escape from passion: equanimity as an awareness-release.’ “And further, there is the case where a monk might say, ‘Although the signless (animittā) has been developed, pursued, handed the reins, taken as a basis, steadied, consolidated, & well undertaken by me as my awareness-release, still my consciousness (viññāṇaṃ) follows the drift of signs (nimitta).’ He should be told, ‘Don’t say that. You shouldn’t speak in that way. Don’t misrepresent the Blessed One, for it’s not right to misrepresent the Blessed One, and the Blessed One wouldn’t say that. It’s impossible, there is no way that—when the signless as an awareness-release (animittā-cetovimutti) has been developed, pursued, handed the reins, taken as a basis, steadied, consolidated, & well undertaken—consciousness would follow the drift of signs. That possibility doesn’t exist, for this is the escape from all signs (sabbanimittānaṃ): the signless as an awareness-release.’ “And further, there is the case where a monk might say, ‘Although “I am” (asmīti) is gone, and I do not assume that “I am this,” still the arrow of uncertainty & perplexity (vicikicchākathaṃkathāsallaṃ) keeps overpowering my mind.’ He should be told, ‘Don’t say that. You shouldn’t speak in that way. Don’t misrepresent the Blessed One, for it’s not right to misrepresent the Blessed One, and the Blessed One wouldn’t say that. It’s impossible, there is no way that—when “I am” is gone, and “I am this” is not assumed— it is impossible that arrow of uncertainty & perplexity would keep overpowering the mind. That possibility doesn’t exist, for this is the escape from the arrow of uncertainty & perplexity: the uprooting of the conceit, “I am” (asmimānasamugghāṭo).’ These six dhammas are hard to penetrate (duppaṭivijjhā). What are the six dhammas that should be made to arise (uppādetabbā)? Six continual abidings. There is the case, friends, where a monk, on seeing a form (rūpaṃ) via the eye (cakkhunā), is neither gladdened nor saddened, but remains equanimous (upekkhako), mindful (sato), & alert (sampajāno). Having heard a sound (saddaṃ) with the ear…Having smelled an odor (gandhaṃ) with the nose… Having experienced a taste (rasaṃ) with the tongue (jivhāya)… Having felt a tactile object (phoṭṭhabbaṃ) with the body (kāyena)… Having cognized a mental phenomenon (dhammaṃ) with the mind (manasā), he is neither joyful nor saddened, but dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending. These six dhammas should be made to arise. What are the six dhammas that should be directly known (abhiññeyyā)? Six unsurpassables (anuttariyāni): unsurpassable seeing (dassanānuttariyaṃ), unsurpassable hearing (savanānuttariyaṃ), unsurpassable gain (lābhānuttariyaṃ), unsurpassable training (sikkhānuttariyaṃ), unsurpassable attendance (pāricariyānuttariyaṃ), unsurpassable recollection (anussatānuttariyaṃ). These six dhammas should be directly known. What are the six dhammas that should be realized (sacchikātabbā)? Six direct knowledges (cha abhiññā): There is the case, friends, where a monk wields manifold supranormal powers. Having been one he becomes many (ekopi hutvā bahudhā hoti), having been many he becomes one. He appears (āvibhāvaṃ). He vanishes (tirobhāvaṃ). He goes unimpeded through walls (tirokuṭṭaṃ), ramparts (tiropākāraṃ), and mountains (tiropabbataṃ) as if through space (ākāse). He dives in and out of the earth (pathaviyā) as if it were water (udake). He walks on the water without sinking, as if it were dry land. Sitting cross-legged, he travels through space like a winged bird. With his hand he touches and strokes even the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful. He exercises mastery over the body as far as the Brahma-world.

Should [they] be realized?

“With the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, he hears both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, those that are far as well as near.

“He discerns the awareness of other beings, other individuals, having encompassed it with his own awareness, he knows the mind with lust as ‘the mind with lust’…he knows the mind without liberation as ‘the mind without liberation.’

“He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth…and so on… Thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives.

“With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, they see beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and they understand how beings pass on according to their actions…and so on…”

“Through the ending of the *āsavas*, he dwells, having realized it himself with direct knowledge, in the taintless deliverance of mind (*ceto-vimutti*) and deliverance through wisdom (*paññā-vimutti*). These six *dharmas* should be realized.

“Thus, these sixty *dharmas*—true, genuine, real, not unreal, not otherwise—have been rightly awakened to by the *Tathāgata*.

Seven *dharmas*.
commentary_pali:
356. Chakkesu sabbaṃ uttānatthameva. Duppaṭivijjhapade panettha maggo kathito. Sesaṃ purimasadisaṃ.

Sattadhammavaṇṇanā
