358. “Eight *dhamma*s, friends, are very helpful…pe… Eight *dhamma*s should be realized.

(ka) “What are the eight *dhamma*s that are very helpful? Eight causes and eight conditions lead to the acquiring of the as-yet-unacquired wisdom (*prajñā*) that is basic to the holy life (*ādibrahmacariyikāya*), and to the increase, plenitude, development, & culmination of that which has already been acquired.

What are the eight? Here, a *bhikkhu* lives in dependence on the Teacher (*satthāraṃ*), or on a respectable companion in the holy life, in whom he has established a strong sense of shame & compunction, love, & respect. This is the first cause, the first requisite condition that leads to the acquiring of the as-yet-unacquired wisdom that is basic to the holy life, and to the increase, plenitude, development, & culmination of that which has already been acquired.

The *bhikkhu* lives in dependence on the Teacher, or on a respectable companion in the holy life, in whom he has established a strong sense of shame & compunction, love, & respect. He approaches him at the appropriate times to quiz & cross-question him: ‘What, venerable sir, is this? What is the meaning of this?’ Then those venerable ones reveal the unrevealed, explain the unexplained, and remove doubt about the many ideas that raise doubts. This is the second cause, the second requisite condition that leads to the acquiring of the as-yet-unacquired wisdom that is basic to the holy life, and to the increase, plenitude, development, & culmination of that which has already been acquired.

Having heard the *dhamma*, he the student achieves a twofold seclusion: seclusion in body & seclusion in mind. This is the third cause, the third requisite condition that leads to the acquiring of the as-yet-unacquired wisdom that is basic to the holy life, and to the increase, plenitude, development, & culmination of that which has already been acquired.

“Again, a *bhikkhu* is virtuous. He dwells restrained in accordance with the *Pāṭimokkha*, consummate in his behavior & sphere of activity. He trains himself, having undertaken the training rules, seeing danger in the slightest faults. This is the fourth cause, the fourth requisite condition that leads to the acquiring of the as-yet-unacquired wisdom that is basic to the holy life, and to the increase, plenitude, development, & culmination of that which has already been acquired.

“Again, a *bhikkhu* has heard much, has retained what he has heard, has stored what he has heard. Such teachings as are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and which affirm a holy life that is utterly perfect and pure—such teachings as these he has learned much of, remembered, mastered verbally, investigated with the mind, and penetrated well by view. This is the fifth cause, the fifth requisite condition that leads to the acquiring of the as-yet-unacquired wisdom that is basic to the holy life, and to the increase, plenitude, development, & culmination of that which has already been acquired.

“He keeps his persistence aroused for abandoning unskillful qualities and for taking on skillful qualities. He is steadfast, solid in his effort, not shirking his duties with regard to skillful qualities. This is the sixth cause, the sixth requisite condition that leads to the acquiring of the as-yet-unacquired wisdom that is basic to the holy life, and to the increase, plenitude, development, & culmination of that which has already been acquired.
Again, friends, a monk is mindful, endowed with the highest skill in mindfulness, remembering and recollecting what was done and spoken long ago.

This is the seventh cause, the seventh condition, that conduces to the gaining of the wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life, to the increase, abundance, development, and perfection of the wisdom that has already been gained.

Again, friends, a monk dwells contemplating the arising and passing away in the five aggregates subject to clinging: ‘Such is form (rūpa), such is the arising of form, such is the passing away of form; such is feeling (vedanā), such is the arising of feeling, such is the passing away of feeling; such is perception (saññā), such is the arising of perception, such is the passing away of perception; such are fabrications (saṅkhārā), such is the arising of fabrications, such is the passing away of fabrications; such is consciousness (viññāṇa), such is the arising of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.’

This is the eighth cause, the eighth condition, that conduces to the gaining of the wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life, to the increase, abundance, development, and perfection of the wisdom that has already been gained.

These eight things are very helpful.

What eight things should be developed? The Noble Eightfold Path (ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo), that is to say: right view (sammādiṭṭhi), right intention (sammāsaṅkappo), right speech (sammāvācā), right action (sammākammanto), right livelihood (sammāājīvo), right effort (sammāvāyāmo), right mindfulness (sammāsati), right concentration (sammāsamādhi).

These eight things should be developed.

What eight things should be fully understood? The eight worldly conditions (aṭṭha lokadhammā): gain (lābho) and loss (alābho), fame (yaso) and disrepute (ayaso), blame (nindā) and praise (pasaṃsā), happiness (sukhañca) and suffering (dukkhañca).

These eight things should be fully understood.

What eight things should be abandoned? The eight wrongnesses (aṭṭha micchattā): wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi), wrong intention (micchāsaṅkappo), wrong speech (micchāvācā), wrong action (micchākammanto), wrong livelihood (micchāājīvo), wrong effort (micchāvāyāmo), wrong mindfulness (micchāsati), wrong concentration (micchāsamādhi).

These eight things should be abandoned.

What eight things lead to decline? The eight grounds for laziness (aṭṭha kusītavatthūni).

Here, friends, a monk has some work to do, and it occurs to him: ‘I have to do some work, and when I am doing it, my body will get tired. So, why don't I lie down?’

He lies down and does not arouse energy for attaining the unachieved, reaching the unreached, and realizing the unrealized.

This is the first ground for laziness.

What eight things lead to decline?

Again, friends, a monk has done some work,

and it occurs to him: ‘I have already done some work, and now that I have done it, my body is tired. So, why don't I lie down?’

He lies down and does not arouse energy… This is the second ground for laziness.

Again, friends, a monk has to go on a journey,

and it occurs to him: ‘I have to go on a journey, and when I am going, my body will get tired. So, why don't I lie down?’

He lies down and does not arouse energy… This is the third ground for laziness.

Again, friends, a monk has gone on a journey,

and it occurs to him: ‘I have already gone on a journey, and now that I have gone, my body is tired. So, why don't I lie down?’

He lies down and does not arouse energy… This is the fourth ground for laziness.

Again, friends, a monk, while wandering for alms in a village or town, does not get enough coarse or fine food to fill his belly,

and it occurs to him: ‘I have been wandering for alms in a village or town, and I did not get enough coarse or fine food to fill my belly. So, my body is tired and unfit for work. Why don't I lie down?’… This is the fifth ground for laziness.

Again, friends, a monk, while wandering for alms in a village or town, gets enough coarse or fine food to fill his belly,

and it occurs to him: ‘I have been wandering for alms in a village or town, and I got enough coarse or fine food to fill my belly…
The thought occurs to him: ‘This body of mine is heavy & unsuitable for work—stuffed with beans, as it were. Why don’t I lie down?’ So he lies down. … This is the sixth ground for laziness.

Again, friends, a monk comes down with a slight illness. The thought occurs to him: ‘I have come down with a slight illness. There’s a need to lie down. Why don’t I lie down?’ So he lies down. … This is the seventh ground for laziness.

Again, friends, a monk has recovered from his illness, not long after his recovery. The thought occurs to him: ‘I have recovered from my illness. It’s not long after my recovery. This body of mine is weak & unsuitable for work. Why don’t I lie down?’ So he lies down. … This is the eighth ground for laziness. These eight **dhamma**s are on the side of decline.

What are the eight **dhamma**s on the side of distinction? The eight grounds for the arousal of energy. Here, friends, a monk has some work to do. The thought occurs to him: ‘I will have to do this work. But when I am doing this work, it will not be easy to attend to the Buddha’s message. Why don’t I make an effort beforehand for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized?’ So he makes an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized. This is the first ground for the arousal of energy.

What are the eight **dhamma**s on the side of distinction?

Again, friends, a monk has done some work. The thought occurs to him: ‘I have done some work. While I was doing work, I couldn’t attend to the Buddha’s message. Why don’t I make an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized?’ So he makes an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized. This is the second ground for the arousal of energy.

Again, friends, a monk will have to go on a journey. The thought occurs to him: ‘I will have to go on this journey. But when I am going on the journey, it will not be easy to attend to the Buddha’s message. Why don’t I make an effort beforehand for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized?’ So he makes an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized. This is the third ground for the arousal of energy.

Again, friends, a monk has gone on a journey. The thought occurs to him: ‘I have gone on a journey. While I was going on the journey, I couldn’t attend to the Buddha’s message. Why don’t I make an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized?’ So he makes an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized. This is the fourth ground for the arousal of energy.

Again, friends, a monk, having gone for alms in a village or town, does not get as much coarse or refined food as he would like for his fill. The thought occurs to him: ‘I, having gone for alms in a village or town, have not gotten as much coarse or refined food as I would like for my fill. This body of mine is light & suitable for work. Why don’t I make an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized?’ So he makes an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized. This is the fifth ground for the arousal of energy.

Again, friends, a monk, having gone for alms in a village or town, gets as much coarse or refined food as he would like for his fill. The thought occurs to him: ‘I, having gone for alms in a village or town, have gotten as much coarse or refined food as I would like for my fill. This body of mine is light & suitable for work. Why don’t I make an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized?’ So he makes an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized. This is the sixth ground for the arousal of energy.

Again, friends, a monk comes down with a slight illness. The thought occurs to him: ‘I have come down with a slight illness. Now, there’s the possibility that it could get worse. Why don’t I make an effort beforehand for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized?’ So he makes an effort for the attaining of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized. This is the seventh ground for the arousal of energy.
“Furthermore, friends, a monk has recovered from his illness, not long after his recovery.

The thought occurs to him: ‘I have recovered from my illness. It’s not long after my recovery. Now, there’s the possibility that the illness could come back. Why don’t I arouse energy for the attainment of the as-yet-unattained, the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, the realization of the as-yet-unrealized?’

So he arouses energy for the attainment of the as-yet-unattained, for the reaching of the as-yet-unreached, for the realization of the as-yet-unrealized.

This is the eighth ground for the arousal of energy (ārambhavatthu).

These eight *dhamma*s are on the side of distinction.

(cha) “What eight *dhamma*s are hard to penetrate (*duppaṭivijjhā*)? The eight inopportune, untimely situations for leading the holy life (*brahmacariyavāsa*).

Here, friends, a *Tathāgata* appears in the world, a worthy one, a rightly self-awakened one (*arahaṃ sammāsambuddho*), and the *Dhamma* is taught that leads to stilling, to total unbinding (*parinibbānika*), to self-awakening (*sambodhagāmī*) as declared by One Well-gone (*sugatāppavedito*).

But this person is reborn in hell (*nirayaṃ upapanno hoti*).

This is the first inopportune, untimely situation for leading the holy life.

“Furthermore, friends, a *Tathāgata* appears in the world, a worthy one, a rightly self-awakened one (*arahaṃ sammāsambuddho*), and the *Dhamma* is taught that leads to stilling, to total unbinding (*parinibbānika*), to self-awakening (*sambodhagāmī*) as declared by One Well-gone (*sugatāppavedito*), but this person is reborn in an animal womb (*tiracchānayoniṃ upapanno hoti*).

This is the second inopportune, untimely situation for leading the holy life.

“Furthermore…he is reborn in the realm of ghosts (*pettivisayaṃ upapanno hoti*).

This is the third inopportune, untimely situation for leading the holy life.

“Furthermore…he is reborn in a certain host of long-lived *deva*s (*dīghāyukaṃ devanikāyaṃ upapanno hoti*).

This is the fourth inopportune, untimely situation for leading the holy life.

“Furthermore…he is born in a border region among ignorant barbarians (*milakkha*s) where there is no opening for monks (*bhikkhu*s), nuns (*bhikkhunī*s), male lay followers (*upāsaka*s), or female lay followers (*upāsika*s) to go.

This is the fifth inopportune, untimely situation for leading the holy life.

“Furthermore…this person is born in the Middle Country, but he has wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhiko*) and skewed vision (*viparītadassano*): ‘There is nothing given (*dinnaṃ*), nothing offered (*yiṭṭhaṃ*), nothing sacrificed (*hutaṃ*). There is no fruit or result (*phalaṃ vipāko*) of good or bad actions (*sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ*). There is no this world (*ayaṃ loko*), no next world (*paro loko*), no mother (*mātā*), no father (*pitā*); there are no spontaneously reborn beings (*sattā opapātikā*); there are no *samaṇa*s or *brāhmaṇa*s who, faring rightly and practicing rightly (*sammāpaṭipannā*), proclaim this world and the next after having directly known and realized it for themselves (*sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedentī*)’.

This is the sixth inopportune, untimely situation for leading the holy life.

“Furthermore…this person is born in the Middle Country, but he is undiscerning (*duppañño*), dull (*jaḷo*), drooling (*eḷamūgo*), incapable of knowing the meaning of what is well-said or ill-said (*subhāsitadubbhāsitānamattham aññātuṃ*).

This is the seventh inopportune, untimely situation for leading the holy life.

“Furthermore…this person is born in the Middle Country, and he is discerning (*paññavā*), not dull (*ajaḷo*), not drooling (*aneḷamūgo*), capable of knowing the meaning of what is well-said or ill-said (*subhāsitadubbhāsitānamattham aññātuṃ*).

This is the eighth inopportune, untimely situation for leading the holy life.

These eight *dhamma*s are hard to penetrate (*duppaṭivijjhā*).

(ja) “What eight *dhamma*s should be developed (*uppādetabbā*)? The eight thoughts of a great man (*mahāpurisavitakka*) – This *Dhamma* is for one who is content with little (*appiccha*), not for one who is of great desires (*mahiccha*).

This *Dhamma* is for one who is content (*santuṭṭha*), not for one who is discontent (*asantuṭṭha*).

This *Dhamma* is for one who is reclusive (*pavivitta*), not for one who delights in society (*saṅgaṇikārāma*).

This *Dhamma* is for one whose energy is aroused (*āraddhavīriya*), not for one who is lazy (*kusīta*).

This *Dhamma* is for one whose mindfulness is established (*upaṭṭhitasati*), not for one whose mindfulness is confused (*muṭṭhassati*).

This *Dhamma* is for one whose mind is concentrated (*samāhita*), not for one whose mind is unconcentrated (*asamāhita*).
This *dharma* is for one endowed with wisdom (*prajñāvatas*), not for one whose wisdom is weak (*duṣprajñasya*).

This *dharma* is for one who is free from proliferation (*niṣprapañcas*), not for one who delights in proliferation. These eight *dharmas* should be cultivated.

What eight *dharmas* should be fully known (*abhijñeyyā*)? The eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhāyatanas*): One with the perception of form internally sees forms externally as limited, beautiful and ugly; mastering them, one is aware that one knows and sees them. This is the first sphere of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*).

One with the perception of form internally sees forms externally as immeasurable, beautiful and ugly; mastering them, one is aware that one knows and sees them. This is the second sphere of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*).

One with the perception of the formless internally sees forms externally as limited, beautiful and ugly; mastering them, one is aware that one knows and sees them. This is the third sphere of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*).

One with the perception of the formless internally sees forms externally as immeasurable, beautiful and ugly; mastering them, one is aware that one knows and sees them. This is the fourth sphere of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*).

One with the perception of the formless internally sees forms externally as blue, blue in their color, blue in their features, blue in their glow. Just as a flax flower is blue, blue in its color, blue in its features, blue in its glow, or just as Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, is blue, blue in its color, blue in its features, blue in its glow; in the same way one with the perception of the formless internally sees forms externally as blue, blue in their color, blue in their features, blue in their glow; mastering them, one is aware that one knows and sees them. This is the fifth sphere of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*).

One with the perception of the formless internally sees forms externally as yellow, yellow in their color, yellow in their features, yellow in their glow. Just as a *kaṇikāra* flower is yellow, yellow in its color, yellow in its features, yellow in its glow, or just as Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, is yellow, yellow in its color, yellow in its features, yellow in its glow; in the same way one with the perception of the formless internally sees forms externally as yellow, yellow in their color, yellow in their features, yellow in their glow; mastering them, one is aware that one knows and sees them. This is the sixth sphere of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*).

One with the perception of the formless internally sees forms externally as red, red in their color, red in their features, red in their glow.
Just as a *bandhujīvaka* flower (*bandhujīvakapupphaṃ*) is red (*lohitakaṃ*), red in its color (*lohitakavaṇṇaṃ*), red in its features (*lohitakanidassanaṃ*), red in its glow (*lohitakanibhāsaṃ*), or just as Vārāṇasī muslin (*vatthaṃ bārāṇaseyyakaṃ*), smooth on both sides (*ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ*), is red (*lohitakaṃ*), red in its color (*lohitakavaṇṇaṃ*), red in its features (*lohitakanidassanaṃ*), red in its glow (*lohitakanibhāsaṃ*), in the same way one percipient of the formless internally (*ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko*) sees forms externally (*bahiddhā rūpāni passati*) as red (*lohitakāni*), red in their color (*lohitakavaṇṇāni*), red in their features (*lohitakanidassanāni*), red in their glow (*lohitakanibhāsāni*). Mastering them, he is percipient of ‘I know; I see.’
This is the seventh dimension of mastery (*idaṃ sattamaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ*).

“One percipient of the formless internally (*ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko*) sees forms externally (*bahiddhā rūpāni passati*) as white (*odātāni*), white in their color (*odātavaṇṇāni*), white in their features (*odātanidassanāni*), white in their glow (*odātanibhāsāni*).
Just as the morning star (*osadhitārakā*) is white (*odātā*), white in its color (*odātavaṇṇā*), white in its features (*odātanidassanā*), white in its glow (*odātanibhāsā*), or just as Vārāṇasī muslin (*vatthaṃ bārāṇaseyyakaṃ*), smooth on both sides (*ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ*), is white (*odātaṃ*), white in its color (*odātavaṇṇaṃ*), white in its features (*odātanidassanaṃ*), white in its glow (*odātanibhāsaṃ*), in the same way one percipient of the formless internally (*ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko*) sees forms externally (*bahiddhā rūpāni passati*) as white (*odātāni*), white in their color (*odātavaṇṇāni*), white in their features (*odātanidassanāni*), white in their glow (*odātanibhāsāni*). Mastering them, he is percipient of ‘I know; I see.’
This is the eighth dimension of mastery (*idaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ*).
These eight *dhammas* should be directly known (*ime aṭṭha dhammā abhiññeyyā*).

(ña) What eight *dhammas* should be realized (*aṭṭha dhammā sacchikātabbā*)? The eight liberations (*aṭṭha vimokkhā*) - Possessed of form, one sees forms (*rūpī rūpāni passati*).
This is the first liberation (*ayaṃ paṭhamo vimokkho*).
What eight *dhammas* should be realized (*aṭṭha dhammā sacchikātabbā*)? One not perceiving material forms internally sees material forms externally (*ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati*).
This is the second liberation (*ayaṃ dutiyo vimokkho*).
Thinking: “It is beautiful” (*subhanteva*), one becomes intent on it (*adhimutto hoti*).
This is the third liberation (*ayaṃ tatiyo vimokkho*).
Through the complete surmounting of perceptions of material form (*sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā*), the passing away of perceptions of impingement (*paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā*), and non-attention to perceptions of diversity (*nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā*), ‘Space is infinite (*ananto ākāso*)’ one enters and dwells in the base of the infinity of space (*ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati*).
This is the fourth liberation (*ayaṃ catuttho vimokkho*).
Having completely surmounted the base of the infinity of space (*sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma*), ‘Consciousness is infinite (*anantaṃ viññāṇaṃ*)’ one enters and dwells in the base of the infinity of consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati*).
This is the fifth liberation (*ayaṃ pañcamo vimokkho*).
By transcending the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma*), thinking: “There is no thing (*natthi kiñcī*)”, one enters and abides in the Sphere of No-Thingness (*ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati*).
This is the sixth liberation (*ayaṃ chaṭṭho vimokkho*).
By utterly transcending the sphere of nothingness (*sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma*), one enters and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati*).
This is the seventh liberation (*ayaṃ sattamo vimokkho*).
By transcending the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*sabbaso nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma*), one enters and abides in the Cessation of Perception and Feeling (*saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ upasampajja viharati*).
This is the eighth liberation (*ayaṃ aṭṭhamo vimokkho*).
These eight *dhammas* should be realized (*ime aṭṭha dhammā sacchikātabbā*).

Thus, these eighty *dhammas*—true (*bhūtā*), genuine (*tacchā*), real (*tathā*), not unreal (*avitathā*), not otherwise (*anaññathā*)—have been rightly awakened to by the Tathāgata (*sammā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā*).

Nine *dhammas*.
commentary_pali:
358. (Ka) ādibrahmacariyikāya paññāyāti sikkhattayasaṅgahassa maggabrahmacariyassa ādibhūtāya pubbabhāge taruṇasamathavipassanāpaññāya . Aṭṭhaṅgikassa vā maggassa ādibhūtāya sammādiṭṭhipaññāya. Tibbanti balavaṃ. Hirottappanti hirī ca ottappañca. Pemanti gehassitapemaṃ. Gāravoti garucittabhāvo. Garubhāvanīyañhi upanissāya viharato kilesā nuppajjanti ovādānusāsaniṃ labhati. Tasmā taṃ nissāya vihāro paññāpaṭilābhassa paccayo hoti.

(Cha) akkhaṇesu yasmā petā asurānaṃ āvāhanaṃ gacchanti, vivāhanaṃ gacchanti, tasmā pettivisayeneva asurakāyo gahitoti veditabbo.

(Ja) appicchassāti ettha paccayaappiccho, adhigamaappiccho, pariyattiappiccho, dhutaṅgaappicchoti cattāro appicchā. Tattha paccayaappiccho bahuṃ dente appaṃ gaṇhāti, appaṃ dente appataraṃ vā gaṇhāti, na vā gaṇhāti, na anavasesagāhī hoti. Adhigamaappiccho majjhantikatthero viya attano adhigamaṃ aññesaṃ jānituṃ na deti. Pariyattiappiccho tepiṭakopi samāno na bahussutabhāvaṃ jānāpetukāmo hoti sāketatissatthero viya. Dhutaṅgaappiccho dhutaṅgapariharaṇabhāvaṃ aññesaṃ jānituṃ na deti dvebhātikattheresu jeṭṭhakatthero viya. Vatthu visuddhimagge kathitaṃ. Ayaṃ dhammoti evaṃ santaguṇanigūhanena ca paccayapaṭiggahaṇe mattaññutāya ca appicchassa puggalassa ayaṃ navalokuttaradhammo sampajjati, no mahicchassa. Evaṃ sabbattha yojetabbaṃ.

appicchassā Ayaṃ dhammo

Santuṭṭhassāti catūsu paccayesu tīhi santosehi santuṭṭhassa. Pavivittassāti kāyacittaupadhivivekehi vivittassa. Tattha kāyaviveko nāma gaṇasaṅgaṇikaṃ vinodetvā aṭṭhaārambhavatthuvasena ekībhāvo. Ekībhāvamattena pana kammaṃ na nipphajjatīti kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbatteti, ayaṃ cittaviveko nāma. Samāpattimatteneva kammaṃ na nipphajjatīti jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā saṅkhāre sammasitvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, ayaṃ upadhiviveko nāma. Tenāha bhagavā – ‘‘kāyaviveko ca vivekaṭṭhakāyānaṃ nekkhammābhiratānaṃ. Cittaviveko ca parisuddhacittānaṃ paramavodānappattānaṃ. Upadhiviveko ca nirupadhīnaṃ puggalānaṃ visaṅkhāragatāna’’nti (mahāni. 49).

Santuṭṭhassā Pavivittassā kāyaviveko cittaviveko upadhiviveko

Saṅgaṇikārāmassāti gaṇasaṅgaṇikāya ceva kilesasaṅgaṇikāya ca ratassa. Āraddhavīriyassāti kāyikacetasikavīriyavasena āraddhavīriyassa. Upaṭṭhitasatissāti catusatipaṭṭhānavasena upaṭṭhitasatissa. Samāhitassāti ekaggacittassa. Paññavatoti kammassakatapaññāya paññavato. Nippapañcassāti vigatamānataṇhādiṭṭhipapañcassa.

Saṅgaṇikārāmassā Āraddhavīriyassā Upaṭṭhitasatissā Samāhitassā Paññavato Nippapañcassā

Idha bhāvetabbapade maggo kathito. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva.

Navadhammavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
358. (ka) *ādibrahmacariyikāya paññāyā* means the wisdom that is the beginning of the path of the holy life, which encompasses the three trainings, or the wisdom of right view that is the beginning of the eightfold path, or the preliminary insight of nascent serenity and insight (*samatha-vipassanā*). *Tibba* means strong. *Hiri-ottappa* means moral shame and dread of evil. *Pema* means household affection. *Gāravo* means having a reverential mind. For when one lives relying on what should be revered, defilements do not arise, and one obtains instruction and guidance. Therefore, living in reliance on that is a condition for gaining wisdom.

(cha) Because at inauspicious times the departed spirits go to invite the demons and go to marry, therefore, it should be understood that the demon host is included in the realm of the departed spirits.

(ja) *Appicchassa* here means four kinds of having few wants: having few wants regarding requisites, having few wants regarding attainment, having few wants regarding learning, and having few wants regarding ascetic practices. There, having few wants regarding requisites means when someone gives much, one takes little, when someone gives little, one takes even less, or one does not take at all; one is not one who takes everything without leaving anything. Having few wants regarding attainment is like the Elder Majjhantika, who does not allow others to know of his attainments. Having few wants regarding learning is like the Elder Saketa Tissa, who, even though being a master of the three baskets (*tipitaka*), does not want to make known that he is very learned. Having few wants regarding ascetic practice is like the elder brother among the two brother elders, who does not allow others to know of his practice of undertaking the ascetic observances (*dhutaṅga*). The subject matter is discussed in the *Path of Purification* (*Visuddhimagga*). *Ayaṃ dhammo* means in this way, this supramundane Dhamma comes to be possessed by a person who has few wants because of concealing one’s virtues and because of knowing the right amount in receiving requisites, not by one who has great desires. Thus, it should be connected everywhere.

*Appicchassā ayaṃ dhammo*

*Santuṭṭhassā* means being content with three kinds of contentment regarding the four requisites. *Pavivittassā* means being secluded by way of physical, mental, and basis of existence seclusion. There, *kāyaviveko* means eliminating association with groups and being alone by way of the eight grounds for exertion. However, since the task is not accomplished by merely being alone, one performs the preliminary work with a colored disc (*kasiṇa*) and brings about the eight attainments; this is called *cittaviveko*. Since the task is not accomplished by mere attainment, one makes the absorption (*jhāna*) a foundation, reflects on conditioned phenomena, and attains arahantship together with the discriminations; this is called *upadhiviveko*. Therefore, the Blessed One said, “Physical seclusion is for those with bodies set apart, delighting in renunciation. Mental seclusion is for those with perfectly pure minds, having attained the highest purity. Basis-of-existence seclusion is for those persons without a basis of existence, who have gone to the unconditioned” (Mahāni. 49).

*Santuṭṭhassā pavivittassā kāyaviveko cittaviveko upadhiviveko*

*Saṅgaṇikārāmassā* means delighting in association with groups and association with defilements. *Āraddhavīriyassā* means having aroused energy by way of physical and mental energy. *Upaṭṭhitasatissā* means having mindfulness established by way of the four establishments of mindfulness. *Samāhitassā* means having one-pointedness of mind. *Paññavato* means possessing wisdom by way of the wisdom of ownership of deeds. *Nippapañcassā* means being free from the proliferation of conceit, craving, views, and so forth.

*Saṅgaṇikārāmassā*
Of one who has aroused his energy, of one who has mindfulness established, of one who is concentrated, of one who is wise, of one who is free from proliferation: Here, in the section on what should be developed, the path is described.

The rest is the same as before.

Description of the nine qualities.

mula_pali:
359. ‘‘Nava dhammā bahukārā…pe… nava dhammā sacchikātabbā.

(Ka) ‘‘katame nava dhammā bahukārā? Nava yonisomanasikāramūlakā dhammā, yonisomanasikaroto pāmojjaṃ jāyati, pamuditassa pīti jāyati, pītimanassa kāyo passambhati, passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedeti, sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati, samāhite citte yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati, yathābhūtaṃ jānaṃ passaṃ nibbindati, nibbindaṃ virajjati, virāgā vimuccati. Ime nava dhammā bahukārā.

bahukārā?

(Kha) ‘‘katame nava dhammā bhāvetabbā? Nava pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgāni – sīlavisuddhi pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ, cittavisuddhi pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ, diṭṭhivisuddhi pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ, kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ, maggāmaggañāṇadassana – visuddhi pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ, paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ, ñāṇadassanavisuddhi pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ, paññāvisuddhi pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ, vimuttivisuddhi pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ. Ime nava dhammā bhāvetabbā.

bhāvetabbā?

(Ga) ‘‘katame nava dhammā pariññeyyā? Nava sattāvāsā – santāvuso, sattā nānattakāyā nānattasaññino, seyyathāpi manussā ekacce ca devā ekacce ca vinipātikā. Ayaṃ paṭhamo sattāvāso.

pariññeyyā?

‘‘Santāvuso , sattā nānattakāyā ekattasaññino, seyyathāpi devā brahmakāyikā paṭhamābhinibbattā. Ayaṃ dutiyo sattāvāso.

‘‘Santāvuso, sattā ekattakāyā nānattasaññino, seyyathāpi devā ābhassarā. Ayaṃ tatiyo sattāvāso.

‘‘Santāvuso, sattā ekattakāyā ekattasaññino, seyyathāpi devā subhakiṇhā. Ayaṃ catuttho sattāvāso.

‘‘Santāvuso, sattā asaññino appaṭisaṃvedino, seyyathāpi devā asaññasattā. Ayaṃ pañcamo sattāvāso.

‘‘Santāvuso, sattā sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanūpagā. Ayaṃ chaṭṭho sattāvāso.

‘‘Santāvuso, sattā sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanūpagā. Ayaṃ sattamo sattāvāso.

‘‘Santāvuso, sattā sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanūpagā. Ayaṃ aṭṭhamo sattāvāso.

‘‘Santāvuso, sattā sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma nevasaññānāsaññāyatanūpagā. Ayaṃ navamo sattāvāso. Ime nava dhammā pariññeyyā.

(Gha) ‘‘katame nava dhammā pahātabbā? Nava taṇhāmūlakā dhammā – taṇhaṃ paṭicca pariyesanā, pariyesanaṃ paṭicca lābho, lābhaṃ paṭicca vinicchayo, vinicchayaṃ paṭicca chandarāgo , chandarāgaṃ paṭicca ajjhosānaṃ, ajjhosānaṃ paṭicca pariggaho, pariggahaṃ paṭicca macchariyaṃ, macchariyaṃ paṭicca ārakkho, ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ paṭicca (syā. pī. ka.) daṇḍādānasatthādānakalahaviggahavivādatuvaṃtuvaṃpesuññamusāvādā aneke pāpakā akusalā dhammā sambhavanti. Ime nava dhammā pahātabbā.

pahātabbā? ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ paṭicca (syā. pī. ka.)

(Ṅa) ‘‘katame nava dhammā hānabhāgiyā? Nava āghātavatthūni – ‘anatthaṃ me acarī’ti āghātaṃ bandhati, ‘anatthaṃ me caratī’ti āghātaṃ bandhati, ‘anatthaṃ me carissatī’ti āghātaṃ bandhati; ‘piyassa me manāpassa anatthaṃ acarī’ti āghātaṃ bandhati…pe… ‘anatthaṃ caratī’ti āghātaṃ bandhati…pe… ‘anatthaṃ carissatī’ti āghātaṃ bandhati; ‘appiyassa me amanāpassa atthaṃ acarī’ti āghātaṃ bandhati…pe… ‘atthaṃ caratī’ti āghātaṃ bandhati…pe… ‘atthaṃ carissatī’ti āghātaṃ bandhati. Ime nava dhammā hānabhāgiyā.

hānabhāgiyā?

(Ca) ‘‘katame nava dhammā visesabhāgiyā? Nava āghātapaṭivinayā – ‘anatthaṃ me acari, taṃ kutettha labbhā’ti āghātaṃ paṭivineti; ‘anatthaṃ me carati, taṃ kutettha labbhā’ti āghātaṃ paṭivineti; ‘anatthaṃ me carissati, taṃ kutettha labbhā’ti āghātaṃ paṭivineti; ‘piyassa me manāpassa anatthaṃ acari…pe… anatthaṃ carati…pe… anatthaṃ carissati, taṃ kutettha labbhā’ti āghātaṃ paṭivineti; ‘appiyassa me amanāpassa atthaṃ acari…pe… atthaṃ carati…pe… atthaṃ carissati, taṃ kutettha labbhā’ti āghātaṃ paṭivineti. Ime nava dhammā visesabhāgiyā.

visesabhāgiyā?

(Cha) ‘‘katame nava dhammā duppaṭivijjhā? Nava nānattā – dhātunānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati phassanānattaṃ, phassanānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati vedanānānattaṃ, vedanānānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati saññānānattaṃ, saññānānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati saṅkappanānattaṃ, saṅkappanānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandanānattaṃ, chandanānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati pariḷāhanānattaṃ, pariḷāhanānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati pariyesanānānattaṃ, pariyesanānānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati lābhanānattaṃ. Ime nava dhammā duppaṭivijjhā.

duppaṭivijjhā?

(Ja) ‘‘katame nava dhammā uppādetabbā? Nava saññā – asubhasaññā, maraṇasaññā, āhārepaṭikūlasaññā , sabbalokeanabhiratisaññā anabhiratasaññā (syā. ka.), aniccasaññā, anicce dukkhasaññā, dukkhe anattasaññā, pahānasaññā, virāgasaññā. Ime nava dhammā uppādetabbā.

uppādetabbā? anabhiratasaññā (syā. ka.)

(Jha) ‘‘katame nava dhammā abhiññeyyā? Nava anupubbavihārā – idhāvuso, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā…pe… dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Pītiyā ca virāgā …pe… tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sukhassa ca pahānā…pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā…pe… ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sabbaso nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ime nava dhammā abhiññeyyā.

abhiññeyyā?

(Ña) ‘‘katame nava dhammā sacchikātabbā? Nava anupubbanirodhā – paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa kāmasaññā niruddhā hoti, dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa vitakkavicārā niruddhā honti, tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa pīti niruddhā hoti, catutthaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa assāsapassāssā niruddhā honti, ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samāpannassa rūpasaññā niruddhā hoti, viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samāpannassa ākāsānañcāyatanasaññā niruddhā hoti, ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samāpannassa viññāṇañcāyatanasaññā niruddhā hoti, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samāpannassa ākiñcaññāyatanasaññā niruddhā hoti, saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpannassa saññā ca vedanā ca niruddhā honti. Ime nava dhammā sacchikātabbā.

sacchikātabbā?

‘‘Iti ime navuti dhammā bhūtā tacchā tathā avitathā anaññathā sammā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā.

Dasa dhammā
mula_english:
359. “Nine *dhammas*, friends, are very helpful... Nine *dhammas* should be realized.

(a) "What are the nine *dhammas* that are very helpful (*bahukārā*)? They are the nine *dhammas* rooted in appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*): In one who is appropriately attentive, joy (*pāmojjaṃ*) is born. When one is joyful, rapture (*pīti*) is born. In one who is enraptured at heart, the body (*kāyo*) grows calm (*passambhati*). When the body is calm, one feels pleasure (*sukhaṃ vedeti*). Feeling pleasure, the mind (*cittaṃ*) becomes concentrated (*samādhiyati*). When the mind is concentrated, one knows and sees (*yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati*) what has come to be. Knowing and seeing what has come to be, one is disenchanted (*nibbindati*). Disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate (*virajjati*). From dispassion, one is released (*vimuccati*). These nine *dhammas* are very helpful.

(b) "What are the nine *dhammas* that should be developed (*bhāvetabbā*)? They are the nine factors in the endeavour for purification (*pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgāni*): purity of moral conduct (*sīlavisuddhi*) is a factor in the endeavour for purification, purity of mind (*cittavisuddhi*) is a factor in the endeavour for purification, purity of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*) is a factor in the endeavour for purification, purity of overcoming doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi*) is a factor in the endeavour for purification, purity of knowledge and vision of what is the path and not the path (*maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi*) is a factor in the endeavour for purification, purity of knowledge and vision of the course of practice (*paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi*) is a factor in the endeavour for purification, purity of knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassanavisuddhi*) is a factor in the endeavour for purification, purity of wisdom (*paññāvisuddhi*) is a factor in the endeavour for purification, purity of release (*vimuttivisuddhi*) is a factor in the endeavour for purification. These nine *dhammas* should be developed.

(c) "What are the nine *dhammas* that should be fully understood (*pariññeyyā*)? They are the nine abodes of beings (*sattāvāsā*): Here, friends, there are beings with diversity of body (*nānattakāyā*) and diversity of perception (*nānattasaññino*), such as human beings (*manussā*), some gods (*devā*), and some beings in the states of loss (*vinipātikā*). This is the first abode for beings (*sattāvāso*).

Here, friends, there are beings with diversity of body and singularity of perception (*ekattasaññino*), such as the gods of the Brahma-world (*brahmakāyikā devā*) generated by the first jhāna (*paṭhamābhinibbattā*). This is the second abode for beings.

Here, friends, there are beings with singularity of body and diversity of perception, such as the gods of streaming radiance (*ābhassarā devā*). This is the third abode for beings.

Here, friends, there are beings with singularity of body and singularity of perception, such as the gods of beautiful glory (*subhakiṇhā devā*). This is the fourth abode for beings.

Here, friends, there are beings without perception (*asaññino*) and without any feeling (*appaṭisaṃvedino*), such as the unpercipient beings (*asaññasattā devā*). This is the fifth abode for beings.

Here, friends, there are beings who, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form (*rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā*), with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact (*paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā*), not attending to perceptions of diversity (*nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā*), [thinking,] ‘Infinite is space,’ arrive at the dimension of the infinity of space (*ākāsānañcāyatanūpagā*). This is the sixth abode for beings.

Here, friends, there are beings who, with the complete surmounting of the dimension of the infinity of space, [thinking,] ‘Infinite is consciousness,’ arrive at the dimension of the infinity of consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatanūpagā*). This is the seventh abode for beings.

Here, friends, there are beings who, with the complete surmounting of the dimension of the infinity of consciousness, [thinking,] ‘There is nothing,’ arrive at the dimension of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatanūpagā*). This is the eighth abode for beings.

Here, friends, there are beings who, with the complete surmounting of the dimension of nothingness, arrive at the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatanūpagā*). This is the ninth abode for beings. These nine *dhammas* should be fully understood.

(d) "What are the nine *dhammas* that should be abandoned (*pahātabbā*)? They are the nine *dhammas* rooted in craving (*taṇhāmūlakā dhammā*): Seeking (*pariyesanā*) is dependent on craving (*taṇhaṃ paṭicca*); acquisition (*lābho*) is dependent on seeking; ascertainment (*vinicchayo*) is dependent on acquisition; desire and passion (*chandarāgo*) is dependent on ascertainment; attachment (*ajjhosānaṃ*) is dependent on desire and passion; possessiveness (*pariggaho*) is dependent on attachment; stinginess (*macchariyaṃ*) is dependent on possessiveness; defensiveness (*ārakkho*) is dependent on stinginess; and because of defensiveness, the taking up of sticks and knives (*daṇḍādānasatthādāna*); conflicts, quarrels, and disputes (*kalahaviggahavivāda*); accusations, divisive speech (*pesuñña*), and lies (*musāvādā*), various evil, unskillful *dhammas* (*anekā pāpakā akusalā dhammā*) come into play (*sambhavanti*). These nine *dhammas* should be abandoned."
(ṅa) "What are the nine dhammas on the side of decline (*hānabhāgiyā*)? Nine grounds for animosity (*āghātavatthūni*) – ‘He has done me harm,’ one binds hatred (*āghātaṃ bandhati*); ‘He is doing me harm,’ one binds hatred; ‘He is going to do me harm,’ one binds hatred; ‘He has done harm to people who are dear & pleasing to me,’ one binds hatred…pe… ‘He is doing harm,’ one binds hatred…pe… ‘He is going to do harm,’ one binds hatred; ‘He has aided people who are not dear or pleasing to me,’ one binds hatred…pe… ‘He is aiding,’ one binds hatred…pe… ‘He is going to aid,’ one binds hatred. These nine dhammas are on the side of decline (*hānabhāgiyā*).

(ca) "What are the nine *dharmas* on the side of distinction (*visesabhāgiyā*)? Nine ways of removing animosity (*āghātapaṭivinayā*) – ‘He has done me harm, what can be gained from that?’ one removes animosity; ‘He is doing me harm, what can be gained from that?’ one removes animosity; ‘He is going to do me harm, what can be gained from that?’ one removes animosity; ‘He has done harm to people who are dear & pleasing to me…pe… he is doing harm…pe… he is going to do harm, what can be gained from that?’ one removes animosity; ‘He has aided people who are not dear or pleasing to me…pe… he is aiding…pe… he is going to aid, what can be gained from that?’ one removes animosity. These nine *dharmas* are on the side of distinction (*visesabhāgiyā*).

(cha) "What are the nine *dharmas* that are hard to penetrate (*duppaṭivijjhā*)? Nine multiplicities (*nānattā*) – dependent on a multiplicity of elements (*dhātunānattaṃ*), there arises a multiplicity of contacts (*phassanānattaṃ*); dependent on a multiplicity of contacts, there arises a multiplicity of feelings (*vedanānānattaṃ*); dependent on a multiplicity of feelings, there arises a multiplicity of perceptions (*saññānānattaṃ*); dependent on a multiplicity of perceptions, there arises a multiplicity of resolves (*saṅkappanānattaṃ*); dependent on a multiplicity of resolves, there arises a multiplicity of desires (*chandanānattaṃ*); dependent on a multiplicity of desires, there arises a multiplicity of burning (*pariḷāhanānattaṃ*); dependent on a multiplicity of burning, there arises a multiplicity of search (*pariyesanānānattaṃ*); dependent on a multiplicity of search, there arises a multiplicity of gains (*lābhanānattaṃ*). These nine *dharmas* are hard to penetrate (*duppaṭivijjhā*).

(ja) "What are the nine *dharmas* that should be developed (*uppādetabbā*)? Nine perceptions (*saññā*) – perception of unattractiveness (*asubhasaññā*), perception of death (*maraṇasaññā*), perception of disgust toward food (*āhārepaṭikūlasaññā*), perception of non-delight in the entire world (*sabbalokeanabhiratisaññā*), perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*), perception of suffering in impermanence (*anicce dukkhasaññā*), perception of not-self in suffering (*dukkhe anattasaññā*), perception of abandonment (*pahānasaññā*), perception of dispassion (*virāgasaññā*). These nine *dharmas* should be developed (*uppādetabbā*).

(jha) "What are the nine *dharmas* that should be directly known (*abhiññeyyā*)? Nine successive dwelling places (*anupubbavihārā*) – Here, friend, a *bhikkhu*, quite secluded from sense pleasures, secluded from unwholesome *dharmas*, enters and dwells in the first *jhāna*, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. With the subsiding of thought and examination… he enters and dwells in the second *jhāna*. With the fading away of rapture… he enters and dwells in the third *jhāna*. With the abandoning of pleasure… he enters and dwells in the fourth *jhāna*. With the complete transcending of perceptions of form… he enters and dwells in the sphere of the infinitude of space (*ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ*). With the complete transcending of the sphere of the infinitude of space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite,’ he enters and dwells in the sphere of the infinitude of consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ*). With the complete transcending of the sphere of the infinitude of consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing,’ he enters and dwells in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ*). With the complete transcending of the sphere of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ*). With the complete transcending of the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, he enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ*). These nine *dharmas* should be directly known (*abhiññeyyā*).
(ña) "Which are the nine *dharmas* to be realized? They are the nine successive cessations (*anupubbanirodhā*): When one has attained the first *jhāna*, the perception of sensuality (*kāmasaññā*) has ceased (*niruddhā hoti*). When one has attained the second *jhāna*, directed thought (*vitakka*) and evaluation (*vicāra*) have ceased (*niruddhā honti*). When one has attained the third *jhāna*, rapture (*pīti*) has ceased (*niruddhā hoti*). When one has attained the fourth *jhāna*, in-and-out breaths (*assāsapassāssā*) have ceased (*niruddhā honti*). When one has attained the dimension of the infinitude of space (*ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ*), the perception of forms (*rūpasaññā*) has ceased (*niruddhā hoti*). When one has attained the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ*), the perception of the dimension of the infinitude of space (*ākāsānañcāyatanasaññā*) has ceased (*niruddhā hoti*). When one has attained the dimension of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ*), the perception of the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatanasaññā*) has ceased (*niruddhā hoti*). When one has attained the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ*), the perception of the dimension of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatanasaññā*) has ceased (*niruddhā hoti*). When one has attained the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ*), perception (*saññā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) have ceased (*niruddhā honti*).

These nine *dharmas* should be realized (*sacchikātabbā*).

"Thus, these ninety *dharmas*—true (*bhūtā*), genuine (*tacchā*), real (*tathā*), not unreal (*avitathā*), not otherwise (*anaññathā*)—have been rightly awakened to (*abhisambuddhā*) by the *Tathāgata*.

Ten *dharmas*.
commentary_pali:
359. (Kha) sīlavisuddhīti visuddhiṃ pāpetuṃ samatthaṃ catupārisuddhisīlaṃ. Pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅganti parisuddhabhāvassa padhānaṅgaṃ. Cittavisuddhīti vipassanāya padaṭṭhānabhūtā aṭṭha paguṇasamāpattiyo. Diṭṭhivisuddhīti sapaccayanāmarūpadassanaṃ. Kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhīti paccayākārañāṇaṃ. Addhattayepi hi paccayavaseneva dhammā pavattantīti passato kaṅkhaṃ vitarati. Maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhīti obhāsādayo na maggo, vīthippaṭipannaṃ udayabbayañāṇaṃ maggoti evaṃ maggāmagge ñāṇaṃ. Paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhīti rathavinīte vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā kathitā, idha taruṇavipassanā. Ñāṇadassanavisuddhīti rathavinīte maggo kathito, idha vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā. Etā pana sattapi visuddhiyo vitthārena visuddhimagge kathitā. Paññāti arahattaphalapaññā. Vimuttipi arahattaphalavimuttiyeva.

(Cha) dhātunānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati phassanānattanti cakkhādidhātunānattaṃ paṭicca cakkhusamphassādinānattaṃ uppajjatīti attho. Phassanānattaṃ paṭiccāti cakkhusamphassādinānattaṃ paṭicca . Vedanānānattanti cakkhusamphassajādivedanānānattaṃ. Saññānānattaṃ paṭiccāti kāmasaññādinānattaṃ paṭicca. Saṅkappanānattanti kāmasaṅkappādinānattaṃ. Saṅkappanānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandanānattanti saṅkappanānattatāya rūpe chando sadde chandoti evaṃ chandanānattaṃ uppajjati. Pariḷāhanānattanti chandanānattatāya rūpapariḷāho saddapariḷāhoti evaṃ pariḷāhanānattaṃ uppajjati. Pariyesanānānattanti pariḷāhanānattatāya rūpapariyesanādinānattaṃ uppajjati. Lābhanānattanti pariyesanānānattatāya rūpapaṭilābhādinānattaṃ uppajjati.

dhātunānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati phassanānatta Phassanānattaṃ paṭiccā Vedanānānatta Saññānānattaṃ paṭiccā Saṅkappanānatta Saṅkappanānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandanānatta Pariḷāhanānatta Pariyesanānānatta Lābhanānatta

(Ja) saññāsu maraṇasaññāti maraṇānupassanāñāṇe saññā. Āhārepaṭikūlasaññāti āhāraṃ pariggaṇhantassa uppannasaññā. Sabbalokeanabhiratisaññāti sabbasmiṃ vaṭṭe ukkaṇṭhantassa uppannasaññā. Sesā heṭṭhā kathitā eva. Idha bahukārapade maggo kathito. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva.

maraṇasaññā Āhārepaṭikūlasaññā Sabbalokeanabhiratisaññā

Dasadhammavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
359. (kha) *sīlavisuddhi* means morality purification: the fourfold morality that is able to bring about purification.

*pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅga* means the principal factor of purity.

*cittavisuddhi* means mind purification: the eight accomplished attainments that are the foundation for insight.

*diṭṭhivisuddhi* means view purification: seeing name and form with their conditions.

*kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi* means the purification of overcoming doubt: knowledge of conditionality.

Indeed, seeing that phenomena occur only through conditions in the three times, one overcomes doubt.

*maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi* means the purification of knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path: lights and so on are not the path; the knowledge of arising and passing away that has entered the path is the path; thus, knowledge of what is the path and what is not.

*paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi* means the purification of knowledge and vision of the way of practice: in the Relay Chariots discourse, the insight leading to abandonment is spoken of; here, it is initial insight.

*ñāṇadassanavisuddhi* means the purification of knowledge and vision: in the Relay Chariots discourse, the path is spoken of; here, it is the insight leading to abandonment.

But all seven of these purifications are spoken of in detail in the *Path of Purification* (*Visuddhimagga*).

*paññā* means wisdom: the wisdom of the fruit of *arahatship*.

*vimutti* also means liberation: just the liberation of the fruit of *arahatship*.

(cha) *dhātunānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati phassanānatta* means, dependent on the diversity of elements, diverse contact arises; the meaning is that dependent on the diversity of elements, such as the eye element, diverse contact, such as eye-contact, arises.

*phassanānattaṃ paṭicca* means, dependent on diverse contact, such as eye-contact.

*vedanānānatta* means diverse feeling, such as diverse feeling born of eye-contact.

*saññānānattaṃ paṭicca* means, dependent on the diversity of perceptions, such as perception of sensual pleasure.

*saṅkappanānatta* means diverse thought, such as diverse thought of sensual pleasure.

*saṅkappanānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandanānatta* means, dependent on diverse thought, diverse desire arises; due to the diversity of thought, desire for forms, desire for sounds, thus diverse desire arises.

*pariḷāhanānatta* means diverse burning: due to the diversity of desire, burning for forms, burning for sounds, thus diverse burning arises.

*pariyesanānānatta* means diverse seeking: due to diverse burning, diverse seeking for forms and so on arises.

*lābhanānatta* means diverse obtaining: due to diverse seeking, diverse obtaining of forms and so on arises.

*dhātunānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati phassanānatta* *phassanānattaṃ paṭicca* *vedanānānatta* *saññānānattaṃ paṭicca* *saṅkappanānatta* *saṅkappanānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandanānatta* *pariḷāhanānatta* *pariyesanānānatta* *lābhanānatta*

(ja) Among perceptions, *maraṇasaññā* means the perception in the knowledge of contemplating death.

*āhārepaṭikūlasaññā* means the perception that arises for one who is taking food.

*sabbalokeanabhiratisaññā* means the perception that arises for one who is disgusted with all of existence.

360. ‘‘Dasa dhammā bahukārā…pe… dasa dhammā sacchikātabbā.

(Ka) ‘‘katame dasa dhammā bahukārā? Dasa nāthakaraṇādhammā – idhāvuso, bhikkhu sīlavā hoti, pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharati ācāragocarasampanno, aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesu, yaṃpāvuso, bhikkhu sīlavā hoti…pe… sikkhati sikkhāpadesu. Ayampi dhammo nāthakaraṇo.

bahukārā?

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu bahussuto …pe… diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhā, yaṃpāvuso, bhikkhu bahussuto…pe… ayampi dhammo nāthakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu kalyāṇamitto hoti kalyāṇasahāyo kalyāṇasampavaṅko. Yaṃpāvuso, bhikkhu…pe… kalyāṇasampavaṅko. Ayampi dhammo nāthakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu suvaco hoti sovacassakaraṇehi dhammehi samannāgato, khamo padakkhiṇaggāhī anusāsaniṃ. Yaṃpāvuso, bhikkhu…pe… anusāsaniṃ. Ayampi dhammo nāthakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu yāni tāni sabrahmacārīnaṃ uccāvacāni kiṃkaraṇīyāni tattha dakkho hoti analaso tatrupāyāya vīmaṃsāya samannāgato, alaṃ kātuṃ, alaṃ saṃvidhātuṃ. Yaṃpāvuso, bhikkhu…pe… alaṃ saṃvidhātuṃ. Ayampi dhammo nāthakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu dhammakāmo hoti piyasamudāhāro abhidhamme abhivinaye uḷārapāmojjo. Yaṃpāvuso, bhikkhu…pe… uḷārapāmojjo. Ayampi dhammo nāthakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu santuṭṭho hoti itarītarehi cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārehi. Yaṃpāvuso, bhikkhu …pe… ayampi dhammo nāthakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu āraddhavīriyo viharati…pe… kusalesu dhammesu. Yaṃpāvuso, bhikkhu…pe… ayampi dhammo nāthakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu satimā hoti, paramena satinepakkena samannāgato, cirakatampi cirabhāsitampi saritā anussaritā. Yaṃpāvuso, bhikkhu…pe… ayampi dhammo nāthakaraṇo.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu paññavā hoti udayatthagāminiyā paññāya samannāgato, ariyāya nibbedhikāya sammā dukkhakkhayagāminiyā. Yaṃpāvuso, bhikkhu…pe… ayampi dhammo nāthakaraṇo. Ime dasa dhammā bahukārā.

(Kha) ‘‘katame dasa dhammā bhāvetabbā? Dasa kasiṇāyatanāni – pathavīkasiṇameko sañjānāti uddhaṃ adho tiriyaṃ advayaṃ appamāṇaṃ. Āpokasiṇameko sañjānāti…pe… tejokasiṇameko sañjānāti… vāyokasiṇameko sañjānāti… nīlakasiṇameko sañjānāti… pītakasiṇameko sañjānāti… lohitakasiṇameko sañjānāti… odātakasiṇameko sañjānāti… ākāsakasiṇameko sañjānāti… viññāṇakasiṇameko sañjānāti uddhaṃ adho tiriyaṃ advayaṃ appamāṇaṃ . Ime dasa dhammā bhāvetabbā.

bhāvetabbā?

(Ga) ‘‘katame dasa dhammā pariññeyyā? Dasāyatanāni – cakkhāyatanaṃ, rūpāyatanaṃ, sotāyatanaṃ, saddāyatanaṃ, ghānāyatanaṃ, gandhāyatanaṃ, jivhāyatanaṃ, rasāyatanaṃ, kāyāyatanaṃ, phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ. Ime dasa dhammā pariññeyyā.

pariññeyyā?

(Gha) ‘‘katame dasa dhammā pahātabbā? Dasa micchattā – micchādiṭṭhi, micchāsaṅkappo, micchāvācā, micchākammanto, micchāājīvo, micchāvāyāmo, micchāsati, micchāsamādhi, micchāñāṇaṃ, micchāvimutti. Ime dasa dhammā pahātabbā.

pahātabbā?

(Ṅa) ‘‘katame dasa dhammā hānabhāgiyā? Dasa akusalakammapathā – pāṇātipāto, adinnādānaṃ, kāmesumicchācāro, musāvādo, pisuṇā vācā, pharusā vācā, samphappalāpo, abhijjhā, byāpādo, micchādiṭṭhi. Ime dasa dhammā hānabhāgiyā.

hānabhāgiyā?

(Ca) ‘‘katame dasa dhammā visesabhāgiyā? Dasa kusalakammapathā – pāṇātipātā veramaṇī, adinnādānā veramaṇī, kāmesumicchācārā veramaṇī, musāvādā veramaṇī, pisuṇāya vācāya veramaṇī, pharusāya vācāya veramaṇī, samphappalāpā veramaṇī, anabhijjhā, abyāpādo, sammādiṭṭhi. Ime dasa dhammā visesabhāgiyā.

visesabhāgiyā?

(Cha) ‘‘katame dasa dhammā duppaṭivijjhā? Dasa ariyavāsā – idhāvuso , bhikkhu pañcaṅgavippahīno hoti, chaḷaṅgasamannāgato, ekārakkho, caturāpasseno, paṇunnapaccekasacco, samavayasaṭṭhesano, anāvilasaṅkappo, passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro, suvimuttacitto, suvimuttapañño.

duppaṭivijjhā?

‘‘Kathañcāvuso , bhikkhu pañcaṅgavippahīno hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno kāmacchando pahīno hoti, byāpādo pahīno hoti, thinamiddhaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, vicikicchā pahīnā hoti. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu pañcaṅgavippahīno hoti.

pañcaṅgavippahīno

‘‘Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu chaḷaṅgasamannāgato hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā neva sumano hoti na dummano, upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno. Sotena saddaṃ sutvā…pe… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya neva sumano hoti na dummano, upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu chaḷaṅgasamannāgato hoti.

‘‘Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu ekārakkho hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu satārakkhena cetasā samannāgato hoti. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu ekārakkho hoti.

‘‘Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu caturāpasseno hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevati, saṅkhāyekaṃ adhivāseti, saṅkhāyekaṃ parivajjeti, saṅkhāyekaṃ vinodeti. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu caturāpasseno hoti.

‘‘Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu paṇunnapaccekasacco hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno yāni tāni puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ puthupaccekasaccāni, sabbāni tāni nunnāni honti paṇunnāni cattāni vantāni muttāni pahīnāni paṭinissaṭṭhāni. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu paṇunnapaccekasacco hoti.

‘‘Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu samavayasaṭṭhesano hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno kāmesanā pahīnā hoti, bhavesanā pahīnā hoti, brahmacariyesanā paṭippassaddhā. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu samavayasaṭṭhesano hoti.

‘‘Kathañcāvuso , bhikkhu anāvilasaṅkappā hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno kāmasaṅkappo pahīno hoti, byāpādasaṅkappo pahīno hoti, vihiṃsāsaṅkappo pahīno hoti. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu anāvilasaṅkappo hoti.

anāvilasaṅkappā

‘‘Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro hoti.

‘‘Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu suvimuttacitto hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno rāgā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ hoti, dosā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ hoti, mohā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu suvimuttacitto hoti.

‘‘Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu suvimuttapañño hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu ‘rāgo me pahīno ucchinnamūlo tālāvatthukato anabhāvaṃkato āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo’ti pajānāti. ‘Doso me pahīno…pe… āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo’ti pajānāti. ‘Moho me pahīno …pe… āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo’ti pajānāti. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu suvimuttapañño hoti. Ime dasa dhammā duppaṭivijjhā.

(Ja) ‘‘katame dasa dhammā uppādetabbā? Dasa saññā – asubhasaññā, maraṇasaññā, āhārepaṭikūlasaññā, sabbalokeanabhiratisaññā, aniccasaññā, anicce dukkhasaññā, dukkhe anattasaññā, pahānasaññā, virāgasaññā, nirodhasaññā. Ime dasa dhammā uppādetabbā.

Sammāsaṅkappassa micchāsaṅkappo…pe… sammāvācassa micchāvācā… sammākammantassa micchākammanto… sammāājīvassa micchāājīvo… sammāvāyāmassa micchāvāyāmo… sammāsatissa micchāsati… sammāsamādhissa micchāsamādhi… sammāñāṇassa micchāñāṇaṃ nijjiṇṇaṃ hoti. Sammāvimuttissa micchāvimutti nijjiṇṇā hoti. Ye ca micchāvimuttipaccayā aneke pāpakā akusalā dhammā sambhavanti, te cassa nijjiṇṇā honti. Ime dasa dhammā abhiññeyyā.

abhiññeyyā?

Ime dasa dhammā sacchikātabbā.

360. “Ten *dhamma*s, friends, are very helpful… Ten *dhamma*s should be realized.” (a) “Which ten *dhamma*s are very helpful (*bahukārā*)? Ten *dhamma*s that create a protector (*nāthakaraṇa*)—Here, friends, a monk is virtuous (*sīlavā*), dwells restrained by the restraint of the *Pātimokkha*, possessing good conduct and proper domain, seeing danger in the slightest faults, undertaking and training himself in the training rules. And the fact that the monk is virtuous…trains himself in the training rules: this *dhamma* is one that creates a protector (*nāthakaraṇa*). “Furthermore (*puna ca paraṃ*), friends, the monk has heard much (*bahussuto*)…is well-penetrated in terms of his views. And the fact that he has heard much…this *dhamma* is one that creates a protector. “Furthermore, friends, the monk has admirable friends (*kalyāṇamitto*), admirable comrades, admirable companions. And the fact that he has admirable friends…admirable companions: this *dhamma* is one that creates a protector. “Furthermore, friends, the monk is easy to speak to (*suvaco*), endowed with qualities that make him easy to speak to, patient, respectful to instruction (*anusāsaniṃ*). And the fact that he is easy to speak to…respectful to instruction: this *dhamma* is one that creates a protector. “Furthermore, friends, the monk is adept at the various affairs involving his companions in the holy life (*sabrahmacārīnaṃ*), is vigorous, quick-witted in the techniques involved in them, is up to doing them or arranging to get them done. And the fact that he is adept at…doing them or arranging to get them done: this *dhamma* is one that creates a protector. “Furthermore, friends, the monk is one who desires the *dharma* (*dharmakāmo*), endearing in his conversation (*piyasamudāhāro*), greatly rejoicing in the higher *dharma* (*abhidhamma*) & higher *Vinaya* (*abhivinaye*). And the fact that the monk…greatly rejoicing: this *dhamma* is one that creates a protector. “Furthermore, friends, the monk is content (*santuṭṭho*) with any old robe cloth at all, any old alms food, any old lodging, any old medicinal requisites for curing sickness at all. And the fact that the monk…this *dhamma* is one that creates a protector. “Furthermore, friends, the monk keeps his persistence aroused (*āraddhavīriyo*)…with regard to skillful qualities (*kusalesu dhammesu*). And the fact that the monk…this *dhamma* is one that creates a protector. “Furthermore, friends, the monk is mindful (*satimā*), endowed with excellent proficiency in mindfulness (*satinepakkena*), remembering & recollecting what was done & said a long time ago. And the fact that the monk…this *dhamma* is one that creates a protector. “Furthermore, friends, the monk is discerning (*paññavā*), endowed with the discernment related to arising & passing away (*udayatthagāminiyā paññāya*)—noble (*ariyāya*), penetrating (*nibbedhikāya*), leading to the right ending of stress (*sammā dukkhakkhayagāminiyā*). And the fact that the monk…this *dhamma* is one that creates a protector. These ten *dhamma*s are very helpful. (b) “Which ten *dhamma*s should be developed (*bhāvetabbā*)? Ten *kasiṇa*-bases: One perceives the earth-*kasiṇa* (*pathavīkasiṇa*) above, below, all around, non-dual, immeasurable (*appamāṇaṃ*). One perceives the water-*kasiṇa* (*āpokasiṇa*)… the fire-*kasiṇa* (*tejokasiṇa*)… the wind-*kasiṇa* (*vāyokasiṇa*)… the blue-*kasiṇa* (*nīlakasiṇa*)… the yellow-*kasiṇa* (*pītakasiṇa*)… the red-*kasiṇa* (*lohitakasiṇa*)… the white-*kasiṇa* (*odātakasiṇa*)… the space-*kasiṇa* (*ākāsakasiṇa*)… the consciousness-*kasiṇa* (*viññāṇakasiṇa*) above, below, all around, non-dual, immeasurable. These ten *dhamma*s should be developed. What ten *dhamma* should be developed? (ga) What ten *dhamma* should be fully understood (*pariññeyyā*)? They are the ten bases (*dasāyatanāni*): the eye-base (*cakkhāyatanaṃ*), the form-base (*rūpāyatanaṃ*), the ear-base (*sotāyatanaṃ*), the sound-base (*saddāyatanaṃ*), the nose-base (*ghānāyatanaṃ*), the odor-base (*gandhāyatanaṃ*), the tongue-base (*jivhāyatanaṃ*), the taste-base (*rasāyatanaṃ*), the body-base (*kāyāyatanaṃ*), and the tangible-base (*phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ*). These ten *dhamma* should be fully understood. (gha) What ten *dhamma* should be abandoned (*pahātabbā*)? They are the ten wrongnesses (*dasa micchattā*): wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*), wrong intention (*micchāsaṅkappo*), wrong speech (*micchāvācā*), wrong action (*micchākammanto*), wrong livelihood (*micchāājīvo*), wrong effort (*micchāvāyāmo*), wrong mindfulness (*micchāsati*), wrong concentration (*micchāsamādhi*), wrong knowledge (*micchāñāṇaṃ*), and wrong liberation (*micchāvimutti*). These ten *dhamma* should be abandoned. (ṅa) What ten *dhamma* are on the side of decline (*hānabhāgiyā*)? They are the ten unskillful courses of action (*dasa akusalakammapathā*): killing (*pāṇātipāto*), taking what is not given (*adinnādānaṃ*), sexual misconduct (*kāmesumicchācāro*), lying (*musāvādo*), divisive speech (*pisuṇā vācā*), harsh speech (*pharusā vācā*), idle chatter (*samphappalāpo*), covetousness (*abhijjhā*), ill will (*byāpādo*), and wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*). These ten *dhamma* are on the side of decline. (ca) What ten *dhamma* are on the side of distinction (*visesabhāgiyā*)? They are the ten skillful courses of action (*dasa kusalakammapathā*): abstaining from killing (*pāṇātipātā veramaṇī*), abstaining from taking what is not given (*adinnādānā veramaṇī*), abstaining from sexual misconduct (*kāmesumicchācārā veramaṇī*), abstaining from lying (*musāvādā veramaṇī*), abstaining from divisive speech (*pisuṇāya vācāya veramaṇī*), abstaining from harsh speech (*pharusāya vācāya veramaṇī*), abstaining from idle chatter (*samphappalāpā veramaṇī*), non-covetousness (*anabhijjhā*), non-ill will (*abyāpādo*), and right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*). These ten *dhamma* are on the side of distinction. (cha) What ten *dhamma* are difficult to penetrate (*duppaṭivijjhā*)? They are the ten noble abodes (*dasa ariyavāsā*): Here, a *bhikkhu* has abandoned five factors (*pañcaṅgavippahīno*), is endowed with six (*chaḷaṅgasamannāgato*), guards one (*ekārakkho*), is supported in four (*caturāpasseno*), has shaken off idiosyncratic truths (*paṇunnapaccekasacco*), has thoroughly given up searching (*samavayasaṭṭhesano*), is undisturbed in his resolves (*anāvilasaṅkappo*), is calmed in his bodily fabrication (*passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro*), is well-released in mind (*suvimuttacitto*), and is well-released in discernment (*suvimuttapañño*). How, friend, is a *bhikkhu* one who has abandoned five factors (*pañcaṅgavippahīno*)? Here, friend, a *bhikkhu* has abandoned sensual desire (*kāmacchando*), has abandoned ill will (*byāpādo*), has abandoned sloth and torpor (*thinamiddhaṃ*), has abandoned restlessness and anxiety (*uddhaccakukkuccaṃ*), and has abandoned uncertainty (*vicikicchā*). This is how a *bhikkhu* has abandoned five factors. How, friend, is a *bhikkhu* one who is endowed with six? Here, friend, having seen a form with the eye, a *bhikkhu* is neither joyful nor saddened, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. Having heard a sound with the ear… Having smelled an odor with the nose… Having tasted a flavor with the tongue… Having felt a tangible object with the body… Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is neither joyful nor saddened, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. This is how a *bhikkhu* is endowed with six. How, friend, is a *bhikkhu* one who guards one? Here, friend, a *bhikkhu* is endowed with a mind guarded by mindfulness. This is how a *bhikkhu* guards one. How, friend, is a *bhikkhu* one who is supported in four? Here, friend, a *bhikkhu*, considering, makes use of one thing; considering, he endures one thing; considering, he avoids one thing; considering, he gets rid of one thing. This is how a *bhikkhu* is supported in four. How, friend, is a *bhikkhu* one who has shaken off idiosyncratic truths (*paṇunnapaccekasacco*)? Here, friend, whatever idiosyncratic truths are held by various ascetics and *brāhmaṇas*, all of them are rejected, dispelled, given up, relinquished, released, abandoned, and forsaken. This is how a *bhikkhu* has shaken off idiosyncratic truths. How, friend, is a *bhikkhu* one who has thoroughly given up searching (*samavayasaṭṭhesano*)? Here, friend, a *bhikkhu* has abandoned the search for sensual pleasures (*kāmesanā*), has abandoned the search for existence (*bhavesanā*), and his search for the spiritual life (*brahmacariyesanā*) is calmed. This is how a *bhikkhu* has thoroughly given up searching. How, friend, is a *bhikkhu* one who is undisturbed in his resolves (*anāvilasaṅkappā*)? Here, friend, a *bhikkhu* has abandoned his resolve for sensuality (*kāmasaṅkappo*), has abandoned his resolve for ill will (*byāpādasaṅkappo*), and has abandoned his resolve for harmfulness (*vihiṃsāsaṅkappo*). This is how a *bhikkhu* is undisturbed in his resolves. "0259"/> **anāvilasaṅkappā** "And how, friends, is a *bhikṣu* calmed in his bodily fabrication? Here, friends, a *bhikṣu*, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and just from the prior disappearance of joy and sadness, achieves and abides in the fourth *jhāna*, which is neither painful nor pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This is how, friends, a *bhikṣu* is calmed in his bodily fabrication. "And how, friends, is a *bhikṣu* well released in mind? Here, friends, a *bhikṣu's* mind is released from *rāga* (greed), his mind is released from *dosa* (aversion), his mind is released from *moha* (delusion). This is how, friends, a *bhikṣu* is well released in mind. "And how, friends, is a *bhikṣu* well-released in discernment? Here, friends, a *bhikṣu* understands, ‘*Rāga* (greed) is abandoned in me, its root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of development, not destined for future arising.’ ‘*Dosa* (aversion) is abandoned in me…pe… not destined for future arising.’ ‘*Moha* (delusion) is abandoned in me …pe… not destined for future arising.’ This is how, friends, a *bhikṣu* is well-released in discernment. These ten *dharmas* are hard to penetrate. (ja) "Which ten *dharmas* should be made to arise? The ten perceptions (*saññā*) – the foulness perception (*asubhasaññā*), the death perception (*maraṇasaññā*), the loathsomeness-of-food perception (*āhārepaṭikūlasaññā*), the non-delight-in-the-entire-world perception (*sabbalokeanabhiratisaññā*), the impermanence perception (*aniccasaññā*), the suffering-in-impermanence perception (*anicce dukkhasaññā*), the not-self-in-suffering perception (*dukkhe anattasaññā*), the abandoning perception (*pahānasaññā*), the dispassion perception (*virāgasaññā*), the cessation perception (*nirodhasaññā*). These ten *dharmas* should be made to arise. **uppādetabbā?** (jha) "Which ten *dharmas* should be directly known (*abhiññeyyā*)? The ten grounds for decay (*nijjaravatthūni*) – In one of right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*), wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*) is abolished. And the many evil unwholesome *dharmas* that originate with wrong view as condition are also abolished. In one of right resolve (*sammāsaṅkappassa*), wrong resolve (*micchāsaṅkappo*)…pe… In one of right speech (*sammāvācassa*), wrong speech (*micchāvācā*)… In one of right action (*sammākammantassa*), wrong action (*micchākammanto*)… In one of right livelihood (*sammāājīvassa*), wrong livelihood (*micchāājīvo*)… In one of right effort (*sammāvāyāmassa*), wrong effort (*micchāvāyāmo*)… In one of right mindfulness (*sammāsatissa*), wrong mindfulness (*micchāsati*)… In one of right concentration (*sammāsamādhissa*), wrong concentration (*micchāsamādhi*)… In one of right knowledge (*sammāñāṇassa*), wrong knowledge (*micchāñāṇaṃ*) is abolished. In one of right deliverance (*sammāvimuttissa*) wrong deliverance (*micchāvimutti*) is abolished. And the many evil unwholesome *dharmas* that originate with wrong deliverance as condition are also abolished. These ten *dharmas* should be directly known (*abhiññeyyā*). **abhiññeyyā?** (ña) "Which ten *dharmas* should be realized (*sacchikātabbā*)? The ten qualities of one beyond training (*asekkhā dhammā*) – the right view of one beyond training (*asekkhā sammādiṭṭhi*), the right resolve of one beyond training (*asekkho sammāsaṅkappo*), the right speech of one beyond training (*asekkhā sammāvācā*), the right action of one beyond training (*asekkho sammākammanto*), the right livelihood of one beyond training (*asekkho sammāājīvo*), the right effort of one beyond training (*asekkho sammāvāyāmo*), the right mindfulness of one beyond training (*asekkhā sammāsati*), the right concentration of one beyond training (*asekkho sammāsamādhi*), the right knowledge of one beyond training (*asekkhaṃ sammāñāṇaṃ*), the right release of one beyond training (*asekkhā sammāvimutti*). These ten *dharmas* should be realized (*sacchikātabbā*). **sacchikātabbā?** "Thus, these one hundred *dharmas* are actual, genuine, true, not false, not otherwise, [and] rightly awakened by the *Tathāgata*. That is what Venerable Sāriputta said. Elated, those *bhikkhus* delighted in Venerable Sāriputta’s statement. The Dasuttara Sutta, the eleventh [sutta], is finished. The Pāthika Vagga is finished. 360. (Jha) nijjaravatthūnīti nijjarakāraṇāni. Micchādiṭṭhi nijjiṇṇā hotīti ayaṃ heṭṭhā vipassanāyapi nijjiṇṇā eva pahīnā. Kasmā puna gahitāti asamucchinnattā. Vipassanāya hi kiñcāpi jiṇṇā, na pana samucchinnā, maggo pana uppajjitvā taṃ samucchindati, na puna vuṭṭhātuṃ deti. Tasmā puna gahitā. Evaṃ sabbapadesu nayo netabbo.

Ettha ca sammādiṭṭhipaccayā catusaṭṭhi dhammā bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchanti. Katame catusaṭṭhi? Sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe adhimokkhaṭṭhena saddhindriyaṃ paripūreti, paggahaṭṭhena vīriyindriyaṃ paripūreti, anussaraṇaṭṭhena satindriyaṃ paripūreti, avikkhepaṭṭhena samādhindriyaṃ paripūreti, dassanaṭṭhena paññindriyaṃ paripūreti, vijānanaṭṭhena manindriyaṃ, abhinandanaṭṭhena somanassindriyaṃ, pavattasantatiadhipateyyaṭṭhena jīvitindriyaṃ paripūreti…pe… arahattaphalakkhaṇe adhimokkhaṭṭhena saddhindriyaṃ, pavattasantatiadhipateyyaṭṭhena jīvitindriyaṃ paripūretīti evaṃ catūsu maggesu catūsu phalesu aṭṭha aṭṭha hutvā catusaṭṭhi dhammā pāripūriṃ gacchanti. Idha abhiññeyyapade maggo kathito. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva.

Idha ṭhatvā pañhā samodhānetabbā. Dasake sataṃ pañhā kathitā. Ekake ca navake ca sataṃ , duke ca aṭṭhake ca sataṃ, tike ca sattake ca sataṃ, catukke ca chakke ca sataṃ, pañcake paññāsāti aḍḍhachaṭṭhāni pañhasatāni kathitāni honti.
